By aligning model attention with structured CRS, the proposed framework offers a promising paradigm for building more interpretable and reliable AI diagnostic systems in complex clinical settings.

papers.title: Learning local discrete features in explainable-by-design convolutional neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we design a convolutional neural network that is both high-performance and explainable by using a lateral inhibition mechanism to learn local discrete features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ExplaiNet, an explainable-by-design CNN that uses a lateral inhibition layer to learn local discrete feature vectors, enabling high accuracy and providing explanations via a probabilistic graph and motif discovery.
papers.conclusion: The ExplaiNet framework breaks the performance-explainability trade-off by introducing an explainable-by-design CNN that retains or surpasses baseline performance while providing causal explanations based on discrete feature motifs.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed ExplaiNet model achieves comparable or better performance than baseline ResNet and DenseNet architectures on tiny image datasets while providing explanations.
The lateral inhibition layer amplifies gradients of winner neurons, leading to ordered activations and the formation of local discrete feature vectors.
Feature motif discovery using the EXTREME algorithm reduces the vocabulary of local discrete features, providing concise explanations.
The explainer probabilistic graph can infer causal relationships between motifs of adjacent levels and attribute the model's output to global motifs.
Experiments show that the explainer can sometimes correctly classify samples that the neural predictor misclassifies, suggesting potential for ensemble use or adversarial sample detection.
papers.limitation:
Further research on regularization aspects of the lateral inhibition function is required to investigate the magnitude of weights and activations during training.
Experiments are limited to tiny image datasets due to computational resources; the method has not been tested on medium-resolution images or high numbers of classes.
future_direction: Investigate the proper amount of weight decay and restriction of input values for positively monotonic gradient amplification in the lateral inhibition function.
Scale up the method to train models on medium-resolution images, high number of classes, and with millions of parameters.
Adjust the EXTREME algorithm to support custom numeric system bases, making the conversion to the quaternary system optional.
papers.abstract: Our proposed framework attempts to break the trade-off between performance and explainability by introducing an explainable-by-design convolutional neural network (CNN) based on the lateral inhibition mechanism. The ExplaiNet model consists of the predictor, that is a high-accuracy CNN with residual or dense skip connections, and the explainer probabilistic graph that expresses the spatial interactions of the network neurons. The value on each graph node is a local discrete feature (LDF) vector, a patch descriptor that represents the indices of antagonistic neurons ordered by the strength of their activations, which are learned with gradient descent. Using LDFs as sequences we can increase the conciseness of explanations by repurposing EXTREME, an EM-based sequence motif discovery method that is typically used in molecular biology. Having a discrete feature motif matrix for each one of intermediate image representations, instead of a continuous activation tensor, allows us to leverage the inherent explainability of Bayesian networks. By collecting observations and directly calculating probabilities, we can explain causal relationships between motifs of adjacent levels and attribute the model's output to global motifs. Moreover, experiments on various tiny image benchmark datasets confirm that our predictor ensures the same level of performance as the baseline architecture for a given count of parameters and/or layers. Our novel method shows promise to exceed this performance while providing an additional stream of explanations. In the solved MNIST classification task, it reaches a comparable to the state-of-the-art performance for single models, using standard training setup and 0.75 million parameters.

papers.title: Multimodal Task Vectors Enable Many-Shot Multimodal In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How to enable Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) to perform many-shot in-context learning without being limited by context length, by compressing examples into implicit representations (task vectors) in the model's attention heads?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Multimodal Task Vectors (MTV), compact implicit representations of in-context examples stored in attention heads, enabling many-shot multimodal in-context learning without fine-tuning and overcoming context length limitations.
papers.conclusion: MTV enables many-shot multimodal in-context learning, scales with examples, and generalizes to similar tasks without requiring fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
MTV outperforms zero-shot and few-shot ICL on various vision-language tasks.
MTV performance scales with the number of compressed examples (shots and iterations).
MTV can be used alongside explicit few-shot examples, freeing up context length.
MTV attention heads extracted on one task can generalize to similar out-of-domain tasks.
papers.limitation:
MTV requires interleaved LMMs and may not work as well on non-interleaved models.
Computing mean activations requires multiple forward passes, which can be computationally expensive.
papers.abstract: The recent success of interleaved Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) in few-shot learning suggests that in-context learning (ICL) with many examples can be promising for learning new tasks. However, this many-shot multimodal ICL setting has one crucial problem: it is fundamentally limited by the model's context length set at pretraining. The problem is especially prominent in the multimodal domain, which processes both text and images, requiring additional tokens. This motivates the need for a multimodal method to compress many shots into fewer tokens without finetuning. In this work, we enable LMMs to perform multimodal, many-shot in-context learning by leveraging Multimodal Task Vectors (MTV) -- compact implicit representations of in-context examples compressed in the model's attention heads. Specifically, we first demonstrate the existence of such MTV in LMMs and then leverage these extracted MTV to enable many-shot in-context learning for various vision-and-language tasks. Our experiments suggest that MTV can scale in performance with the number of compressed shots and generalize to similar out-of-domain tasks without additional context length for inference. Code: https://github.com/Brandon3964/MultiModal-Task-Vector

papers.title: Counterfactual reasoning: an analysis of in-context emergence
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether language models can perform in-context counterfactual reasoning, i.e., predicting consequences of hypothetical scenarios by inferring unobserved latent concepts and copying contextual noise from factual observations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that language models are capable of in-context counterfactual reasoning, and through analysis of Transformers, finds that self-attention, model depth, and pre-training data diversity drive performance, with mechanistic evidence that the latent concept is linearly represented in the residual stream and that designated noise abduction heads emerge.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can perform counterfactual reasoning by leveraging self-attention and depth, and this ability extends to sequential data, suggesting potential for counterfactual story generation.
papers.key_findings:
Language models can perform in-context counterfactual reasoning on synthetic linear regression tasks.
Self-attention is crucial for counterfactual reasoning; MLP-only models fail.
Model depth improves counterfactual reasoning performance.
Pre-training data diversity improves performance and out-of-distribution generalization.
The latent parameter is linearly encoded in the residual stream, and designated noise abduction heads emerge in attention layers.
papers.limitation: The synthetic setup may not fully capture the complexity of natural language counterfactual reasoning.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to natural language tasks and more complex functions.
Further exploration of the role of attention heads in counterfactual reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large-scale neural language models exhibit remarkable performance in in-context learning: the ability to learn and reason about the input context on the fly. This work studies in-context counterfactual reasoning in language models, that is, the ability to predict consequences of a hypothetical scenario. We focus on a well-defined, synthetic linear regression task that requires noise abduction. Accurate prediction is based on (1) inferring an unobserved latent concept and (2) copying contextual noise from factual observations. We show that language models are capable of counterfactual reasoning. Further, we enhance existing identifiability results and reduce counterfactual reasoning for a broad class of functions to a transformation on in-context observations. In Transformers, we find that self-attention, model depth and pre-training data diversity drive performance. Moreover, we provide mechanistic evidence that the latent concept is linearly represented in the residual stream and we introduce designated \textit{noise abduction heads} central to performing counterfactual reasoning. Lastly, our findings extend to counterfactual reasoning under SDE dynamics and reflect that Transformers can perform noise abduction on sequential data, providing preliminary evidence on the potential for counterfactual story generation. Our code is available under https://github.com/mrtzmllr/iccr.

papers.title: From Sequence to Structure: Uncovering Substructure Reasoning in Transformers
papers.research_question: How can a decoder-only Transformer architecture understand underlying graph structures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Induced Substructure Filtration (ISF) perspective to explain how transformers extract substructures from graph data, and shows that this perspective applies to LLMs and can be extended to attributed graphs.
papers.conclusion: The ISF process explains how transformers understand graph structures and can be extended to complex graph reasoning, offering a new perspective for graph foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers perform a layer-wise node aggregation process (ISF) to detect substructures.
The number of transformer layers needed correlates with the size of the substructure.
Transformers can extract multiple substructures simultaneously.
Both adjacency list and edge list representations can be used, but adjacency list is more efficient.
Transformers abstract substructures into a sequence of tokens in the question prompt.
papers.limitation: The work focuses primarily on the fundamentals of substructure extraction, leaving other substructure-related tasks and more detailed theoretical analysis for future research.
future_direction: Extend to other substructure-related tasks.
Develop a more comprehensive theoretical understanding.
papers.abstract: Recent studies suggest that large language models (LLMs) possess the capability to solve graph reasoning tasks. Notably, even when graph structures are embedded within textual descriptions, LLMs can still effectively answer related questions. This raises a fundamental question: How can a decoder-only Transformer architecture understand underlying graph structures? To address this, we start with the substructure extraction task, interpreting the inner mechanisms inside the transformers and analyzing the impact of the input queries. Specifically, through both empirical results and theoretical analysis, we present Induced Substructure Filtration (ISF), a perspective that captures the substructure identification in the multi-layer transformers. We further validate the ISF process in LLMs, revealing consistent internal dynamics across layers. Building on these insights, we explore the broader capabilities of Transformers in handling diverse graph types. Specifically, we introduce the concept of thinking in substructures to efficiently extract complex composite patterns, and demonstrate that decoder-only Transformers can successfully extract substructures from attributed graphs, such as molecular graphs. Together, our findings offer a new insight on how sequence-based Transformers perform the substructure extraction task over graph data.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning is Subgraph Search: A New Lens on Learning Dynamics
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how fine-tuning works from a mechanistic interpretability perspective, viewing fine-tuning as a search for and optimization of a subgraph within the model's computational graph.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit-tuning, a fine-tuning method that dynamically localizes and optimizes subgraphs (circuits) within a model's computational graph, enabling analysis of learning dynamics and balancing task performance with general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Circuit-tuning provides a new method for studying learning dynamics from a mechanistic interpretability perspective, offering insights into how fine-tuning works and enabling more precise fine-tuning that balances task performance and general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit-tuning provides better training stability and preserves language modeling ability better than full fine-tuning.
The functionality of specific attention heads (Subject Attribute Heads) can reverse during fine-tuning to adapt to new tasks.
Some attention heads (Subject Identification Heads) preserve their functions and are shared before and after fine-tuning.
Nodes within a circuit cooperate through division of labor and indirect interactions to complete tasks.
Edges in the computational graph exhibit strengthening and weakening akin to Hebbian learning during fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: The study of mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer a model to explain its behaviors. While recent studies have focused on the static mechanism of a certain behavior, the learning dynamics inside a model remain to be explored. In this work, we develop a fine-tuning method for analyzing the mechanism behind learning. Inspired by the concept of intrinsic dimension, we view a model as a computational graph with redundancy for a specific task, and treat the fine-tuning process as a search for and optimization of a subgraph within this graph. Based on this hypothesis, we propose circuit-tuning, an algorithm that iteratively builds the subgraph for a specific task and updates the relevant parameters in a heuristic way. We first validate our hypothesis through a carefully designed experiment and provide a detailed analysis of the learning dynamics during fine-tuning. Subsequently, we conduct experiments on more complex tasks, demonstrating that circuit-tuning could strike a balance between the performance on the target task and the general capabilities. Our work offers a new analytical method for the dynamics of fine-tuning, provides new findings on the mechanisms behind the training process, and inspires the design of superior algorithms for the training of neural networks.

papers.title: Site-Net: Using global self-attention and real-space supercells to capture long-range interactions in crystal structures
papers.research_question: How can global self-attention and real-space supercells be used to capture long-range interactions in crystal structures for property prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Site-Net is a transformer architecture that uses global self-attention and real-space supercells to capture long-range interactions in crystal structures, achieving state-of-the-art performance on band gap prediction.
papers.conclusion: Site-Net effectively captures long-range interactions in crystal structures and achieves competitive performance on band gap prediction, with potential for improvement via more extensive hyperparameter tuning and the use of larger supercells.
papers.key_findings:
Site-Net achieves a mean absolute error of 0.251 eV on the Matbench band gap regression task, demonstrating competitive performance.
Attention heads in Site-Net become specialized to deal with primarily short- or long-range interactions.
Enforcing a distance cutoff limit of 5 Å on the attention decreases model performance, confirming that longer-range interactions meaningfully contribute to predictions.
Site-Net learns from interactions beyond the nearest neighbor atomic sites.
The model performance is consistent across band gap values.
papers.limitation:
The model is computationally intensive and has a quadratic dependence on the number of atoms in the crystal in terms of VRAM and computational load.
The hyperparameter search was only preliminary, and the hyperparameters used are likely far from optimal.
The cutoff limit of 100 atoms excludes about 3% of crystal structures in the dataset during training due to memory constraints.
Model performance may be limited by the size of the supercell and could improve with larger supercells.
future_direction: More extensive hyperparameter tuning.
Using larger supercells to improve performance.
Applying the method to disordered crystal structures.
papers.abstract: Site-Net is a transformer architecture that models the periodic crystal structures of inorganic materials as a labelled point set of atoms and relies entirely on global self-attention and geometric information to guide learning. Site-Net processes standard crystallographic information files to generate a large real-space supercell, and the importance of interactions between all atomic sites is flexibly learned by the model for the prediction task presented. The attention mechanism is probed to reveal Site-Net can learn long-range interactions in crystal structures, and that specific attention heads become specialized to deal with primarily short- or long-range interactions. We perform a preliminary hyperparameter search and train Site-Net using a single graphics processing unit (GPU), and show Site-Net achieves state-of-the-art performance on a standard band gap regression task.

papers.title: Hierarchical Sparse Circuit Extraction from Billion-Parameter Language Models through Scalable Attribution Graph Decomposition
papers.research_question: How can sparse computational circuits be efficiently extracted from billion-parameter language models using hierarchical decomposition and attribution graphs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Hierarchical Attribution Graph Decomposition (HAGD), a framework that reduces circuit discovery complexity from exponential to polynomial, enabling extraction of interpretable circuits from billion-parameter models with high behavioral preservation.
papers.conclusion: HAGD enables circuit extraction from large models with preserved behavior, but limitations include incomplete attention modeling, reconstruction residuals, and interpretability challenges for large circuits.
papers.key_findings:
HAGD reduces circuit discovery complexity to O(n^2 log n) and extracts circuits from models up to 70B parameters.
Behavioral preservation ranges from 82% to 97% on algorithmic tasks and 74% to 88% on natural language benchmarks.
Cross-architecture transfer shows 52%-82% structural similarity, indicating shared computational patterns.
Circuit size grows sublinearly with model parameters, but natural language tasks yield larger, less modular circuits.
The method outperforms baselines like ACDC in scalability while maintaining comparable circuit quality.
papers.limitation:
Attention circuits are not modeled, leaving significant computational pathways unanalyzed.
Reconstruction dark matter of 15-20% unexplained variance means extracted circuits are incomplete.
Validation circularity arises from using ablation experiments that assume circuit completeness.
GNN meta-model requires ground-truth circuit labels that are expensive to obtain.
Large circuits with hundreds of nodes may exceed human interpretability limits.
future_direction: Integrate attention and MLP circuit analysis.
Characterize reconstruction residuals (dark matter).
Develop label-efficient training methods for GNN meta-model.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to reverse-engineer neural network computations into human-understandable algorithms, yet extracting sparse computational circuits from billion-parameter language models remains challenging due to exponential search complexity and pervasive polysemanticity. The proposed Hierarchical Attribution Graph Decomposition (HAGD) framework reduces circuit discovery complexity from O(2^n) exhaustive enumeration to O(n^2 log n) through multi-resolution abstraction hierarchies and differentiable circuit search. The methodology integrates cross-layer transcoders for monosemantic feature extraction, graph neural network meta-learning for topology prediction, and causal intervention protocols for validation. Empirical evaluation spans GPT-2 variants, Llama-7B through Llama-70B, and Pythia suite models across algorithmic tasks and natural language benchmarks. On modular arithmetic tasks, the framework achieves up to 91% behavioral preservation ($\pm$2.3\% across runs) while maintaining interpretable subgraph sizes. Cross-architecture transfer experiments suggest that discovered circuits exhibit moderate structural similarity (averaging 67%) across model families, indicating potential shared computational patterns. These results provide preliminary foundations for interpretability at larger model scales while identifying significant limitations in current attribution methodologies that require future advances.

papers.title: Exploring Cancer Genomics with Graph Convolutional Networks: A Comparative Explainability Study with Integrated Gradients and SHAP
papers.research_question: How do SHAP and Integrated Gradients compare in explaining the predictions of Graph Convolutional Networks applied to multiomics cancer data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a framework that integrates SHAP and Integrated Gradients to improve the interpretability of Graph Convolutional Networks for cancer gene identification from multiomics data.
papers.conclusion: SHAP is ideal for tasks requiring interpretability and consistency, while IG is better for faster, scalable analyses in explaining GCN predictions.
papers.key_findings:
SHAP provides more intuitive visualizations and consistent feature importance rankings for GCN predictions.
Integrated Gradients is computationally more efficient but has diffused attributions and variability for lower-impact genes.
The GCN model achieves 76% accuracy and 0.78 AUC-ROC in cancer gene identification.
SHAP and IG are complementary methods, with SHAP better for interpretability and IG for scalability.
papers.limitation:
SHAP is computationally intensive due to its game-theoretic approach.
IG shows variability in identifying lower-impact genes across runs.
future_direction: Improving scalability of GCNs for larger datasets.
Integrating explainability techniques for more robust feature attributions.
Exploring GCN applications in clinical settings for real-time predictions.
papers.abstract: In the rapidly advancing field of cancer genomics, identifying new cancer genes and understanding their molecular mechanisms are essential for advancing targeted therapies and improving patient outcomes. This study explores the capability of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) for integrating complex multiomics data to uncover intricate biological relationships. However, the inherent complexity of GCNs often limits their interpretability, posing challenges for practical applications in clinical settings. To enhance explainability, we systematically compare two state-of-the-art interpretability methods: Integrated Gradients (IG) and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). We quantify model performance through various metrics, achieving an accuracy of 76% and an Area Under the ROC curve is 0.78, indicating the model’s effective identification of both overall predictions and positive instances. We analyze and compare explanations provided by IG and SHAP to gain more knowledge in the decision-making processes of GCNs. Our framework interpret the contributions of various omics features in GCN models, with the highest SHAP score observed for feature MF:UCEC and the highest IG score for KIF11. This approach identifies novel cancer genes and clarifies their molecular mechanisms, enhancing GCN interpretability. The study improves GCN accessibility in personalized medicine and contributes to understanding cancer biology.

papers.title: The Molecular Structure of Thought: Mapping the Topology of Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models learn and represent effective Long Chain-of-Thought?
papers.core_contribution: The paper models Long Chain-of-Thought as a molecular structure with three bond types and introduces Mole-Syn, a method to synthesize effective Long CoT structures, improving performance and RL stability.
papers.conclusion: The molecular structure view explains how LLMs learn Long CoT, and Mole-Syn enables effective synthesis of these structures for improved reasoning performance.
papers.key_findings:
Long CoT reasoning exhibits stable molecular-like structures formed by deep-reasoning, self-reflection, and self-exploration bonds.
Semantic isomers with compatible bond structures are crucial for effective Long CoT learning, while incompatible structures lead to instability.
Distillation from strong reasoning LLMs successfully imparts Long CoT structures, but distillation from weak instruction LLMs or human traces fails.
Mole-Syn can synthesize effective Long CoT structures by transferring behavior distributions, boosting performance across benchmarks.
Conflict between two stable molecular structures during training causes structural chaos and degrades performance.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often fail to learn effective long chain-of-thought (Long CoT) reasoning from human or non-Long-CoT LLMs imitation. To understand this, we propose that effective and learnable Long CoT trajectories feature stable molecular-like structures in unified view, which are formed by three interaction types: Deep-Reasoning (covalent-like), Self-Reflection (hydrogen-bond-like), and Self-Exploration (van der Waals-like). Analysis of distilled trajectories reveals these structures emerge from Long CoT fine-tuning, not keyword imitation. We introduce Effective Semantic Isomers and show that only bonds promoting fast entropy convergence support stable Long CoT learning, while structural competition impairs training. Drawing on these findings, we present Mole-Syn, a distribution-transfer-graph method that guides synthesis of effective Long CoT structures, boosting performance and RL stability across benchmarks.

papers.title: Physics Steering: Causal Control of Cross-Domain Concepts in a Physics Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Whether scientific foundation models learn abstract, domain-general representations of physical phenomena that can be causally manipulated via activation steering.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that a physics foundation model learns linearly steerable representations of physical concepts (e.g., vorticity, diffusion, temporal progression), and that injecting these directions during inference enables fine-grained causal control over simulation behavior. The concept directions are domain-general and transfer across unrelated physical systems.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability techniques from LLMs can be successfully adapted to scientific foundation models, providing evidence that these models develop abstract, domain-general representations of fundamental physical concepts that are linearly encoded and causally steerable.
papers.key_findings:
Single directions in the model's activation space correspond to specific physical concepts like vorticity, diffusion, and simulation speed.
Injecting (adding or subtracting) these concept directions during inference causally steers model predictions, allowing induction or suppression of vortices, enhancement or suppression of diffusion, and speeding up or slowing down simulations.
The extracted concept directions transfer successfully between unrelated physical systems (e.g., from fluid dynamics to chemical reaction-diffusion), indicating they represent abstract, domain-general physical principles.
The results support the Linear Representation Hypothesis for scientific foundation models, showing physical concepts are represented linearly in activation space.
Steering effects are more physically plausible and interpretable when using spatially-averaged concept directions that discard spatial structure, compared to using full spatial tensors.
papers.limitation:
The physical plausibility of the steered results is an open question; including spatial dimensions in the steering tensor can lead to less physically realistic outcomes.
The effectiveness of steering depends on the initial conditions of the simulation; steering becomes more difficult and can produce distorted fields when the initial state is far from the target regime.
future_direction: Exploring the layer-dependence of concept representations and steering effects.
Further work to definitively assess the physicality and self-consistency of steered simulation results.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have revealed that large language models (LLMs) develop internal representations corresponding not only to concrete entities but also distinct, human-understandable abstract concepts and behaviour. Moreover, these hidden features can be directly manipulated to steer model behaviour. However, it remains an open question whether this phenomenon is unique to models trained on inherently structured data (ie. language, images) or if it is a general property of foundation models. In this work, we investigate the internal representations of a large physics-focused foundation model. Inspired by recent work identifying single directions in activation space for complex behaviours in LLMs, we extract activation vectors from the model during forward passes over simulation datasets for different physical regimes. We then compute "delta" representations between the two regimes. These delta tensors act as concept directions in activation space, encoding specific physical features. By injecting these concept directions back into the model during inference, we can steer its predictions, demonstrating causal control over physical behaviours, such as inducing or removing some particular physical feature from a simulation. These results suggest that scientific foundation models learn generalised representations of physical principles. They do not merely rely on superficial correlations and patterns in the simulations. Our findings open new avenues for understanding and controlling scientific foundation models and has implications for AI-enabled scientific discovery.

papers.title: Negative Pre-activations Differentiate Syntax
papers.research_question: Whether and how negative pre-activations are leveraged by models, specifically for syntactic processing.
papers.core_contribution: Negative pre-activations in a sparse subpopulation of Wasserstein neurons are actively used as a substrate for syntax in smooth-activation language models.
papers.conclusion: Negative pre-activations are not an inert byproduct but a functional substrate that certain neurons leverage to implement grammar, reframing ReLU-era intuitions.
papers.key_findings:
Wasserstein neurons, which have non-Gaussian pre-activation distributions, emerge early in training and track grammatical competence.
Zeroing negative pre-activations of top Wasserstein neurons disproportionately increases perplexity and degrades grammatical performance on BLiMP and TSE, while random or perplexity-matched ablations of non-Wasserstein neurons do not.
The same ablation has a milder effect on non-grammatical benchmarks, showing a double dissociation between syntax and other capabilities.
Layerwise ablations reveal that early layers are most critical for grammar, and damage compounds across depth.
Wasserstein neurons implement 'negative differentiation', mapping similar inputs (e.g., syntactic tokens) to distinct negative pre-activation values.
papers.limitation: The ablation method zeroing negative pre-activations disproportionately collapses negative-negative pairs, so correlations between negative-negative pair prevalence and grammatical vulnerability may partly reflect the intervention mechanics.
papers.abstract: A recently discovered class of entangled neurons, known as Wasserstein neurons, is disproportionately critical in large language models despite constituting only a very small fraction of the network: their targeted removal collapses the model, consistent with their unique role in differentiating similar inputs. Interestingly, in Wasserstein neurons immediately preceding smooth activation functions, such differentiation manifests in the negative pre-activation space, especially in early layers. Pairs of similar inputs are driven to highly distinct negative values, and these pairs involve syntactic tokens such as determiners and prepositions. We show that this negative region is functional rather than simply favorable for optimization. A minimal, sign-specific intervention that zeroes only the negative pre-activations of a small subset of entangled neurons significantly weakens overall model function and disrupts grammatical behavior, while both random and perplexity-matched controls leave grammatical performance largely unchanged. Part of speech analysis localizes the excess surprisal to syntactic scaffolding tokens, and layer-specific interventions reveal that small local degradations accumulate across depth. Over training checkpoints, the same ablation impairs grammatical behavior as Wasserstein neurons emerge and stabilize. Together, these results identify negative differentiation in a sparse subset of entangled neurons as a crucial mechanism that language models rely on for syntax.

papers.title: GOAt: Explaining Graph Neural Networks via Graph Output Attribution
papers.research_question: How to generate faithful, discriminative, and stable explanations for Graph Neural Networks by attributing graph outputs to input features.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces GOAt, a training-free method for explaining GNNs by attributing outputs to input features, which achieves high fidelity, discriminability, and stability.
papers.conclusion: GOAt overcomes limitations of existing GNN explainers in terms of discriminability and stability, and enhances the transparency of GNN decision-making.
papers.key_findings:
GOAt outperforms state-of-the-art GNN explainers in fidelity across different sparsity levels.
GOAt generates explanations with higher discriminability, effectively separating classes in embedding space.
GOAt exhibits higher stability, covering more data samples with fewer explanation motifs.
GOAt provides human-understandable explanations, such as identifying chemical motifs in mutagenicity datasets.
GOAt is computationally efficient compared to search-based baselines like SubgraphX.
papers.limitation: Requires expert knowledge to design explaining processes for various GNNs
papers.abstract: Understanding the decision-making process of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) is crucial to their interpretability. Most existing methods for explaining GNNs typically rely on training auxiliary models, resulting in the explanations remain black-boxed. This paper introduces Graph Output Attribution (GOAt), a novel method to attribute graph outputs to input graph features, creating GNN explanations that are faithful, discriminative, as well as stable across similar samples. By expanding the GNN as a sum of scalar products involving node features, edge features and activation patterns, we propose an efficient analytical method to compute contribution of each node or edge feature to each scalar product and aggregate the contributions from all scalar products in the expansion form to derive the importance of each node and edge. Through extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world data, we show that our method not only outperforms various state-ofthe-art GNN explainers in terms of the commonly used fidelity metric, but also exhibits stronger discriminability, and stability by a remarkable margin.

papers.title: Do We Really Need GNNs with Explicit Structural Modeling? MLPs Suffice for Language Model Representations
papers.research_question: Do we really need GNNs with explicit structural modeling to enhance language model representations for improved performance on downstream NLP tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that feature-transformation operations (as in MLPs) are the primary drivers of performance improvements in structure-aware tasks, while message-passing operations (the core of GNNs) contribute minimally or negatively, suggesting MLPs are sufficient for enhancing language model representations.
papers.conclusion: Explicit structural information may not be critical for enhancing language model representations in probing tasks, and MLPs without explicit structural modeling are sufficient, efficient, and scalable alternatives to GNNs.
papers.key_findings:
MLPs, when used as feature-transformation modules, consistently improve the linguistic knowledge captured in LM representations across different architectures.
GNNs that incorporate feature-transformation operations show beneficial effects, but models relying solely on message-passing operations tend to underperform.
Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks (KANs) show performance comparable to MLPs, further underscoring the importance of feature-transformation operations.
Random graph structures cause a performance decline, with the message-passing module being more sensitive to structural noise than the full GNN module.
The performance gains from control modules vary across language model architectures, with T5 and BERT benefiting more than Llama-3-8B.
papers.abstract: Explicit structural information has been proven to be encoded by Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), serving as auxiliary knowledge to enhance model capabilities and improve performance in downstream NLP tasks. However, recent studies indicate that GNNs fail to fully utilize structural information, whereas Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs), despite lacking the message-passing mechanisms inherent to GNNs, exhibit a surprising ability in structure-aware tasks. Motivated by these findings, this paper introduces a comprehensive probing framework from an information-theoretic perspective. The framework is designed to systematically assess the role of explicit structural modeling in enhancing language model (LM) representations and to investigate the potential of MLPs as efficient and scalable alternatives to GNNs. We extend traditional probing classifiers by incorporating a control module that allows for selective use of either the full GNN model or its decoupled components, specifically, the message-passing and feature-transformation operations.This modular approach isolates and assesses the individual contributions of these operations, avoiding confounding effects from the complete GNN architecture. Using the Edge Probing Suite, a diagnostic tool for evaluating the linguistic knowledge encoded in LMs, we find that MLPs, when used as feature-transformation modules, consistently improve the linguistic knowledge captured in LM representations across different architectures. They effectively encode both syntactic and semantic patterns. Similarly, GNNs that incorporate feature-transformation operations show beneficial effects. In contrast, models that rely solely on message-passing operations tend to underperform, often leading to negative impacts on probing task performance.

papers.title: Exploiting Hypergraph Topologies: Advancing Explainable AI for Predicting Drug Synergies
papers.research_question: The paper investigates the use of Hyper Graph Neural Networks (HGNNs) in modeling and predicting the interactions between drug combinations and their consequent effects on certain cell lines.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes an explainable Hyper Graph Neural Network (Ex-HGNN) model for predicting drug synergy and antagonism, demonstrating high predictive performance and interpretability through SHAP and LIME.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates the effectiveness of the Ex-HGNN model for drug synergy prediction and highlights the importance of explainable AI for building trust and transparency in healthcare applications.
papers.key_findings:
The Ex-HGNN model achieved a test accuracy of 86.70% and high AUC/AUPR scores, indicating strong predictive capability for drug combination efficacy.
SHAP and LIME analyses provided transparency by revealing the contribution of individual features (e.g., specific drugs and cell lines) to the model's predictions.
The model showed robust performance across different evaluation metrics, balancing precision and recall for synergistic and antagonistic drug combinations.
papers.abstract: Background: Considering the importance of drug therapy as a dominant approach in cancer treatment, monotherapy has been successful in advancing disease treatments, but its effectiveness can be limited due to different drug responses. To overcome these challenges, the drug combination strategy involving the use of multiple drugs to treat a specific disease has been advocated. Objective: The objective of this research was to investigate the use of Hyper Graph Neural Networks (HGNNs) in modeling and predicting the interactions between drug combinations and their consequent effects on certain cell lines. Method: The methodology involved extensive data preprocessing, exploratory data analysis (EDA), and the implementation of an HGNN model tailored to capture the complex inter-relations of multidimensional data. The Ex-HGNN model showed superior performance metrics, including high accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-scores, and portrayed efficiency in categorizing drug interactions and their effects as either synergistic or antagonistic. A critical detail of this study was the implementation of explainable AI approaches, such as SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) and LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations). These methods brought transparency into the decisions of the Ex-HGNN model, rendering them more interpretable and trustworthy. They allowed insight into the contribution of individual features on the prediction decisions of the Ex-HGNN model, an essential component in the field of drug efficiency analysis. Results: Experimental results validated the proposed drug synergy prediction model and its significant enhancement compared to state-of-the-art methods. Conclusion: These findings provide a stepping-stone for future research using machine learning and deep learning approaches in resolving other drug-related issues. This work demonstrates the effectiveness of Hyper Graph neural network modeling for high-dimensional data analysis and emphasizes the importance of explainable artificial intelligence in the fields of healthcare and precision medicine.

papers.title: Transformers are Graph Neural Networks
papers.core_contribution: The paper establishes that Transformers are Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) operating on fully connected graphs, and that their efficiency on modern hardware gives them an advantage over sparse GNNs.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are Graph Neural Networks that are currently winning the hardware lottery due to their efficient implementation on modern parallel hardware.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can be viewed as message passing GNNs on fully connected graphs, where self-attention captures the relative importance of all tokens.
The self-attention mechanism in Transformers is equivalent to the message passing in Graph Attention Networks (GATs) but with global attention over all tokens.
Transformers are implemented via dense matrix operations that are significantly more efficient on modern hardware (GPUs/TPUs) than the sparse message passing typical of GNNs.
The connection has inspired Graph Transformers, which aim to combine local message passing and global multi-head attention.
Transformers are expressive set processing networks that can learn relationships among input elements without being constrained by a priori graph structures.
papers.abstract: We establish connections between the Transformer architecture, originally introduced for natural language processing, and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for representation learning on graphs. We show how Transformers can be viewed as message passing GNNs operating on fully connected graphs of tokens, where the self-attention mechanism capture the relative importance of all tokens w.r.t. each-other, and positional encodings provide hints about sequential ordering or structure. Thus, Transformers are expressive set processing networks that learn relationships among input elements without being constrained by apriori graphs. Despite this mathematical connection to GNNs, Transformers are implemented via dense matrix operations that are significantly more efficient on modern hardware than sparse message passing. This leads to the perspective that Transformers are GNNs currently winning the hardware lottery.

papers.title: A Comparison of Explainable Artificial Intelligence Methods in the Phase Classification of Multi-Principal Element Alloys
papers.research_question: How do two model-agnostic local post hoc interpretability methods (breakDown and SHAP) compare in explaining the predictions of a black-box classification model for phase classification of multi-principal element alloys? Which method produces explanations more consistent with domain knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that SHAP and breakDown, two local post hoc interpretability methods, produce similar explanations for a dataset with independent and non-interacting features, with SHAP being marginally more consistent with existing literature.
papers.conclusion: Both breakDown and SHAP are effective for local post hoc interpretability in materials science, with SHAP being more robust but computationally expensive, and breakDown being a greedy alternative that yields similar results when features are independent.
papers.key_findings:
Both breakDown and SHAP identify similar key features for phase classification, such as maxdiff_AtomicWeight and mean_CovalentRadius for BCC and AM phases.
SHAP results are more consistent with existing literature on phase formation in multi-principal element alloys.
Despite differences in variable attribution at the instance level, clustering of compositions based on breakDown and SHAP values yields similar groups of alloys.
Ceteris-Paribus profile plots show similar functional dependencies between features and predicted phases for clusters identified by both methods.
The similarity between breakDown and SHAP explanations is attributed to the independent and non-interacting nature of the input features in the dataset.
papers.limitation: The dataset used has independent and non-interacting features, which may not be generalizable to other datasets with correlated features.
papers.abstract: Abstract We demonstrate the capabilities of two model-agnostic local post hoc model interpretability methods, namely breakDown (BD) and shapley (SHAP), to explain the predictions of a black-box classification learning model that establishes a quantitative relationship between chemical composition and multi-principal element alloys phase formation. We trained an ensemble of support vector machines using a dataset with 1,821 instances, 12 features with low pair-wise correlation, and seven phase labels. Feature contributions to the model prediction are computed by BD and SHAP for each composition. The resulting BD and SHAP transformed data are then used as inputs to identify similar composition groups using k-means clustering. Explanation-of-clusters by features reveal that the results from SHAP agree more closely with the literature. Visualization of compositions within a cluster using Ceteris-Paribus (CP) profile plots show the functional dependencies between the feature values and predicted response. Despite the differences between BD and SHAP in variable attribution, only minor changes were observed in the CP profile plots. Explanation-of-clusters by examples show that the clusters that share a common phase label contain similar compositions, which clarifies the similar-looking CP profile trends. In the limits of a dataset with independent and non-interacting features, SHAP and BD appear to capture similar pattern.

papers.title: Lost in the Prompt Order: Revealing the Limitations of Causal Attention in Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the mechanism behind the performance gap between CQO (context-question-option) and QOC (question-option-context) prompt orderings in multiple-choice question answering for decoder-only large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The performance gap between CQO and QOC orderings in multiple-choice question answering is primarily due to causal attention masking in decoder-only LLMs, which prevents option tokens from attending to context tokens in the QOC order.
papers.conclusion: The study identifies causal attention as the key mechanism behind prompt order sensitivity in decoder-only LLMs for MCQA, providing mechanistic insight and practical guidance for prompt design.
papers.key_findings:
CQO ordering outperforms QOC by over 14% across 21 decoder-only LLMs and four datasets.
The gap is not explained by training data bias or failure to recall options.
Causal attention masking is the core mechanism: in QOC, the causal mask prevents option tokens from attending to context tokens, making context effectively inaccessible.
Encoder models with bidirectional attention show no performance gap, confirming the role of causal masking.
Targeted interventions (attention pruning, activation patching, option repetition) degrade CQO or improve QOC performance, further supporting the causal attention explanation.
papers.limitation:
Evaluations are primarily focused on MCQA tasks with four-option formats.
Models are evaluated only up to 9B parameters due to computational constraints.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit surprising sensitivity to the structure of the prompt, but the mechanisms underlying this sensitivity remain poorly understood. In this work, we conduct an in-depth investigation on a striking case: in multiple-choice question answering, placing context before the questions and options (CQO) outperforms the reverse order (QOC) by over 14%p, consistently over a wide range of models and datasets. Through systematic architectural analysis, we identify causal attention as the core mechanism: in QOC prompts, the causal mask prevents option tokens from attending to context, creating an information bottleneck where context becomes invisible to options.

papers.title: How Graph Neural Networks Learn: Lessons from Training Dynamics
papers.research_question: Do GNNs indeed learn the desired function that can generalize during the training process, and if so, how?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that GNN training dynamics implicitly align the Neural Tangent Kernel with the graph adjacency (kernel-graph alignment), which explains generalization on homophilic graphs and failure on heterophilic graphs, and proposes a parameter-free Residual Propagation algorithm that matches GNN performance while being orders-of-magnitude faster.
papers.conclusion: The graph implicit bias in optimization explains the generalization and limitations of GNNs, and the proposed Residual Propagation algorithm offers a simple, fast, and effective alternative for semi-supervised learning on graphs.
papers.key_findings:
The optimization of GNNs implicitly leverages graph structure through kernel-graph alignment.
This alignment promotes generalization on homophilic graphs but harms it on heterophilic graphs.
The proposed Residual Propagation algorithm, which explicitly uses graph adjacency to propagate residuals, achieves performance comparable to trained GNNs while being much faster and requiring no trainable parameters.
Theoretical analysis in the overparameterized regime shows how the graph structure integrates into the Neural Tangent Kernel.
Empirical verification shows that the NTK of real-world GNNs aligns with the message passing matrix used in the forward pass.
papers.limitation:
The analysis may only explain a limited part of an under-explored complex problem.
The theoretical analysis relies on the overparameterized regime approximation.
future_direction: Dissecting other graph learning tasks such as link prediction and representation learning.
Using the analytical framework to gain insights and develop methods for other practically relevant GNN issues.
papers.abstract: A long-standing goal in deep learning has been to characterize the learning behavior of black-box models in a more interpretable manner. For graph neural networks (GNNs), considerable advances have been made in formalizing what functions they can represent, but whether GNNs will learn desired functions during the optimization process remains less clear. To fill this gap, we study their training dynamics in function space. In particular, we find that the gradient descent optimization of GNNs implicitly leverages the graph structure to update the learned function, as can be quantified by a phenomenon which we call \emph{kernel-graph alignment}. We provide theoretical explanations for the emergence of this phenomenon in the overparameterized regime and empirically validate it on real-world GNNs. This finding offers new interpretable insights into when and why the learned GNN functions generalize, highlighting their limitations in heterophilic graphs. Practically, we propose a parameter-free algorithm that directly uses a sparse matrix (i.e. graph adjacency) to update the learned function. We demonstrate that this embarrassingly simple approach can be as effective as GNNs while being orders-of-magnitude faster.

papers.title: Transformers learn factored representations
papers.research_question: Do transformers learn to factor their world into parts from next-token prediction, and why would they have an inductive bias for factored representations?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers learn to factor their world into parts, representing each factor in orthogonal subspaces of the residual stream, and show an inductive bias toward factored representations even when it is lossy.
papers.conclusion: Transformers decompose the world into parts and represent them in orthogonal subspaces due to an inductive bias from next-token prediction, suggesting interpretable low-dimensional structure may persist in models trained on complex data.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers learn factored representations in orthogonal subspaces when data has conditionally independent factors.
The dimensionality of activations collapses to the linearly growing factored prediction, not the exponentially growing joint representation.
Factor subspaces become approximately orthogonal over training, as measured by subspace overlap and dimensionality additivity.
Factoring begins at the token embedding layer, with the embedding matrix developing low-rank structure corresponding to factor subspaces.
Transformers exhibit an inductive bias toward factored representations, learning them early even when data is not perfectly factorable, sacrificing fidelity for dimensional efficiency.
papers.limitation: Experiments are conducted on synthetic data with known latent structure, which may not fully capture real-world complexity.
future_direction: Investigate whether differences in factorization behavior between transformers, RNNs, and LSTMs are due to training dynamics or inductive bias.
papers.abstract: Transformers pretrained via next token prediction learn to factor their world into parts, representing these factors in orthogonal subspaces of the residual stream. We formalize two representational hypotheses: (1) a representation in the product space of all factors, whose dimension grows exponentially with the number of parts, or (2) a factored representation in orthogonal subspaces, whose dimension grows linearly. The factored representation is lossless when factors are conditionally independent, but sacrifices predictive fidelity otherwise, creating a tradeoff between dimensional efficiency and accuracy. We derive precise predictions about the geometric structure of activations for each, including the number of subspaces, their dimensionality, and the arrangement of context embeddings within them. We test between these hypotheses on transformers trained on synthetic processes with known latent structure. Models learn factored representations when factors are conditionally independent, and continue to favor them early in training even when noise or hidden dependencies undermine conditional independence, reflecting an inductive bias toward factoring at the cost of fidelity. This provides a principled explanation for why transformers decompose the world into parts, and suggests that interpretable low dimensional structure may persist even in models trained on complex data.

papers.title: Encoding Concepts in Graph Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can Graph Neural Networks be made more interpretable by design through a differentiable concept-discovery approach?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Concept Encoder Module, a differentiable concept-discovery approach that makes Graph Neural Networks explainable by design, achieving comparable accuracy, meaningful concept discovery, and supporting test-time interventions.
papers.conclusion: The Concept Encoder Module successfully makes Graph Neural Networks explainable by design, enabling concept discovery, interpretable predictions, and effective human interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Concept Graph Networks (CGNs) achieve comparable or better task accuracy than equivalent vanilla GNNs.
The Concept Encoder Module (CEM) discovers a more complete set of concepts than the post-hoc GCExplainer.
CEM identifies meaningful, fine-grained, and rare graph concepts that align with human expectations or ground truth.
CEM provides accurate and simple logic explanations for model predictions.
CEM supports effective test-time interventions at the concept level, which can significantly improve model performance and human trust.
papers.abstract: The opaque reasoning of Graph Neural Networks induces a lack of human trust. Existing graph network explainers attempt to address this issue by providing post-hoc explanations, however, they fail to make the model itself more interpretable. To fill this gap, we introduce the Concept Encoder Module, the first differentiable concept-discovery approach for graph networks. The proposed approach makes graph networks explainable by design by first discovering graph concepts and then using these to solve the task. Our results demonstrate that this approach allows graph networks to: (i) attain model accuracy comparable with their equivalent vanilla versions, (ii) discover meaningful concepts that achieve high concept completeness and purity scores, (iii) provide high-quality concept-based logic explanations for their prediction, and (iv) support effective interventions at test time: these can increase human trust as well as significantly improve model performance.

papers.title: Open Sesame: Getting inside BERT’s Linguistic Knowledge
papers.research_question: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information?
papers.core_contribution: BERT encodes positional information in lower layers and switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. The paper also introduces a 'confusion score' to quantify intrusion effects in BERT's self-attention mechanism.
papers.conclusion: BERT composes increasingly abstract hierarchical representations of linguistic structure using self-attention, but does not show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure found in human processing.
papers.key_findings:
Diagnostic classifiers show BERT's lower layers encode positional information well, while higher layers encode hierarchical information.
The proposed confusion score reveals BERT's attention is sensitive to syntactic structure and grammatical features (number, gender) in subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora.
BERT's attention is not perfectly syntactic; it sometimes attends to grammatically inaccessible or mismatched distractors.
Confusion scores decrease with layer depth, and there is an increase in confusion at layer 4, coinciding with the degradation of positional information.
BERT's performance on possessive constructions in the subject noun task is poor, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
papers.limitation:
BERT performed poorly on possessive constructions in the subject noun task, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
BERT's attention is only incompletely modulated by structural and featural properties, and attention is sometimes spread across grammatically irrelevant elements.
future_direction: Investigate or visualize layer-on-layer changes in BERT’s structural and positional information, particularly between layers 3 and 4.
Retrieve the increasingly hierarchical representations of BERT across layers via the self-attention mechanism.
papers.abstract: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information? Recent work has shown that contextual representations like BERT perform well on tasks that require sensitivity to linguistic structure. We present here two studies which aim to provide a better understanding of the nature of BERT's representations. The first of these focuses on the identification of structurally-defined elements using diagnostic classifiers, while the second explores BERT's representation of subject-verb agreement and anaphor-antecedent dependencies through a quantitative assessment of self-attention vectors. In both cases, we find that BERT encodes positional information about word tokens well on its lower layers, but switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. We conclude then that BERT's representations do indeed model linguistically relevant aspects of hierarchical structure, though they do not appear to show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure that is found in human processing of reflexive anaphora.

papers.title: CoulGAT: An Experiment on Interpretability of Graph Attention Networks
papers.research_question: How can a screened Coulomb potential-inspired attention mechanism be used to interpret Graph Attention Network layers and the training dataset?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a scalable graph attention model framework (CoulGAT) with a screened Coulomb potential-based attention mechanism, whose learned parameters provide interpretability of node-node and node-feature interactions.
papers.conclusion: The Coulomb attention mechanism provides an effective tool for interpreting Graph Attention Networks and can be used to extract an empirical standard model for graph structure and hidden layers.
papers.key_findings:
The Coulomb attention mechanism enables building deep graph models (up to 140 layers) and provides stable training.
The learned attention parameters (a and P) reveal interaction strengths and ranges between nodes and features, allowing interpretation of the graph structure.
The distributions of a and P parameters can be used to compare different models and optimize hidden layer representations.
The model learns interaction patterns that can be classified as confinement, Coulomb, or distance-independent, analogous to physical potentials.
The framework scales well and can be used to extract an empirical standard model for the graph structure of a dataset.
future_direction: Evaluation of the attention mechanism with different transductive and inductive graph datasets.
Using better input embeddings to improve model performance.
Applying the approach to other high capacity models such as transformers.
papers.abstract: We present an attention mechanism inspired from definition of screened Coulomb potential. This attention mechanism was used to interpret the Graph Attention (GAT) model layers and training dataset by using a flexible and scalable framework (CoulGAT) developed for this purpose. Using CoulGAT, a forest of plain and resnet models were trained and characterized using this attention mechanism against CHAMPS dataset. The learnable variables of the attention mechanism are used to extract node-node and node-feature interactions to define an empirical standard model for the graph structure and hidden layer. This representation of graph and hidden layers can be used as a tool to compare different models, optimize hidden layers and extract a compact definition of graph structure of the dataset.

papers.title: $\mathcal{V}isi\mathcal{P}runer$: Decoding Discontinuous Cross-Modal Dynamics for Efficient Multimodal LLMs
papers.research_question: How do Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) process and fuse visual and textual information across layers, and how can this understanding be used to design an efficient pruning framework?
papers.core_contribution: This paper uncovers a three-stage, discontinuous cross-modal interaction process in MLLMs (shallow task recognition, sparse middle-layer fusion, deep linguistic alignment) and introduces VisiPruner, a training-free pruning framework that exploits this dynamic to significantly reduce computational overhead.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a three-stage framework for understanding MLLM mechanics, introduces an efficient pruning method (VisiPruner) based on these insights, and provides actionable guidelines for future efficient MLLM design that aligns with intrinsic layer-wise processing dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Shallow layers in MLLMs recognize task intent from text instructions, with visual tokens acting as passive 'attention sinks' rather than contributing to meaningful cross-modal fusion.
Cross-modal fusion occurs abruptly in middle layers and is driven by a sparse subset of critical visual tokens, which can be identified by their influence on attention outputs rather than by attention weights.
Deep layers discard vision tokens and focus solely on linguistic refinement and alignment of the generated content with natural language conventions.
Attention scores are a poor proxy for information utility in shallow layers, as highly attended visual tokens can be masked or merged without performance degradation.
VisiPruner, based on these insights, reduces up to 99% of vision-related attention computations and 53.9% of total FLOPs while maintaining competitive performance across diverse MLLMs and benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
Training the projector to align vision tokens with semantic representations and inserting them until later layers could further strengthen the findings regarding intra-modal processing in shallow layers.
Due to hardware constraints, the analysis was limited to models with up to 13 billion parameters.
future_direction: Truncate shallow visual layers and eliminate cross/self-attention.
Train models to attend sparsely in middle layers.
Enable early exiting in deep visual layers once modality fusion is established.
papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong performance across vision-language tasks, but suffer from significant computational overhead due to the quadratic growth of attention computations with the number of multimodal tokens. Though efforts have been made to prune tokens in MLLMs, \textit{they lack a fundamental understanding of how MLLMs process and fuse multimodal information.} Through systematic analysis, we uncover a \textbf{three-stage} cross-modal interaction process: (1) Shallow layers recognize task intent, with visual tokens acting as passive attention sinks; (2) Cross-modal fusion occurs abruptly in middle layers, driven by a few critical visual tokens; (3) Deep layers discard vision tokens, focusing solely on linguistic refinement. Based on these findings, we propose \emph{VisiPruner}, a training-free pruning framework that reduces up to 99\% of vision-related attention computations and 53.9\% of FLOPs on LLaVA-v1.5 7B. It significantly outperforms existing token pruning methods and generalizes across diverse MLLMs. Beyond pruning, our insights further provide actionable guidelines for training efficient MLLMs by aligning model architecture with its intrinsic layer-wise processing dynamics. Our code is available at: https://github.com/EIT-NLP/VisiPruner.

papers.title: Beyond Sight: Probing Alignment Between Image Models and Blind V1
papers.research_question: Does representational alignment between deep neural networks (DNNs) and neural activity hold for the primary visual cortex (V1) of a blind human? Specifically, can DNN activations predict neural activity evoked by electrical stimulation or mental imagery in blind V1?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates significant representational alignment between DNN activations and neural activity in the primary visual cortex (V1) of a blind human, showing that DNNs with higher ImageNet accuracy or higher sighted primate neural predictivity are more predictive of blind V1 activity. It also proposes a proof-of-concept approach for interpreting blind V1 neurons using feature visualization.
papers.conclusion: The findings suggest that some form of natural visual processing is preserved in blind V1 and that DNNs can be used to model and interpret blind V1 activity, with implications for visual prostheses and understanding cortical plasticity.
papers.key_findings:
DNN activations are significantly aligned with neural activity in blind V1 during electrical stimulation and, to a lesser extent, during mental imagery.
DNN-blind V1 alignment scores are positively correlated with DNN-sighted neural predictivity and ImageNet top-1 accuracy.
ResNet-50 activations show strong correlations with multi-unit spiking and local field potential responses during stimulation, with fewer correlations during delay and recall periods.
A proof-of-concept method using maximally exciting images (MEIs) derived from DNN activations shows promise for interpreting blind V1 neuron properties.
Neural activity patterns during working memory tasks allow classification of the stimulating electrode with high accuracy, suggesting shared representations across stimulation, delay, and recall periods.
papers.limitation:
The dataset contains a limited number of neural responses and visual percepts.
The method relies on phosphene drawings for predicting neural activity, which may not fully capture the perceived phosphenes.
future_direction: Delve deeper into distinct neural activities across different phases of the working memory task.
Use topographic networks to predict neural activity without relying on phosphene drawings.
Collect a more diverse dataset of neural recordings and phosphenes to better understand neuron properties and refine stimulation strategies for visual prostheses.
papers.abstract: Neural activity in the visual cortex of blind humans persists in the absence of visual stimuli. However, little is known about the preservation of visual representation capacity in these cortical regions, which could have significant implications for neural interfaces such as visual prostheses. In this work, we present a series of analyses on the shared representations between evoked neural activity in the primary visual cortex (V1) of a blind human with an intracortical visual prosthesis, and latent visual representations computed in deep neural networks (DNNs). In the absence of natural visual input, we examine two alternative forms of inducing neural activity: electrical stimulation and mental imagery. We first quantitatively demonstrate that latent DNN activations are aligned with neural activity measured in blind V1. On average, DNNs with higher ImageNet accuracy or higher sighted primate neural predictivity are more predictive of blind V1 activity. We further probe blind V1 alignment in ResNet-50 and propose a proof-of-concept approach towards interpretability of blind V1 neurons. The results of these studies suggest the presence of some form of natural visual processing in blind V1 during electrically evoked visual perception and present unique directions in mechanistically understanding and interfacing with blind V1.

papers.title: Exposing the limitations of molecular machine learning with activity cliffs.
papers.abstract: Machine learning has become a crucial tool in drug discovery and chemistry at large, e.g., to predict molecular properties, such as bioactivity, with high accuracy. However, activity cliffs – pairs of molecules that are highly similar in their structure but exhibit large differences in potency – have been underinvestigated for their effect on model performance. Not only are these edge cases informative for molecule discovery and optimization, but models that are well-equipped to accurately predict the potency of activity cliffs have an increased potential for prospective applications. Our work aims to fill the current knowledge gap on best-practice machine learning methods in the presence of activity cliffs. We benchmarked a total of 720 machine and deep learning models on curated bioactivity data from 30 macromolecular targets for their performance on activity cliff compounds. While all methods struggled in the presence of activity cliffs, machine learning approaches based on molecular descriptors outperformed more complex deep learning methods. Our findings highlight large case-by-case differences in performance, advocating for (a) the inclusion of dedicated “activity-cliff-centered” metrics during model development and evaluation, and (b) the development of novel algorithms to better predict the properties of activity cliffs. To this end, the methods, metrics, and results of this study have been encapsulated into an open-access benchmarking platform named MoleculeACE (Activity Cliff Estimation, available on GitHub at: https://github.com/molML/MoleculeACE). MoleculeACE is designed to steer the community towards addressing the pressing but overlooked limitation of molecular machine learning models posed by activity cliffs.

papers.title: A systematic study of key elements underlying molecular property prediction
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has been widely applied in drug discovery with a major task as molecular property prediction. Despite booming techniques in molecular representation learning, key elements underlying molecular property prediction remain largely unexplored, which impedes further advancements in this field. Herein, we conduct an extensive evaluation of representative models using various representations on the MoleculeNet datasets, a suite of opioids-related datasets and two additional activity datasets from the literature. To investigate the predictive power in low-data and high-data space, a series of descriptors datasets of varying sizes are also assembled to evaluate the models. In total, we have trained 62,820 models, including 50,220 models on fixed representations, 4200 models on SMILES sequences and 8400 models on molecular graphs. Based on extensive experimentation and rigorous comparison, we show that representation learning models exhibit limited performance in molecular property prediction in most datasets. Besides, multiple key elements underlying molecular property prediction can affect the evaluation results. Furthermore, we show that activity cliffs can significantly impact model prediction. Finally, we explore into potential causes why representation learning models can fail and show that dataset size is essential for representation learning models to excel.

papers.title: Evolving Concept of Activity Cliffs
papers.abstract: Activity cliffs (ACs) are generally defined as pairs or groups of structurally similar compounds that are active against the same target but have large differences in potency. Accordingly, ACs capture chemical modifications that strongly influence biological activity. Therefore, they are of particular interest in structure-activity relationship (SAR) analysis and compound optimization. The AC concept is much more complex than it may appear at a first glance, especially if one aims to represent ACs computationally and identify them systematically. To these ends, molecular similarity and potency difference criteria must be carefully considered for AC assessment. Furthermore, ACs are often perceived differently in medicinal and computational chemistry, depending on whether they are studied on a case-by-case basis or systematically. For practical applications, intuitive access to AC information plays a major role. Over the years, the AC concept has been further refined and extended. Herein, we review the evolution of the AC concept, emphasizing new analysis schemes and findings that help to better understand ACs and extract SAR knowledge from them.

papers.title: Unraveling Key Elements Underlying Molecular Property Prediction: A Systematic Study
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has been widely applied in drug discovery with a major task as molecular property prediction. Despite booming techniques in molecular representation learning, key elements underlying molecular property prediction remain largely unexplored, which impedes further advancements in this field. Herein, we conduct an extensive evaluation of representative models using various representations on the MoleculeNet datasets, a suite of opioids-related datasets and two additional activity datasets from the literature. To investigate the predictive power in low-data and high-data space, a series of descriptors datasets of varying sizes are also assembled to evaluate the models. In total, we have trained 62,820 models, including 50,220 models on fixed representations, 4,200 models on SMILES sequences and 8,400 models on molecular graphs. Based on extensive experimentation and rigorous comparison, we show that representation learning models exhibit limited performance in molecular property prediction in most datasets. Besides, multiple key elements underlying molecular property prediction can affect the evaluation results. Furthermore, we show that activity cliffs can significantly impact model prediction. Finally, we explore into potential causes why representation learning models can fail and show that dataset size is essential for representation learning models to excel.

papers.title: Spectral Decomposition of Chemical Semantics for Activity Cliffs‐Aware Molecular Property Prediction
papers.abstract: Accurately predicting physicochemical and biological properties of molecules is vital for modern drug discovery, yet existing deep learning models struggle to replicate the multi-level reasoning of chemists.
