Our work represents the first attempt to explain GNNs via identifying subgraphs explicitly and directly. Experimental results show that our SubgraphX achieves significantly improved explanations, while keeping computations at a reasonable level.

papers.title: Atomic-level interpretable multimodal graph neural network for predicting carbon dioxide adsorption in metal-organic frameworks
papers.research_question: How can we predict CO₂ adsorption in metal-organic frameworks using an interpretable multimodal graph neural network?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MMAGNN, a multimodal graph neural network that integrates graph and 3D point cloud data to predict CO₂ adsorption in MOFs with atomic-level interpretability via attention weights.
papers.conclusion: MMAGNN utilizes spatial features and atomic interactions to accurately predict CO₂ adsorption and identify adsorption sites, enhancing prediction accuracy and aiding in MOF design for carbon capture.
papers.key_findings:
MMAGNN achieves higher prediction accuracy than CGCNN and ALIGNN across various pressures, with improvements in MAE, RMSE, and R².
The multimodal design reduces redundant information and feature interference, improving prediction accuracy and stability.
The attention-based interpreter identifies atoms with high attention scores that coincide with CO₂ adsorption sites, validating model interpretability.
MMAGNN effectively captures both local atomic interactions and global pore structure features.
The model generalizes well to modified MOFs like UiO-66-NH₂, correctly shifting attention to new adsorption sites.
papers.abstract: Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are porous crystalline materials with strong potential for CO₂ capture because their structures and chemistries are highly tunable. However, their vast compositional and structural search space hampers efficient prediction of adsorption performance. Here we introduce MMAGNN, a multimodal MOF adsorption graph neural network that integrates graph representations and three-dimensional atomic coordinates. MMAGNN employs graph neural networks (GNNs) with attention mechanisms to extract and fuse molecular and spatial features, and incorporates a Transformer-based interpreter to quantify the contribution of individual atoms to adsorption. We find that the multimodal design reduces redundant information and feature interference, improving prediction accuracy and stability. Validation against adsorption density distributions confirms that MMAGNN learns interatomic interactions and pore-structure information and accurately predicts CO₂ adsorption sites. This interpretable framework provides high-throughput screening and rational design of high-performance MOFs for carbon-capture applications. Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are porous crystalline materials with tunable chemistry and pores, making them promising for CO₂ capture. This work introduces the Multimodal MOF Adsorption Graph Neural Network, fusing atomic graphs and 3D point clouds to predict CO₂ adsorption and produce atom-level attention maps highlighting adsorption sites.

papers.title: Understanding the patterns that neural networks learn from chemical spectra
papers.research_question: How does a neural network learn to classify infrared spectra of small organic molecules by functional groups, and what specific patterns (both intuitive and non-intuitive) does it use for classification?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a simpler 1D CNN that achieves state-of-the-art performance for functional group classification in infrared spectra and introduces a two-step explainability approach, revealing the network uses both characteristic group frequencies and non-intuitive patterns like tails and overtones.
papers.conclusion: The simplified CNN model is effective for spectral classification, and the explainability approach reveals the network uses both intuitive and non-intuitive spectral patterns, which can help assess generalization and guide future model design incorporating physics-based knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
The 1D CNN achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art models while being significantly less complex.
The model consistently attends to the same spectral regions across different random initializations, indicating robust feature learning.
The network learns to use characteristic group frequencies (peaks) for classification, aligning with expert knowledge.
The network also uses non-intuitive patterns such as tails and anharmonic vibrations (overtones and combination bands) to improve classification certainty.
For some functional groups (e.g., nitriles), class imbalance and the presence of only one characteristic band lead to poor classification accuracy, highlighting dataset limitations.
papers.limitation:
Class imbalance leads to poor classification accuracy for rare functional groups like nitriles.
The network sometimes uses non-characteristic vibrations (e.g., C-H wags for halides) which may not generalize to new datasets.
future_direction: Incorporate physics-based intuition into model design, e.g., using IR tables to initialize parameters or filters that optimally recognize peaks.
Transfer understanding from pretrained models to new datasets (potentially from different spectral regions).
papers.abstract: We train a convolutional neural network to classify functional groups from infrared spectra. With explainability methods, we show the model uses the presence and absence of peaks, at fundamental and anharmonic frequencies for accurate classification.

papers.title: Structure and Representation in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we find modular structure in neural networks, and does this structure have functional relevance in terms of local specialization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that trained neural networks exhibit clusterability (modular structure) and that clustering can find locally specialized groups of neurons. It also shows that interpretability tools reveal shortcomings in reward models' feature representation and generalization.
papers.conclusion: The dissertation advances understanding of neural network structure and representation, and highlights the need for better interpretability tools to understand generalization behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Trained neural networks are more clusterable than randomly initialized networks.
Clustering finds groups of neurons that are important and coherent, indicating local specialization.
Interpretability tools applied to reward models show they do not adequately represent relevant features and mispredict reward out of distribution.
These tools do not reveal a clear picture of the computation the networks are performing.
There is a need for better interpretability tools to understand generalization behavior.
papers.limitation: Interpretability tools do not reveal a clear picture of what computation the networks are performing.
future_direction: Applying the methods to larger networks.
Studying the dynamics of clusterability during training.
Developing better interpretability tools for understanding generalization.
papers.abstract: Since neural networks have become dominant within the field of artificial intelligence, a sub-field of research has emerged attempting to understand their inner workings. One standard method within this sub-field has been to primarily understand neural networks as representing human-comprehensible features. Another possibility that has been less explored is to understand them as multi-step computer programs. A seeming prerequisite for this is some form of modularity: for different parts of the network to operate independently enough to be understood in isolation, and to implement distinct interpretable sub-routines.To find modular structure inside neural networks, we initially use the tools of graphical clustering. A network is clusterable in this sense if it can be divided into groups of neurons with strong internal connectivity but weak external connectivity. We find that a trained neural network is typically more clusterable than randomly initialized networks, and often clusterable relative to random networks with the same distribution of weights as the trained network. We investigate factors that promote clusterability, and also develop novel methods targeted at that end.For modularity to be valuable for understanding neural networks, it needs to have some sort of functional relevance.The type of functional relevance we target is local specialization of functionality. A neural network is locally specialized to the extent that parts of its computational graph can be abstractly represented as performing some comprehensible sub-task relevant to the overall task. We propose two proxies for local specialization: importance, which reflects how valuable sets of neurons are to network performance; and coherence, which reflects how consistently their neurons associate with features of the inputs. We then operationalize these proxies using techniques conventionally used to interpret individual neurons, applying them instead to groups of neurons produced by graph clustering algorithms. Our results show that clustering succeeds at finding groups of neurons that are important and coherent, although not all groups of neurons found are so.We conclude with a case study of using more standard interpretability tools, designed to understand the features being represented by directions in activation space, applying them to the analysis of neural networks trained on the reward function of the game CoinRun. Despite our networks achieving a low test loss, the application of interpretability tools shows that networks do not adequately represent relevant features and badly mispredict reward out of distribution. That said, these tools do not reveal a clear picture of what computation the networks are in fact performing. This not only illustrates the need for better interpretability tools to understand generalization behaviour, but motivates it: if we take these networks as models of 'motivation systems' of policies trained by reinforcement learning, the conclusion is that such networks may competently pursue the wrong objectives when deployed in richer environments, indicating a need for interpretability techniques to shed light on generalization behaviour.

papers.title: Geometric Properties and Graph-Based Optimization of Neural Networks: Addressing Non-Linearity, Dimensionality, and Scalability
papers.research_question: How do geometric properties and graph structures of neural networks affect their performance and scalability?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes geometric and graph-based optimization methods, including hierarchical gap encoding, to improve neural network performance in handling non-linearity, dimensionality, and scalability.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that geometric and graph-based optimization techniques effectively address key challenges in neural networks, leading to more efficient and scalable models.
papers.key_findings:
Advanced activation functions like polynomial neurons and radial basis functions (RBFs) improve classification accuracy and decision boundary complexity for non-linear datasets.
Pruning can reduce network complexity while maintaining accuracy, as demonstrated on MNIST.
Hierarchical gap encoding significantly reduces memory usage and improves computational efficiency for large-scale graphs compared to adjacency matrices.
Dimensionality reduction techniques like PCA and autoencoders can reduce training time but may compromise accuracy if not properly configured.
The proposed methods collectively enhance neural network efficiency and scalability across synthetic and real-world datasets.
papers.limitation: Dimensionality reduction techniques like PCA and autoencoders underperformed in some experiments, indicating potential issues with feature retention or suboptimal hyperparameters.
future_direction: Explore hybrid models combining dimensionality reduction, advanced activation functions, and graph-based optimizations.
Investigate the impact of these techniques on other architectures like transformers or recurrent networks.
Optimize hierarchical gap encoding for dynamic graphs with advanced partitioning and encoding strategies.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models are often considered black boxes due to their complex hierarchical transformations. Identifying suitable architectures is crucial for maximizing predictive performance with limited data. Understanding the geometric properties of neural networks involves analyzing their structure, activation functions, and the transformations they perform in high-dimensional space. These properties influence learning, representation, and decision-making. This research explores neural networks through geometric metrics and graph structures, building upon foundational work in arXiv:2007.06559. It addresses the limited understanding of geometric structures governing neural networks, particularly the data manifolds they operate on, which impact classification, optimization, and representation. We identify three key challenges: (1) overcoming linear separability limitations, (2) managing the dimensionality-complexity trade-off, and (3) improving scalability through graph representations. To address these, we propose leveraging non-linear activation functions, optimizing network complexity via pruning and transfer learning, and developing efficient graph-based models. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of neural network geometry, supporting the development of more robust, scalable, and interpretable models.

papers.title: Concept-Based Mechanistic Interpretability Using Structured Knowledge Graphs
papers.research_question: How can concept-based interpretability methods be extended to provide a global, mechanistic understanding of how semantic concepts emerge, interact, and propagate through a model's internal components?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces BAGEL, a scalable framework and interactive tool for global, concept-based mechanistic interpretability that models how semantic concepts are represented and interact across a model's internal layers, enabling systematic analysis of bias alignment between datasets and models.
papers.conclusion: BAGEL offers a global perspective for dissecting concept-based biases in DNNs, bridging the gap between dataset-driven and model-learned concept representations to provide deeper insight into model decision-making processes.
papers.key_findings:
BAGEL provides a global view of concept distributions and their alignment with external semantic priors, bridging dataset-driven and model-learned concept representations.
Early network layers tend to mix concepts with limited class relevance, while deeper layers filter and emphasize concepts more aligned with the input class.
The method can identify spurious correlations and model-specific biases not present in the dataset, visualized via an interactive knowledge graph.
BAGEL demonstrates strong and consistent performance in detecting dataset biases compared to baseline methods like TCAV and SAE.
Rudimentary concepts (e.g., materials, textures) manifest in initial layers, while deeper layers show higher probabilities for more complex concepts (e.g., object parts).
papers.limitation: The logistic regression classifiers used for concept prediction assume a linear relation between features and concepts, which may limit the ability to capture more complex patterns.
future_direction: Extending BAGEL to multimodal architectures.
Refining concept definitions through automated discovery.
papers.abstract: While concept-based interpretability methods have traditionally focused on local explanations of neural network predictions, we propose a novel framework and interactive tool that extends these methods into the domain of mechanistic interpretability. Our approach enables a global dissection of model behavior by analyzing how high-level semantic attributes (referred to as concepts) emerge, interact, and propagate through internal model components. Unlike prior work that isolates individual neurons or predictions, our framework systematically quantifies how semantic concepts are represented across layers, revealing latent circuits and information flow that underlie model decision-making. A key innovation is our visualization platform that we named BAGEL (for Bias Analysis with a Graph for global Explanation Layers), which presents these insights in a structured knowledge graph, allowing users to explore concept-class relationships, identify spurious correlations, and enhance model trustworthiness. Our framework is model-agnostic, scalable, and contributes to a deeper understanding of how deep learning models generalize (or fail to) in the presence of dataset biases. The demonstration is available at https://knowledge-graph-ui-4a7cb5.gitlab.io/.

papers.title: SALSA: Semantically-Aware Latent Space Autoencoder
papers.research_question: How can we learn semantically meaningful latent representations for molecules that respect structural similarities, using SMILES-based autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SALSA, a transformer-autoencoder with a contrastive loss, to learn molecular representations that capture graph-to-graph similarities, resulting in a semantically organized latent space.
papers.conclusion: SALSA learns semantically meaningful latent representations for molecules that respect structural similarities, with improved interpolation and property awareness, and can be applied to other domains with user-defined semantics.
papers.key_findings:
SALSA achieves higher correlation between graph edit distance and Euclidean distance in latent space compared to a naive autoencoder.
SALSA generates more semantically reasonable interpolations between molecules, indicating better semantic continuity.
SALSA implicitly encodes physicochemical properties better than baselines, showing improved property awareness.
The contrastive loss improves structural awareness, while the reconstruction loss acts as a regularizer to prevent degenerative mappings.
SALSA's performance degrades only at very low latent dimensions (e.g., 2 or 4), suggesting robustness down to 8 dimensions.
papers.limitation: The correlation between graph edit distance and Euclidean distance may not hold for molecules that are substantially different
papers.abstract: In deep learning for drug discovery, chemical data are often represented as simplified molecular-input line-entry system (SMILES) sequences which allow for straightforward implementation of natural language processing methodologies, one being the sequence-to-sequence autoencoder. However, we observe that training an autoencoder solely on SMILES is insufficient to learn molecular representations that are semantically meaningful, where semantics are defined by the structural (graph-to-graph) similarities between molecules. We demonstrate by example that autoencoders may map structurally similar molecules to distant codes, resulting in an incoherent latent space that does not respect the structural similarities between molecules. To address this shortcoming we propose Semantically-Aware Latent Space Autoencoder (SALSA), a transformer-autoencoder modified with a contrastive task, tailored specifically to learn graph-to-graph similarity between molecules. Formally, the contrastive objective is to map structurally similar molecules (separated by a single graph edit) to nearby codes in the latent space. To accomplish this, we generate a novel dataset comprised of sets of structurally similar molecules and opt for a supervised contrastive loss that is able to incorporate full sets of positive samples. We compare SALSA to its ablated counterparts, and show empirically that the composed training objective (reconstruction and contrastive task) leads to a higher quality latent space that is more 1) structurally-aware, 2) semantically continuous, and 3) property-aware.

papers.title: Attention over learned object embeddings enables complex visual\n reasoning
papers.research_question: Can a neural-network-based approach combining learned object-centric representations, self-attention, and self-supervised dynamics learning achieve state-of-the-art performance on complex visual reasoning tasks without task-specific modular components?
papers.core_contribution: The Aloe model, which combines learned object-centric representations, self-attention, and self-supervised dynamics learning, achieves state-of-the-art performance on three visual reasoning tasks without task-specific modular components, demonstrating that flexibility and performance need not be traded off.
papers.conclusion: The success of Aloe suggests that with the right soft biases and learning objectives—object-centric representations, self-attention, and self-supervised dynamics learning—neural networks can achieve strong performance on spatiotemporal reasoning tasks without resorting to task-specific modular components.
papers.key_findings:
Aloe outperforms previous state-of-the-art models on CLEVRER, CATER, and ACRE across various question and reasoning types.
The combination of object-level discretization, global self-attention, and self-supervised learning is crucial for strong performance; ablations of any component lead to significant drops.
Aloe is data-efficient, matching previous SOTA performance on CLEVRER with only 50-60% of the training data.
The model generalizes across three distinct visual reasoning tasks (CLEVRER, CATER, ACRE) without any architectural modifications.
Qualitative analysis of attention weights shows the model aligns objects across time and focuses on relevant objects and words for answering questions.
papers.limitation:
Applied only to synthetic datasets due to a lack of real-world datasets testing higher-order spatiotemporal reasoning.
The domains used may not fully evaluate the intended capacities due to hidden biases or other factors.
May perpetuate biases found in training data and could invite problematic applications involving automated assignment of blame.
future_direction: Applying the approach to real-world datasets, such as the upcoming Traffic QA.
Investigating other self-supervised losses and masking schemes to further improve dynamics learning.
Designing and developing more challenging tasks that better approximate human-level visual, spatiotemporal, and causal reasoning.
papers.abstract:
Neural networks have achieved success in a wide array of perceptual tasks but
often fail at tasks involving both perception and higher-level reasoning. On
these more challenging tasks, bespoke approaches (such as modular symbolic
components, independent dynamics models or semantic parsers) targeted towards
that specific type of task have typically performed better. The downside to
these targeted approaches, however, is that they can be more brittle than
general-purpose neural networks, requiring significant modification or even
redesign according to the particular task at hand. Here, we propose a more
general neural-network-based approach to dynamic visual reasoning problems that
obtains state-of-the-art performance on three different domains, in each case
outperforming bespoke modular approaches tailored specifically to the task. Our
method relies on learned object-centric representations, self-attention and
self-supervised dynamics learning, and all three elements together are required
for strong performance to emerge. The success of this combination suggests that
there may be no need to trade off flexibility for performance on problems
involving spatio-temporal or causal-style reasoning. With the right soft biases
and learning objectives in a neural network we may be able to attain the best
of both worlds.

papers.title: InterPLM: Discovering Interpretable Features in Protein Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: What do protein language models (PLMs) learn internally, and how can we extract and analyze interpretable features from their representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a systematic framework using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to extract and analyze interpretable features from protein language models, revealing features that correlate with known biological concepts and enabling applications like filling missing annotations and steering sequence generation.
papers.conclusion: Protein language models encode rich, interpretable representations of protein biology, and the SAE-based framework successfully extracts these features, recovering both known biology and potentially new protein motifs.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features capture significantly more biological annotations (up to 2,548 features per layer) than individual neurons in ESM-2 (up to 46 per layer).
Features cluster based on shared functional and structural roles, revealing hierarchical relationships and subtle specializations.
Large language models (Claude-3.5 Sonnet) can generate meaningful descriptions of SAE features, with high correlation between predicted and actual activation patterns.
Feature activation patterns can identify missing annotations in protein databases and suggest novel biological motifs.
Targeted steering of specific feature activations can influence the model's sequence predictions in interpretable ways.
papers.limitation:
Scaling this approach to structure-prediction models like ESMFold or AlphaFold is a crucial next step.
Steering experiments are currently limited to simple contexts (e.g., periodic glycine patterns); extending steering to more complex biological concepts remains challenging.
The analysis focuses only on representations of unmasked amino acids, leaving open questions about masked token embeddings and the CLS token.
future_direction: Scaling the approach to structure-prediction models like ESMFold or AlphaFold.
Improving feature interpretability through advances in SAE training and additional evaluation metrics.
Mapping how features combine into interpretable circuits for specific capabilities like 3D contact prediction.
papers.abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) have demonstrated remarkable success in protein modeling and design, yet their internal mechanisms for predicting structure and function remain poorly understood. Here we present a systematic approach to extract and analyze interpretable features from PLMs using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). By training SAEs on embeddings from the PLM ESM-2, we identify up to 2,548 human-interpretable latent features per layer that strongly correlate with up to 143 known biological concepts such as binding sites, structural motifs, and functional domains. In contrast, examining individual neurons in ESM-2 reveals up to 46 neurons per layer with clear conceptual alignment across 15 known concepts, suggesting that PLMs represent most concepts in superposition. Beyond capturing known annotations, we show that ESM-2 learns coherent concepts that do not map onto existing annotations and propose a pipeline using language models to automatically interpret novel latent features learned by the SAEs. As practical applications, we demonstrate how these latent features can fill in missing annotations in protein databases and enable targeted steering of protein sequence generation. Our results demonstrate that PLMs encode rich, interpretable representations of protein biology and we propose a systematic framework to extract and analyze these latent features. In the process, we recover both known biology and potentially new protein motifs. As community resources, we introduce InterPLM (interPLM.ai), an interactive visualization platform for exploring and analyzing learned PLM features, and release code for training and analysis at github.com/ElanaPearl/interPLM.

papers.title: The Next Five Hurdles What is a Linear Representation? What is a Multidimensional Feature? The Dark Matter of Neural Networks? Attention Pivot Tables Measuring feature sensitivity using dataset filtering
papers.research_question: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement?
papers.core_contribution: This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering.
papers.conclusion: The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.
papers.key_findings:
Current sparse autoencoder methods may miss many rare features, suggesting a 'dark matter' of neural networks that is difficult to observe.
Linear representations can be mathematically linear even with multidimensional features, requiring a revised definition.
Attention pivot tables reveal interpretable skip-trigrams in one-layer transformers, but their clarity depends on training details and dataset.
Feature sensitivity measured via Claude-filtered datasets shows that individual features often have low sensitivity, and concepts are represented by multiple cooperating features.
Different versions of Claude agree well with each other and with human judgments when rating concept relevance in text snippets.
papers.limitation:
Dictionary learning may be unable to resolve extremely rare features, limiting comprehensiveness.
Features identified by sparse autoencoders often have imperfect sensitivity and specificity, with concepts distributed across multiple features.
Attention pivot table results are sensitive to training hyperparameters and dataset composition, making interpretation unreliable under suboptimal conditions.
future_direction: Developing more efficient dictionary learning algorithms to capture rare features.
Automating the discovery of complementary features that collectively represent concepts.
Further investigation into attention superposition and cross-layer superposition.
papers.abstract: What are the major hurdles facing mechanistic interpretability, and how can we improve feature analysis and measurement? This blog post outlines five key hurdles in mechanistic interpretability, refines the concept of linear representations to include multidimensional features, introduces the idea of 'dark matter' features, provides practical guidance for using attention pivot tables, and demonstrates a method to measure feature sensitivity using LLM-assisted dataset filtering. The authors are optimistic about progress in mechanistic interpretability despite challenges, and highlight the need for further research into feature cooperation and improved analysis methods.

papers.title: DeepFRI Demystified: Interpretability vs. Accuracy in AI Protein Function Prediction
papers.research_question: How interpretable and robust is the DeepFRI model for protein function prediction, and how do different explainability methods compare in highlighting influential residues?
papers.core_contribution: The study reveals that DeepFRI's predictions prioritize conserved structural motifs over functional residues, and different explainability methods offer varying levels of granularity, highlighting trade-offs between accuracy and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: DeepFRI has strengths in conserved domains but limitations in complex proteins, and interpretability methods must be chosen carefully to balance robustness and precision for biological insights.
papers.key_findings:
DeepFRI's predictions often prioritize structural motifs like beta sheets over functional residues, leading to potential misinterpretations.
GradCAM provides broad heatmaps with low sparsity, Excitation Backpropagation offers binary masks with high sparsity, and PGExplainer gives precise per-residue scores.
The model is robust to mutations, requiring over 200 mutations in some cases to cause misclassification, but this may overlook biologically significant changes.
Sparsity analysis shows that explainability methods vary significantly, with GradCAM being the least sparse and Excitation Backpropagation the most sparse.
Using an ensemble of explainability methods can highlight high-confidence residues and areas of epistemic uncertainty.
papers.limitation:
DeepFRI prioritizes structural motifs over functional residues, potentially leading to inaccurate interpretations of protein function.
The model's robustness to mutations may cause it to overlook biologically significant changes unless a large fraction of the structure is disrupted.
DeepFRI's message-passing can overlook long-range or allosteric effects in complex regulatory proteins.
future_direction: Guide experimental validation through targeted mutagenesis based on explainability results.
Fuse GCN topology with per-residue embeddings from protein language models for improved sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Machine learning technologies for protein function prediction are black box models. Despite their potential to identify key drug targets with high accuracy and accelerate therapy development, the adoption of these methods depends on verifying their findings. This study evaluates DeepFRI, a leading Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) based tool, using advanced explainability techniques (GradCAM, Excitation Backpropagation, and PGExplainer) and adversarial robustness tests. Our findings reveal that the model's predictions often prioritize conserved motifs over truly deterministic residues, complicating the identification of functional sites. Quantitative analyses show that explainability methods differ significantly in granularity, with GradCAM providing broad relevance and PGExplainer pinpointing specific active sites. These results highlight tradeoffs between accuracy and interpretability, suggesting areas for improvement in DeepFRI's architecture to enhance its trustworthiness in drug discovery and regulatory settings.

papers.title: MolEdit: Knowledge Editing for Multimodal Molecule Language Models
papers.research_question: How to edit knowledge in multimodal molecule language models (MoLMs) to correct inaccuracies while preserving unrelated knowledge, specifically for molecule-to-caption and caption-to-molecule generation tasks.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MolEdit, a framework for editing multimodal molecule language models, and MEBench, a benchmark for evaluating such editing, addressing molecule-specific challenges of multifaceted expertise and cross-molecule interdependence.
papers.conclusion: MolEdit provides an effective framework for editing multimodal molecule language models, enabling precise knowledge updates while preserving unrelated information, and MEBench offers a comprehensive evaluation benchmark, charting a path toward safer, continuously updatable scientific foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
MolEdit outperforms fine-tuning, gradient-based (MEND), and memory-based (GRACE) baselines across Reliability, Locality, and Generality metrics on both MoMu and MolFM backbones.
MolEdit achieves up to 18.8% higher Reliability and 12.0% better Locality than state-of-the-art editing baselines.
Editing molecule generation is more challenging than editing caption generation, and performance is generally better on MoMu than on MolFM.
The Multi-Expert Knowledge Adapter (MEKA) effectively routes different facets of molecular knowledge to specialized experts, and the Expertise-Aware Editing Switcher (EAES) accurately activates edits only for relevant inputs.
Ablation studies confirm the contribution of each component (MEKA and EAES) to MolEdit's overall performance.
papers.limitation:
Editing molecular SMILES strings is inherently more complex and abstract than editing captions, lacking explicit semantic structure.
Potential misuse of editing to amplify unsafe molecular knowledge and inadvertent propagation of dataset biases.
future_direction: Future work on editing MoLMs.
papers.abstract: Understanding and continuously refining multimodal molecular knowledge is crucial for advancing biomedicine, chemistry, and materials science. Molecule language models (MoLMs) have become powerful tools in these domains, integrating structural representations (e.g., SMILES strings, molecular graphs) with rich contextual descriptions (e.g., physicochemical properties). However, MoLMs can encode and propagate inaccuracies due to outdated web-mined training corpora or malicious manipulation, jeopardizing downstream discovery pipelines. While knowledge editing has been explored for general-domain AI, its application to MoLMs remains uncharted, presenting unique challenges due to the multifaceted and interdependent nature of molecular knowledge. In this paper, we take the first step toward MoLM editing for two critical tasks: molecule-to-caption generation and caption-to-molecule generation. To address molecule-specific challenges, we propose MolEdit, a powerful framework that enables targeted modifications while preserving unrelated molecular knowledge. MolEdit combines a Multi-Expert Knowledge Adapter that routes edits to specialized experts for different molecular facets with an Expertise-Aware Editing Switcher that activates the adapters only when input closely matches the stored edits across all expertise, minimizing interference with unrelated knowledge. To systematically evaluate editing performance, we introduce MEBench, a comprehensive benchmark assessing multiple dimensions, including Reliability (accuracy of the editing), Locality (preservation of irrelevant knowledge), and Generality (robustness to reformed queries). Across extensive experiments on two popular MoLM backbones, MolEdit delivers up to 18.8% higher Reliability and 12.0% better Locality than baselines while maintaining efficiency. The code is available at: https://github.com/LzyFischer/MolEdit.

papers.title: Interpretable Neuron Structuring with Graph Spectral Regularization
papers.research_question: How can we make hidden layers of neural networks more interpretable by enforcing graph structure on neuron activations without significantly impacting performance on the primary task?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Graph Spectral Regularization, a method to enforce graph structure on neuron activations in hidden layers to improve interpretability, and a procedure to learn the graph structure from data.
papers.conclusion: Graph Spectral Regularization is a biologically inspired method that can reveal important structure in data and make neural networks more interpretable, with applicability to real-world biological datasets.
papers.key_findings:
GSR can create interpretable receptive fields in dense networks, localizing activations for similar inputs to specific regions of a graph.
GSR enforces consistent feature ordering across capsules in capsule networks, making the encoding more ordered and interpretable.
GSR can learn graph structures that reflect cluster or trajectory patterns in biological data, revealing hierarchical and developmental structures.
The computational cost of GSR is similar to other regularization methods like L1 and L2, adding minimal overhead.
GSR does not require an information bottleneck and can be applied to wide layers while maintaining interpretability.
papers.limitation:
GSR adds some computational overhead compared to elementwise activation penalties, though the cost is similar to L1 and L2 regularization.
GSR does not increase the representation power of the model; it is a regularization method for interpretability.
papers.abstract: While neural networks are powerful approximators used to classify or embed data into lower dimensional spaces, they are often regarded as black boxes with uninterpretable features. Here we propose Graph Spectral Regularization for making hidden layers more interpretable without significantly impacting performance on the primary task. Taking inspiration from spatial organization and localization of neuron activations in biological networks, we use a graph Laplacian penalty to structure the activations within a layer. This penalty encourages activations to be smooth either on a predetermined graph or on a feature-space graph learned from the data via co-activations of a hidden layer of the neural network. We show numerous uses for this additional structure including cluster indication and visualization in biological and image data sets.

papers.title: Graph-Aware Isomorphic Attention for Adaptive Dynamics in Transformers
papers.research_question: How can graph-aware relational reasoning be integrated into Transformer attention mechanisms to improve the model's ability to capture complex dependencies and generalize across tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces graph-aware attention mechanisms (GIN-Attention and Sparse-GIN-Attention) that integrate graph neural network principles into Transformers, improving relational reasoning and generalization.
papers.conclusion: Integrating graph-based reasoning into Transformers improves their performance and generalization, offering a new perspective on attention mechanisms and paving the way for more interpretable and adaptable architectures.
papers.key_findings:
GIN-Attention outperforms standard attention in training efficiency and validation performance, with reduced overfitting.
Sparse-GIN fine-tuning achieves lower validation perplexity compared to LoRA and other configurations.
The trainable sharpening parameter in GIN-Attention shows a strategic distribution across layers.
PNA-Attention did not improve upon the standard attention in the experiments conducted.
The proposed methods bridge graph theory and Transformer architectures, revealing latent graph-like structures in attention.
future_direction: Exploring the use of external adjacency matrices added to attention mechanisms.
Developing trainable methods to construct adjacency matrices that could replace or complement attention.
Exploring natural transformations for designing more robust and adaptive attention mechanisms.
papers.abstract: We present an approach to modifying Transformer architectures by integrating graph-aware relational reasoning into the attention mechanism, merging concepts from graph neural networks and language modeling. Building on the inherent connection between attention and graph theory, we reformulate the Transformer's attention mechanism as a graph operation and propose Graph-Aware Isomorphic Attention. This method leverages advanced graph modeling strategies, including Graph Isomorphism Networks (GIN) and Principal Neighborhood Aggregation (PNA), to enrich the representation of relational structures. Our approach captures complex dependencies and generalizes across tasks, as evidenced by a reduced generalization gap and improved learning performance. Additionally, we expand the concept of graph-aware attention to introduce Sparse GIN-Attention, a fine-tuning approach that employs sparse GINs. By interpreting attention matrices as sparse adjacency graphs, this technique enhances the adaptability of pre-trained foundational models with minimal computational overhead, endowing them with graph-aware capabilities. Sparse GIN-Attention fine-tuning achieves improved training dynamics and better generalization compared to alternative methods like low-rank adaption (LoRA). We discuss latent graph-like structures within traditional attention mechanisms, offering a new lens through which Transformers can be understood. By evolving Transformers as hierarchical GIN models for relational reasoning. This perspective suggests profound implications for foundational model development, enabling the design of architectures that dynamically adapt to both local and global dependencies. Applications in bioinformatics, materials science, language modeling, and beyond could benefit from this synthesis of relational and sequential data modeling, setting the stage for interpretable and generalizable modeling strategies.

papers.title: A Survey on Explainability of Graph Neural Networks
papers.core_contribution: This survey provides a comprehensive overview of explainability techniques for Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), introducing a novel taxonomy to categorize these methods and discussing their strengths, limitations, and applications.
papers.conclusion: The survey provides a comprehensive overview of explainability methods for GNNs, categorizing them into a novel taxonomy and discussing their strengths, limitations, and applications, while also identifying gaps and future directions for research in interpretable graph-based machine learning.
papers.key_findings:
The survey categorizes explainability methods for GNNs into factual and counterfactual, and further into subcategories based on their objective and methodology.
It discusses the strengths and limitations of each category of explainability methods, including self-interpretable and post-hoc approaches.
The survey highlights key evaluation metrics and datasets commonly used to assess the explainability of GNNs.
It identifies gaps in the existing literature, such as the need for more work on temporal GNNs and causality-based explainers.
The survey emphasizes the importance of human-centered evaluations for real-world applications of explainable GNNs.
future_direction: More work on explainability of temporal GNNs.
Development of causality-based explainers.
Human-centered evaluations for real-world applications.
papers.abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are powerful graph-based deep-learning models that have gained significant attention and demonstrated remarkable performance in various domains, including natural language processing, drug discovery, and recommendation systems. However, combining feature information and combinatorial graph structures has led to complex non-linear GNN models. Consequently, this has increased the challenges of understanding the workings of GNNs and the underlying reasons behind their predictions. To address this, numerous explainability methods have been proposed to shed light on the inner mechanism of the GNNs. Explainable GNNs improve their security and enhance trust in their recommendations. This survey aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the existing explainability techniques for GNNs. We create a novel taxonomy and hierarchy to categorize these methods based on their objective and methodology. We also discuss the strengths, limitations, and application scenarios of each category. Furthermore, we highlight the key evaluation metrics and datasets commonly used to assess the explainability of GNNs. This survey aims to assist researchers and practitioners in understanding the existing landscape of explainability methods, identifying gaps, and fostering further advancements in interpretable graph-based machine learning.

papers.title: The Local Interaction Basis: Identifying Computationally-Relevant and Sparsely Interacting Features in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Can the Local Interaction Basis (LIB) method find interpretable and sparsely-interacting features in neural networks, particularly in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Local Interaction Basis (LIB), a method to transform neural network activations into a basis of computationally-relevant and sparsely-interacting features, and shows it works on toy models but not on language models.
papers.conclusion: LIB is promising on toy models but does not achieve interpretable and sparsely-interacting features on language models, likely due to the assumption of a linear non-overcomplete basis.
papers.key_findings:
LIB identifies more computationally-relevant features than PCA in modular addition and CIFAR-10 models.
LIB features interact more sparsely than PCA features in CIFAR-10 and some layers of language models.
LIB does not produce more interpretable features than PCA in language models.
Integrated gradient interaction graphs can aid circuit discovery in toy models.
LIB does not reveal modular structure in language models.
papers.limitation: LIB does not yield substantial improvements in interpretability or interaction sparsity when applied to language models.
future_direction: Generalizing LIB to overcomplete bases to handle features in superposition.
Exploring other ways to average attributions over the dataset.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand the behavior of neural networks by reverse-engineering their internal computations. However, current methods struggle to find clear interpretations of neural network activations because a decomposition of activations into computational features is missing. Individual neurons or model components do not cleanly correspond to distinct features or functions. We present a novel interpretability method that aims to overcome this limitation by transforming the activations of the network into a new basis - the Local Interaction Basis (LIB). LIB aims to identify computational features by removing irrelevant activations and interactions. Our method drops irrelevant activation directions and aligns the basis with the singular vectors of the Jacobian matrix between adjacent layers. It also scales features based on their importance for downstream computation, producing an interaction graph that shows all computationally-relevant features and interactions in a model. We evaluate the effectiveness of LIB on modular addition and CIFAR-10 models, finding that it identifies more computationally-relevant features that interact more sparsely, compared to principal component analysis. However, LIB does not yield substantial improvements in interpretability or interaction sparsity when applied to language models. We conclude that LIB is a promising theory-driven approach for analyzing neural networks, but in its current form is not applicable to large language models.

papers.title: Everybody Needs a Little HELP: Explaining Graphs via Hierarchical Concepts
papers.research_question: How can we explain graph neural networks by discovering hierarchical concepts that show how concepts from different layers compose to new ones in later steps?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces HELP, a hierarchical explainable graph pooling method that reveals how concepts from different GNN layers compose, and proposes concept conformity, a novel metric to measure noise in discovered concepts.
papers.conclusion: HELP provides hierarchical explanations for GNNs and represents a first step towards understanding the complex interplay of concepts on different levels.
papers.key_findings:
HELP performs on-par with standard GCNs and popular pooling methods in terms of accuracy.
HELP yields explanations that are aligned with expert knowledge in chemistry and social network domains.
The discovered concepts are significantly easier to fully understand than those from previous work, as measured by concept conformity.
HELP is more than 1-WL expressive, enabling it to solve tasks that message-passing GNNs cannot.
HELP is the first non-spectral, end-to-end-learnable hierarchical graph pooling method that can learn to pool a variable number of arbitrary connected components.
papers.limitation: The method requires specifying the number of clusters (concepts) in advance as a hyperparameter.
papers.abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have led to major breakthroughs in a variety of domains such as drug discovery, social network analysis, and travel time estimation. However, they lack interpretability which hinders human trust and thereby deployment to settings with high-stakes decisions. A line of interpretable methods approach this by discovering a small set of relevant concepts as subgraphs in the last GNN layer that together explain the prediction. This can yield oversimplified explanations, failing to explain the interaction between GNN layers. To address this oversight, we provide HELP (Hierarchical Explainable Latent Pooling), a novel, inherently interpretable graph pooling approach that reveals how concepts from different GNN layers compose to new ones in later steps. HELP is more than 1-WL expressive and is the first non-spectral, end-to-end-learnable, hierarchical graph pooling method that can learn to pool a variable number of arbitrary connected components. We empirically demonstrate that it performs on-par with standard GCNs and popular pooling methods in terms of accuracy while yielding explanations that are aligned with expert knowledge in the domains of chemistry and social networks. In addition to a qualitative analysis, we employ concept completeness scores as well as concept conformity, a novel metric to measure the noise in discovered concepts, quantitatively verifying that the discovered concepts are significantly easier to fully understand than those from previous work. Our work represents a first step towards an understanding of graph neural networks that goes beyond a set of concepts from the final layer and instead explains the complex interplay of concepts on different levels.

papers.title: Challenges in Mechanistically Interpreting Model Representations
papers.research_question: What are the challenges in mechanistically interpreting model representations, and how do current mechanistic interpretability tools fall short in understanding complex behaviors like dishonesty?
papers.core_contribution: The paper formalizes the importance of studying feature and behavior representations in models, performs an exploratory study of dishonesty representations in Mistral-7B, and shows that current mechanistic interpretability tools are insufficient for understanding such representations, advocating for new frameworks.
papers.conclusion: Studying representations for features and behaviors is crucial for understanding models, but current mechanistic interpretability tooling is inadequate for answering key questions about representations, necessitating new frameworks.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations for dishonesty can be found and used to steer model behavior, but they are not simply boosting generically dishonest tokens.
Continual injections of the dishonesty direction are required for open-ended dishonest generation, not just at the first token.
Direct logit attribution shows that directional injections affect many components, with MLPs having a more direct effect than attention heads.
Activation patching reveals that many components are involved in the dishonesty behavior, making sparse circuit analysis difficult and less helpful.
Current mechanistic interpretability tooling (e.g., patching) is insufficient for understanding how representations are formed and how they affect long-term generation.
papers.limitation: Patching methods (activation and path patching) do not rigorously prove that circuits found are indeed reserved to that task, and patching only one component at a time might not isolate components if multiple perform the same job.
future_direction: Study how different components interact with representations and alter them.
Explore the training dynamics of a model and study the emergence of representations as a model trains.
Develop new frameworks to think about and study representations.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability (MI) aims to understand AI models by reverse-engineering the exact algorithms neural networks learn. Most works in MI so far have studied behaviors and capabilities that are trivial and token-aligned. However, most capabilities important for safety and trust are not that trivial, which advocates for the study of hidden representations inside these networks as the unit of analysis. We formalize representations for features and behaviors, highlight their importance and evaluation, and perform an exploratory study of dishonesty representations in `Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.1'. We justify that studying representations is an important and under-studied field, and highlight several challenges that arise while attempting to do so through currently established methods in MI, showing their insufficiency and advocating work on new frameworks for the same.

papers.title: Comparing the latent features of universal machine-learning interatomic potentials
papers.research_question: How do different universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) encode chemical information in their latent features, and how do these encodings compare across models, training datasets, and training strategies?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically analyzes the latent features of universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) using feature reconstruction errors, revealing that different models encode chemical information in distinct ways and that these differences can be quantified.
papers.conclusion: Predictive accuracy alone is insufficient to characterize atomistic ML models; feature reconstruction error metrics provide a principled foundation for more transparent, interpretable, and robust model design.
papers.key_findings:
uMLIPs encode the chemical space in significantly distinct ways, with substantial cross-model feature reconstruction errors.
When variants of the same model architecture are considered, trends become dependent on the dataset, target, and training protocol.
Fine-tuning of a uMLIP retains a strong pre-training bias in the latent features.
Atom-level features can be compressed into global structure-level features via concatenation of progressive cumulants, each adding significantly new information.
Backbone features contain more information than last-layer features and are more consistent across models.
papers.abstract: The past few years have seen the development of ``universal'' machine-learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) capable of approximating the ground-state potential energy surface across a wide range of chemical structures and compositions with reasonable accuracy. While these models differ in the architecture and the dataset used, they share the ability to compress a staggering amount of chemical information into descriptive latent features. Herein, we systematically analyze what the different uMLIPs have learned by quantitatively assessing the relative information content of their latent features with feature reconstruction errors, and observing how the trends are affected by the choice of training set and training protocol. We find that uMLIPs encode the chemical space in significantly distinct ways, with substantial cross-model feature reconstruction errors. When variants of the same model architecture are considered, trends become dependent on the dataset, target, and training protocol of choice. We also observe that fine-tuning of a uMLIP retains a strong pre-training bias in the latent features. Finally, we discuss how atom-level features, which are directly output by MLIPs, can be compressed into global structure-level features via concatenation of progressive cumulants, each adding significantly new information about the variability across the atomic environments within a given system.

papers.title: Using Degeneracy in the Loss Landscape for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How does degeneracy in neural network parameterizations obfuscate internal structure for mechanistic interpretability, and how can we remove these degeneracies to obtain more interpretable representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the concept of degeneracy in neural network parameterizations as an obstacle to interpretability, characterizes three sources of degeneracy, and proposes the Interaction Basis, a technique to obtain a representation invariant to these degeneracies, which may lead to sparser and more interpretable representations.
papers.conclusion: The paper argues that degeneracy in neural network parameterizations hinders interpretability, identifies sources of degeneracy, and proposes the Interaction Basis to remove degeneracies, potentially yielding sparser and more interpretable representations.
papers.key_findings:
Neural network parameters can be degenerate due to linear dependence between activations in a layer, linear dependence between gradients passed back to a layer, and ReLUs which fire on the same subset of datapoints.
Modular networks are likely to be more degenerate, and a metric for identifying modules is developed based on this argument.
The Interaction Basis is a tractable technique to obtain a representation invariant to degeneracies from linear dependence of activations or Jacobians.
Representations invariant to degeneracies are likely to have sparser interactions.
The effective parameter count, derived from the local learning coefficient, measures the number of computationally relevant parameters in the network.
papers.limitation: The derivation of the Interaction Basis relies on two simplifying assumptions of independence about the Hessian, which are strong assumptions.
future_direction: Investigate alternative techniques for finding a basis without the simplifying assumptions about the Hessian.
Determine how to choose an appropriate behavioral loss cutoff epsilon for finite data singular learning theory.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability aims to reverse engineer the algorithms implemented by neural networks by studying their weights and activations. An obstacle to reverse engineering neural networks is that many of the parameters inside a network are not involved in the computation being implemented by the network. These degenerate parameters may obfuscate internal structure. Singular learning theory teaches us that neural network parameterizations are biased towards being more degenerate, and parameterizations with more degeneracy are likely to generalize further. We identify 3 ways that network parameters can be degenerate: linear dependence between activations in a layer; linear dependence between gradients passed back to a layer; ReLUs which fire on the same subset of datapoints. We also present a heuristic argument that modular networks are likely to be more degenerate, and we develop a metric for identifying modules in a network that is based on this argument. We propose that if we can represent a neural network in a way that is invariant to reparameterizations that exploit the degeneracies, then this representation is likely to be more interpretable, and we provide some evidence that such a representation is likely to have sparser interactions. We introduce the Interaction Basis, a tractable technique to obtain a representation that is invariant to degeneracies from linear dependence of activations or Jacobians.

papers.title: MARGIN: Uncovering Deep Neural Networks Using Graph Signal Analysis
papers.research_question: Can a large family of interpretability tasks be addressed by a single central problem of identifying relative change in a model's prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MARGIN, a general framework for interpretability that uses graph signal analysis to identify influential nodes in a graph, addressing a wide range of post-hoc interpretability tasks.
papers.conclusion: MARGIN is a simple yet general framework for interpretability that can incorporate rich semantic information and is applicable to many tasks, as demonstrated through several case studies.
papers.key_findings:
MARGIN effectively selects prototypes and criticisms from a dataset, outperforming MMD-critic in unsupervised settings.
MARGIN generates sparse, interpretable saliency maps for image classification without accessing model internals, comparable to white-box methods like Grad-CAM.
MARGIN efficiently detects incorrectly labeled samples in training data, outperforming influence function-based approaches.
MARGIN improves the discriminative power of statistical measures for detecting adversarial examples by incorporating graph structure.
MARGIN-based sampling for active learning on graphs achieves higher label propagation accuracy compared to baseline methods, especially with small training sets.
papers.limitation:
Scalability may be an issue for massive datasets due to graph construction and memory requirements.
Graph construction (choice of neighborhood size) may affect results.
future_direction: Scaling MARGIN to massive datasets
Applying MARGIN to other interpretability tasks
papers.abstract: Interpretability has emerged as a crucial aspect of building trust in machine learning systems, aimed at providing insights into the working of complex neural networks that are otherwise opaque to a user. There are a plethora of existing solutions addressing various aspects of interpretability ranging from identifying prototypical samples in a dataset to explaining image predictions or explaining mis-classifications. While all of these diverse techniques address seemingly different aspects of interpretability, we hypothesize that a large family of interepretability tasks are variants of the same central problem which is identifying relative change in a model's prediction. This paper introduces MARGIN, a simple yet general approach to address a large set of interpretability tasks MARGIN exploits ideas rooted in graph signal analysis to determine influential nodes in a graph, which are defined as those nodes that maximally describe a function defined on the graph. By carefully defining task-specific graphs and functions, we demonstrate that MARGIN outperforms existing approaches in a number of disparate interpretability challenges.

papers.title: Interpretation of machine learning models using shapley values: application to compound potency and multi-target activity predictions
papers.research_question: How can Shapley values (SHAP) be used to interpret machine learning models, and how does the model-independent kernel SHAP compare to the exact tree SHAP for decision tree models? Additionally, how can SHAP be applied to interpret compound potency predictions and multi-target activity predictions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper evaluates and applies the SHAP methodology for interpreting machine learning models in chemoinformatics, demonstrating that kernel SHAP provides reliable approximations compared to exact tree SHAP, and shows SHAP's utility for interpreting compound potency predictions and multi-target activity predictions.
papers.conclusion: The SHAP methodology enables interpretation of ML models and their predictions, providing feature importance values for individual predictions. The kernel SHAP approach is generally applicable and yields reliable approximations compared to exact tree SHAP, shedding light on the black box nature of ML models for practical applications in drug discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Kernel SHAP and tree SHAP yield highly correlated feature importance rankings for decision tree-based models in activity and potency prediction.
SHAP analysis provides meaningful explanations for compound potency predictions and multi-target activity predictions, revealing features that drive model decisions.
SHAP helps rationalize model errors by identifying features whose absence or presence leads to incorrect predictions.
papers.limitation: SHAP-based feature prioritization identifies features that determine ML predictions, but these features may not always be responsible for specific activities.

papers.title: Model Metamers Reveal Invariances in Graph Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do the invariance properties of graph neural networks (GNNs) compare to human perceptual invariances, and can we quantify and mitigate excessive invariance in GNNs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a metamer generation technique for Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to investigate their representational invariance, revealing excessive invariance in standard architectures and proposing architectural and training modifications to mitigate it.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a framework for generating model metamers in GNNs to uncover and quantify representational invariance, exposing a misalignment with human perception and providing tools for benchmarking and improving sensitivity.
papers.key_findings:
Standard GNN architectures exhibit pronounced over-invariance, mapping structurally or semantically different graphs to nearly identical internal activations.
Architectural and training modifications (e.g., replacing ReLU with ELU, adversarial training, adding residual connections) can mitigate over-invariance.
Increasing the hidden layer dimension of a GNN reduces over-invariance by increasing the rank of the model's Jacobian.
Invariance increases with network depth, as feature metamers generated from deeper layers become less similar to the original input.
Cross-model invariance analysis reveals that invariances learned by GNNs comprise both shared components and architecture-specific features.
future_direction: Extend the approach to more graph tasks.
Apply the method to broader model families.
Develop improved metamer generation techniques.
papers.abstract: In recent years, deep neural networks have been extensively employed in perceptual systems to learn representations endowed with invariances, aiming to emulate the invariance mechanisms observed in the human brain. However, studies in the visual and auditory domains have confirmed that significant gaps remain between the invariance properties of artificial neural networks and those of humans. To investigate the invariance behavior within graph neural networks (GNNs), we introduce a model ``metamers'' generation technique. By optimizing input graphs such that their internal node activations match those of a reference graph, we obtain graphs that are equivalent in the model's representation space, yet differ significantly in both structure and node features. Our theoretical analysis focuses on two aspects: the local metamer dimension for a single node and the activation-induced volume change of the metamer manifold. Utilizing this approach, we uncover extreme levels of representational invariance across several classic GNN architectures. Although targeted modifications to model architecture and training strategies can partially mitigate this excessive invariance, they fail to fundamentally bridge the gap to human-like invariance. Finally, we quantify the deviation between metamer graphs and their original counterparts, revealing unique failure modes of current GNNs and providing a complementary benchmark for model evaluation.

papers.title: A Mathematical Philosophy of Explanations in Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the nature of explanations in mechanistic interpretability, and how can we define and demarcate mechanistic interpretability as a scientific practice?
papers.core_contribution: The paper defines mechanistic interpretability as the practice of producing model-level, ontic, causal-mechanistic, and falsifiable explanations of neural networks, and argues that the Principle of Explanatory Optimism is a necessary precondition for its success.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that mechanistic interpretability is a valuable scientific practice for understanding neural networks, grounded in the Explanatory View and dependent on the Principle of Explanatory Optimism, and provides a framework for defining and pursuing faithful explanations.
papers.key_findings:
The Explanatory View Hypothesis posits that neural networks contain implicit explanations of their behavior that can be extracted and understood.
Explanatory faithfulness is defined as the extent to which an explanation matches the model's internal mechanisms (ur-explanations), not just its input-output behavior.
Mechanistic interpretability is formally defined as seeking explanations that are model-level, ontic, causal-mechanistic, and falsifiable.
Mechanistic interpretability has inherent limits due to the value-ladenness and theory-ladenness of explanations, and its focus on model-level explanations excludes system-level complexities.
The Principle of Explanatory Optimism states that the algorithmic structure learned by generalizing neural networks is human-understandable, and without this assumption, mechanistic interpretability is intractable.
papers.limitation:
Explanations in mechanistic interpretability are value-laden, as the choice of precision and metrics depends on the interpreter's goals and values.
Explanations are theory-laden, as interpretability methods rely on theoretical commitments (e.g., sparse autoencoders assume sparsity and linearity).
Mechanistic interpretability focuses on model-level explanations, but AI systems involve additional components beyond the model, limiting the scope of MI for understanding system behavior.
future_direction: Increased focus on criteria that make explanations accessible to diverse humans, involving human-computer interaction and social sciences.
Development of a new field focusing on system-level explanations, building on mechanistic interpretability.
Collaboration between philosophy, computational complexity, and machine learning to investigate the Principle of Explanatory Optimism.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability aims to understand neural net- works through causal explanations. We argue for the Explanatory View Hypothesis: that Mechanistic Interpretability re- search is a principled approach to understanding models be- cause neural networks contain implicit explanations which can be extracted and understood. We hence show that Explanatory Faithfulness, an assessment of how well an explanation fits a model, is well-defined. We propose a definition of Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) as the practice of producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations of neural networks, allowing us to distinguish MI from other interpretability paradigms and detail MI’s inherent limits. We formulate the Principle of Explanatory Optimism, a conjecture which we argue is a necessary precondition for the success of Mechanistic Interpretability.

papers.title: Representational models: A common framework for understanding encoding, pattern-component, and representational-similarity analysis
papers.research_question: How do encoding analysis, pattern component modeling (PCM), and representational similarity analysis (RSA) relate to each other, and what is their relative power for adjudicating between competing representational models of neural activity?
papers.core_contribution: Provides a common mathematical framework showing that encoding analysis, pattern component modeling (PCM), and representational similarity analysis (RSA) all evaluate the second moment of the distribution of neural activity profiles, which determines representational geometry and feature decodability.
papers.conclusion: Encoding analysis, PCM, and RSA are closely related methods that test hypotheses about the distribution of neural activity profiles and should be considered complementary components of a unified analytical framework for understanding neural representations.
papers.key_findings:
Pattern component modeling (PCM) implements a likelihood-ratio test and provides the most powerful test between representational models if its assumptions hold.
Encoding analysis, when appropriately regularized (effectively imposing a prior on activity profiles), can perform similarly to PCM.
Representational similarity analysis (RSA) can achieve near-optimal inference power when the unequal variances and statistical dependencies of dissimilarity estimates are properly accounted for.
The three methods are complementary: PCM is analytically tractable and powerful, RSA provides intuitive summary statistics, and encoding analysis enables voxel-wise mapping of features.
All three methods are properly construed as components of a single toolkit for testing hypotheses about neural representations.
papers.limitation:
The methods focus on the second moment of the activity profile distribution; higher-order moments, which may be important for distinguishing between population codes with the same decodability, are not considered.
The framework is based on observational data and does not test causal effects of activity patterns on downstream neural or behavioral responses.
future_direction: Investigating the presence and computational function of non-Gaussian distributions of activity profiles in fMRI or single-cell data.
Extending the framework to include free parameters that change the model structure and to incorporate more detailed measurement models for indirect brain activity measures.
papers.abstract: Representational models specify how activity patterns in populations of neurons (or, more generally, in multivariate brain-activity measurements) relate to sensory stimuli, motor responses, or cognitive processes. In an experimental context, representational models can be defined as hypotheses about the distribution of activity profiles across experimental conditions. Currently, three different methods are being used to test such hypotheses: encoding analysis, pattern component modeling (PCM), and representational similarity analysis (RSA). Here we develop a common mathematical framework for understanding the relationship of these three methods, which share one core commonality: all three evaluate the second moment of the distribution of activity profiles, which determines the representational geometry, and thus how well any feature can be decoded from population activity. Using simulated data for three different experimental designs, we compare the power of the methods to adjudicate between competing representational models. PCM implements a likelihood-ratio test and therefore provides the most powerful test if its assumptions hold. However, the other two approaches-when conducted appropriately-can perform similarly. In encoding analysis, the linear model needs to be appropriately regularized, which effectively imposes a prior on the activity profiles. With such a prior, an encoding model specifies a well-defined distribution of activity profiles. In RSA, the unequal variances and statistical dependencies of the dissimilarity estimates need to be taken into account to reach near-optimal power in inference. The three methods render different aspects of the information explicit (e.g. single-response tuning in encoding analysis and population-response representational dissimilarity in RSA) and have specific advantages in terms of computational demands, ease of use, and extensibility. The three methods are properly construed as complementary components of a single data-analytical toolkit for understanding neural representations on the basis of multivariate brain-activity data.

papers.title: Ensuring Medical AI Safety: Interpretability-Driven Detection and Mitigation of Spurious Model Behavior and Associated Data
papers.research_question: How can interpretability methods be used to detect and mitigate spurious correlations (shortcut learning) in deep neural networks for medical AI, and how can bias annotation be semi-automated to reduce manual labeling effort?
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends the Reveal2Revise framework with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities, enabling sample- and feature-level annotation of spurious correlations to reduce manual labeling and improve bias mitigation in medical AI models.
papers.conclusion: The interpretability-driven Reveal2Revise framework, enhanced with bias annotation capabilities, provides a comprehensive approach to improve medical AI safety by detecting and mitigating spurious model behavior, ultimately increasing model robustness for real-world deployment.
papers.key_findings:
