The extended Reveal2Revise framework successfully identifies and mitigates both controlled and real-world spurious correlations across four medical datasets and multiple model architectures.
The framework provides sample-level bias annotation via data retrieval using concept representations (e.g., CAVs) and feature-level annotation via spatial localization of artifacts.
Bias mitigation methods like RRR and RR-ClArC, when integrated with the framework, improve model robustness by reducing reliance on spurious features while maintaining accuracy on clean data.
The approach reduces the need for extensive manual annotation by domain experts, making bias detection and mitigation more practical.
The framework is applicable across different modalities (image and ECG) and model types (CNNs and Vision Transformers).
papers.limitation:
The framework requires human validation to distinguish between clinically valid and spurious outlier behavior.
Some artifacts are non-localizable (e.g., brightness shifts), limiting spatial bias localization.
Bias representations (e.g., CAVs) may be inaccurate if the initial set of biased samples is small or noisy.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other modalities and data types.
Improving the automation of bias detection and validation to further reduce human effort.
Integrating the framework with a wider range of bias mitigation techniques.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are increasingly employed in high-stakes medical applications, despite their tendency for shortcut learning in the presence of spurious correlations, which can have potentially fatal consequences in practice. Whereas a multitude of works address either the detection or mitigation of such shortcut behavior in isolation, the Reveal2Revise approach provides a comprehensive bias mitigation framework combining these steps. However, effectively addressing these biases often requires substantial labeling efforts from domain experts. In this work, we review the steps of the Reveal2Revise framework and enhance it with semi-automated interpretability-based bias annotation capabilities. This includes methods for the sample- and feature-level bias annotation, providing valuable information for bias mitigation methods to unlearn the undesired shortcut behavior. We show the applicability of the framework using four medical datasets across two modalities, featuring controlled and real-world spurious correlations caused by data artifacts. We successfully identify and mitigate these biases in VGG16, ResNet50, and contemporary Vision Transformer models, ultimately increasing their robustness and applicability for real-world medical tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/frederikpahde/medical-ai-safety.

papers.title: Integrating Evolutionary and Compositional Features with ML and DL for Robust and Interpretable Druggable Protein Prediction
papers.research_question: How can evolutionary and compositional features be integrated with machine learning and deep learning for robust and interpretable druggable protein prediction?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a hybrid feature representation combining Average Block-based PSSM and Dipeptide Composition for druggable protein prediction, achieving high accuracy with statistical validation and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The hybrid feature representation enables strong predictive performance for druggable protein prediction, with SVM and CapsBiLSTM achieving high accuracy and AUC scores, validated statistically, and providing interpretable insights into sequence descriptors.
papers.key_findings:
Hybrid features (AB-PSSM + DPC) significantly outperform individual descriptors in predicting druggable proteins.
SVM and CapsBiLSTM models achieve classification accuracies above 90% and ROC-AUC/PR-AUC scores above 95%.
Statistical tests (DeLong's test, McNemar's test, bootstrap confidence intervals) confirm the robustness and significance of the improvements.
Interpretability analyses using SHAP and t-SNE reveal biologically significant sequence descriptors influencing druggability.
The proposed framework outperforms existing machine learning and ensemble-based methods in accuracy and interpretability.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Druggable proteins are essential targets in contemporary therapeutic discovery, and their precise identification is necessary for the progression of rational drug design. Traditional biochemical screening techniques are costly, laborious, and protracted, whereas current computational models typically attain only moderate efficacy and seldom offer robust statistical validation or biological interpretability. To mitigate these limitations, we offer a hybrid computational approach that amalgamates evolutionary and compositional information by merging Average Block-based Position-Specific Scoring Matrix (AB-PSSM) characteristics with Dipeptide Composition (DPC) into a 600-dimensional representation. The hybrid feature space was assessed utilizing three machine learning algorithms (support vector machine, random forest, and XGBoost) alongside three deep learning architectures (CapsBiLSTM, ResCapsNetPlus, and ResNet1D) following a rigorous five-fold out-of-fold cross-validation protocol to guarantee fairness and reproducibility. A thorough assessment revealed that the hybrid attributes significantly surpassed individual descriptors, with the SVM and CapsBiLSTM classifiers attaining classification accuracies of 90% and ROC-AUC and PR-AUC values surpassing 95%. The robustness and reliability were further validated by statistical analyses, including DeLong’s test, McNemar’s test, and bootstrap confidence intervals, demonstrating that the observed enhancements were substantial and consistent. Furthermore, interpretability investigations employing SHAP feature attribution and t-SNE visualization underscored biologically significant sequence descriptors as pivotal factors influencing druggability, thus mitigating the "black box" constraint inherent in numerous deep learning methodologies. This study presents a statistically validated, interpretable, and high-performing framework for predicting druggable proteins, which outperforms current machine learning and ensemble-based methods, establishing a clear basis for future applications in precision medicine and drug discovery.

papers.title: Studying Cross-cluster Modularity in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What are the effects of training neural networks to be modular using a clusterability loss on interpretability, such as task specialization and circuit size?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a clusterability measure and loss function to train neural networks to be modular. Shows that modular models do not exhibit more task specialization but have smaller circuits, aiding interpretability.
papers.conclusion: A simple regularizer can split neural network layers into non-interacting modules, but these modules do not yield expected interpretability benefits like task specialization. However, modularity improves circuit size and search space without performance loss.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained models are not modular; clusters are highly enmeshed.
Training with clusterability loss effectively increases modularity in models.
Modular models do not show increased task specialization compared to non-modular models.
Modular models have smaller effective circuits, reducing circuit size.
Theoretical analysis indicates modularity simplifies function spaces and reduces the number of features.
papers.limitation: The modularity metric does not lead to clear interpretability benefits such as task specialization.
future_direction: Investigate alternative regularizers for interpretability benefits.
Build an automated subtask detection mechanism.
papers.abstract: An approach to improve neural network interpretability is via clusterability, i.e., splitting a model into disjoint clusters that can be studied independently. We define a measure for clusterability and show that pre-trained models form highly enmeshed clusters via spectral graph clustering. We thus train models to be more modular using a "clusterability loss" function that encourages the formation of non-interacting clusters. We then investigate the emerging properties of these highly clustered models. We find our trained clustered models do not exhibit more task specialization, but do form smaller circuits. We investigate CNNs trained on MNIST and CIFAR, small transformers trained on modular addition, and GPT-2 and Pythia on the Wiki dataset, and Gemma on a Chemistry dataset. This investigation shows what to expect from clustered models.

papers.title: The geometry of hidden representations of large transformer models
papers.research_question: How do the geometric and statistical properties of hidden representations evolve across layers in large transformer models, and can the intrinsic dimension profile be used to identify layers with maximal semantic content?
papers.core_contribution: The intrinsic dimension profile of hidden representations in large transformers has a characteristic shape (peak, plateau, etc.), and the layers with minimal intrinsic dimension correspond to those with maximal semantic content, providing an unsupervised strategy to identify optimal layers for downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: Large transformers behave like sophisticated autoencoders, with an encoding phase (expansion and compression) and a decoding phase, and the low-ID representations in the intermediate layers are semantically rich.
papers.key_findings:
Representations evolve in distinct phases: an initial expansion (high ID), a compression phase (low ID), and a decoding phase.
The ID profile shows a peak in early layers, a plateau/low-ID region in intermediate layers, and sometimes a second peak in later layers.
Semantic information (e.g., protein remote homology, image class labels) is best encoded in the low-ID regions.
The ID profile can be used in an unsupervised manner to identify layers optimal for downstream learning tasks.
The geometric evolution is consistent across transformers trained on different data modalities (protein sequences and images).
papers.limitation:
The use of average pooling to handle variable-length sequences may affect the intrinsic dimension estimates.
Differences in ID profiles between models may be attributed to data modality, training objectives, and preprocessing choices.
The analysis of NLP representations is preliminary and not as extensive as for protein and image models.
future_direction: Analyzing the similarity of representations in ID minima with those from models trained in a supervised setting.
Further investigation of the second peak in iGPT models and its relation to the decoding phase.
Extending the geometric analysis to a broader range of NLP tasks and models.
papers.abstract: Large transformers are powerful architectures used for self-supervised data analysis across various data types, including protein sequences, images, and text. In these models, the semantic structure of the dataset emerges from a sequence of transformations between one representation and the next. We characterize the geometric and statistical properties of these representations and how they change as we move through the layers. By analyzing the intrinsic dimension (ID) and neighbor composition, we find that the representations evolve similarly in transformers trained on protein language tasks and image reconstruction tasks. In the first layers, the data manifold expands, becoming high-dimensional, and then contracts significantly in the intermediate layers. In the last part of the model, the ID remains approximately constant or forms a second shallow peak. We show that the semantic information of the dataset is better expressed at the end of the first peak, and this phenomenon can be observed across many models trained on diverse datasets. Based on our findings, we point out an explicit strategy to identify, without supervision, the layers that maximize semantic content: representations at intermediate layers corresponding to a relative minimum of the ID profile are more suitable for downstream learning tasks.

papers.title: Interpretability in Parameter Space: Minimizing Mechanistic Description Length with Attribution-based Parameter Decomposition
papers.research_question: How can we decompose neural network parameters into faithful, minimal, and simple mechanistic components?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Attribution-based Parameter Decomposition (APD), a method to decompose neural network parameters into mechanistic components that are faithful, minimal, and simple, optimizing for minimal description length.
papers.conclusion: APD offers a promising approach for mechanistic interpretability, suggesting solutions to open problems like identifying minimal circuits in superposition and providing an architecture-agnostic framework for neural network decomposition, though challenges remain for scaling.
papers.key_findings:
APD successfully recovers ground truth mechanisms in a toy model of superposition, decomposing the weight matrix into columns corresponding to individual features.
APD identifies parameter components representing individual functions in a toy model of compressed computation, where the model computes more nonlinear functions than it has neurons.
APD learns components that represent individual functions even when they span multiple layers in a toy model of cross-layer distributed representations.
APD's components are faithful to the original parameters, minimal in number per input, and simple in terms of rank.
papers.limitation:
High computational cost due to the need for multiple forward and backward passes.
Sensitivity to hyperparameters, such as the batch top-k value and loss coefficients.
Attributions are approximated using gradients, which may not perfectly capture causal importance.
future_direction: Improving computational cost
Improving robustness to hyperparameters
Improving attributions
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand the internal mechanisms learned by neural networks. Despite recent progress toward this goal, it remains unclear how best to decompose neural network parameters into mechanistic components. We introduce Attribution-based Parameter Decomposition (APD), a method that directly decomposes a neural network's parameters into components that (i) are faithful to the parameters of the original network, (ii) require a minimal number of components to process any input, and (iii) are maximally simple. Our approach thus optimizes for a minimal length description of the network's mechanisms. We demonstrate APD's effectiveness by successfully identifying ground truth mechanisms in multiple toy experimental settings: Recovering features from superposition; separating compressed computations; and identifying cross-layer distributed representations. While challenges remain to scaling APD to non-toy models, our results suggest solutions to several open problems in mechanistic interpretability, including identifying minimal circuits in superposition, offering a conceptual foundation for 'features', and providing an architecture-agnostic framework for neural network decomposition.

papers.title: FSX: Message Flow Sensitivity Enhanced Structural Explainer for Graph Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we explain Graph Neural Network predictions by synergistically combining internal message flow dynamics with external graph structure to achieve both high fidelity and computational efficiency?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes FSX, a novel hybrid explanation framework for GNNs that integrates internal message flow sensitivity analysis with a flow-aware cooperative game on external graph structure to generate faithful and efficient subgraph-level explanations.
papers.conclusion: FSX provides a systematic approach for generating faithful and efficient graph-level explanations by tightly coupling a GNN's internal message flow dynamics with external graph structure valuation, paving the way for more principled and insightful explainable AI for graph-structured data.
papers.key_findings:
FSX consistently outperforms baseline methods (FlowX, GNNExplainer, GraphEXT, PGExplainer) in Fidelity+ and Fidelity- across multiple datasets and sparsity levels.
FSX achieves significantly lower computational time compared to baseline methods by focusing evaluation on compact subgraphs derived from flow sensitivity.
The flow-sensitivity analysis directly identifies causally important message flows, leading to more faithful explanations than purely perturbation-based or game-theoretic methods.
The flow-aware cooperative game with a weighted Shapley-like value fairly allocates node contributions by considering both feature importance and role in sustaining critical flows.
FSX effectively bridges the gap between explanation fidelity and efficiency for GNN interpretability.
papers.abstract: Despite the widespread success of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), understanding the reasons behind their specific predictions remains challenging. Existing explainability methods face a trade-off that gradient-based approaches are computationally efficient but often ignore structural interactions, while game-theoretic techniques capture interactions at the cost of high computational overhead and potential deviation from the model's true reasoning path. To address this gap, we propose FSX (Message Flow Sensitivity Enhanced Structural Explainer), a novel hybrid framework that synergistically combines the internal message flows of the model with a cooperative game approach applied to the external graph data. FSX first identifies critical message flows via a novel flow-sensitivity analysis: during a single forward pass, it simulates localized node perturbations and measures the resulting changes in message flow intensities. These sensitivity-ranked flows are then projected onto the input graph to define compact, semantically meaningful subgraphs. Within each subgraph, a flow-aware cooperative game is conducted, where node contributions are evaluated fairly through a Shapley-like value that incorporates both node-feature importance and their roles in sustaining or destabilizing the identified critical flows. Extensive evaluation across multiple datasets and GNN architectures demonstrates that FSX achieves superior explanation fidelity with significantly reduced runtime, while providing unprecedented insights into the structural logic underlying model predictions--specifically, how important sub-structures exert influence by governing the stability of key internal computational pathways.

papers.title: What Does Loss Optimization Actually Teach, If Anything? Knowledge Dynamics in Continual Pre-training of LLMs
papers.research_question: How does loss optimization during continual pre-training (CPT) relate to the acquisition and retention of factual knowledge in LLMs, and does it provide a reliable signal for learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that loss optimization is misaligned with knowledge acquisition in continual pre-training (CPT); factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic despite monotonic loss decrease, and circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of internal knowledge pathways.
papers.conclusion: Loss optimization is not a reliable indicator of learning in CPT; probe-based trajectories reveal narrow learning windows invisible to loss curves, motivating task-based stopping criteria.
papers.key_findings:
Optimization and learning systematically diverge: loss decreases monotonically while factual knowledge acquisition is unstable and non-monotonic.
Acquired facts are rarely consolidated; learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure (entity frequency).
Out-of-domain (OOD) task performance degrades from early epochs during CPT.
Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, explaining narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) provides a much higher upper bound for factual recall, indicating the limitation is in the optimization process, not the data.
future_direction: Novel training objectives, evaluation protocols, and diagnostic tools that make learning dynamics observable during model adaptation.
Task-based stopping criteria that rely on task-level performance rather than next-token prediction.
papers.abstract: Continual Pre-Training (CPT) is widely used for acquiring and updating factual knowledge in LLMs. This practice treats loss as a proxy for knowledge learning, while offering no grounding into how it changes during training. We study CPT as a knowledge learning process rather than a solely optimization problem. We construct a controlled, distribution-matched benchmark of factual documents and interleave diagnostic probes directly into the CPT loop, enabling epoch-level measurement of knowledge acquisition dynamics and changes in Out-Of-Domain (OOD) general skills (e.g., math). We further analyze how CPT reshapes knowledge circuits during training. Across three instruction-tuned LLMs and multiple CPT strategies, optimization and learning systematically diverge as loss decreases monotonically while factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic. Acquired facts are rarely consolidated, learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure, and OOD performance degrades from early epochs. Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, providing an explanation for narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting. These results show that loss optimization is misaligned with learning progress in CPT and motivate evaluation of stopping criteria based on task-level learning dynamics.

papers.title: GPCR-BERT: Interpreting Sequential Design of G Protein Coupled Receptors Using Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the correlation between variations in conserved motifs of GPCRs and other amino acids? Can we predict missing residues and identify key contributing amino acids?
papers.core_contribution: Developed GPCR-BERT, a fine-tuned protein language model, to interpret sequential design of GPCRs, achieving high accuracy in predicting masked residues and identifying residue correlations through attention analysis.
papers.conclusion: GPCR-BERT effectively predicts residues and distinguishes GPCR classes, providing insights into functional relationships and potential applications in mutation studies and drug development.
papers.key_findings:
GPCR-BERT achieved high accuracy (up to 100%) in predicting masked residues in conserved motifs.
The model successfully clustered GPCRs of the same class in embedding space, indicating it captures class-specific features.
Attention analysis revealed correlations between masked residues and other amino acids, some of which align with experimental mutagenesis data.
The model's predictions for CWxP motif were less accurate, likely due to smaller dataset size.
GPCR-BERT outperformed BERT and SVM on the prediction tasks, demonstrating the advantage of protein-specific pre-training.
papers.limitation: The conserved motifs are not 100% conserved (e.g., CWxP motif is only 71% conserved), so the model might not apply to GPCRs with varied versions of the motifs.
papers.abstract: With the rise of Transformers and Large Language Models (LLMs) in Chemistry and Biology, new avenues for the design and understanding of therapeutics have opened up to the scientific community. Protein sequences can be modeled as language and can take advantage of recent advances in LLMs, specifically with the abundance of our access to the protein sequence datasets. In this paper, we developed the GPCR-BERT model for understanding the sequential design of G Protein-Coupled Receptors (GPCRs). GPCRs are the target of over one-third of FDA-approved pharmaceuticals. However, there is a lack of comprehensive understanding regarding the relationship between amino acid sequence, ligand selectivity, and conformational motifs (such as NPxxY, CWxP, E/DRY). By utilizing the pre-trained protein model (Prot-Bert) and fine-tuning with prediction tasks of variations in the motifs, we were able to shed light on several relationships between residues in the binding pocket and some of the conserved motifs. To achieve this, we took advantage of attention weights, and hidden states of the model that are interpreted to extract the extent of contributions of amino acids in dictating the type of masked ones. The fine-tuned models demonstrated high accuracy in predicting hidden residues within the motifs. In addition, the analysis of embedding was performed over 3D structures to elucidate the higher-order interactions within the conformations of the receptors.

papers.title: OrphicX: A Causality-Inspired Latent Variable Model for Interpreting Graph Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How to generate causal, compact, and faithful explanations for any graph neural networks (GNNs) by identifying causal factors in the latent space?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes OrphicX, a generative model that provides causal explanations for any GNN by isolating causal factors in the latent space using information flow measurements and backdoor adjustment to circumvent confounder effects.
papers.conclusion: OrphicX offers a promising tool for explaining GNNs and mining patterns in subgraphs by identifying causal semantics in the latent space via information flow measurements.
papers.key_findings:
OrphicX consistently outperforms baseline explanation methods (Gem, GNNExplainer, PGExplainer) in explanation accuracy and sparsity across synthetic and real-world graph datasets.
OrphicX effectively identifies causal semantics in the latent space, as validated by information flow measurements and perturbation experiments.
The framework is model-agnostic, does not require access to the target GNN's internal structure, and does not rely on linear-independence assumptions of explained features.
OrphicX generates explanatory subgraphs that are faithful (high fidelity) and compact (high sparsity), aligning with human-interpretable motifs in molecular graphs.
The causal analysis identifies node attributes as confounders and uses backdoor adjustment to accurately measure causal influence from latent features to predictions.
papers.limitation:
The generated explanations for GNNs may expose private information of the training data, posing privacy risks in domains like finance and healthcare.
Additional user studies are needed to confirm how well explanations in other domains (e.g., visual scene graphs) align with practitioner needs.
future_direction: Conduct additional user studies to evaluate the alignment of OrphicX explanations with practitioner needs in real-world settings, such as visual scene graphs.
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a new eXplanation framework, called OrphicX, for generating causal explanations for any graph neural networks (GNNs) based on learned latent causal factors. Specifically, we construct a distinct generative model and design an objective function that encourages the generative model to produce causal, compact, and faithful explanations. This is achieved by isolating the causal factors in the latent space of graphs by maximizing the information flow measurements. We theoretically analyze the cause-effect relationships in the proposed causal graph, identify node attributes as confounders between graphs and GNN predictions, and circumvent such confounder effect by leveraging the backdoor adjustment formula. Our framework is compatible with any GNNs, and it does not require access to the process by which the target GNN produces its predictions. In addition, it does not rely on the linear-independence assumption of the explained features, nor require prior knowledge on the graph learning tasks. We show a proof-of-concept of OrphicX on canonical classification problems on graph data. In particular, we analyze the explanatory subgraphs obtained from explanations for molecular graphs (i.e., Mutag) and quantitatively evaluate the explanation performance with frequently occurring subgraph patterns. Empirically, we show that OrphicX can effectively identify the causal semantics for generating causal explanations, significantly outperforming its alternatives.

papers.title: Exact Computation of Any-Order Shapley Interactions for Graph Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can exact any-order Shapley Interactions be efficiently computed for Graph Neural Networks to explain their predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces GraphSHAP-IQ, an efficient method to compute exact any-order Shapley Interactions for GNNs by exploiting the graph structure and GNN architecture, substantially reducing the exponential complexity.
papers.conclusion: GraphSHAP-IQ enables efficient, exact computation of Shapley Interactions for GNNs, offering a flexible and faithful framework for interpretability with an adjustable complexity-accuracy trade-off.
papers.key_findings:
GraphSHAP-IQ reduces the exponential complexity of computing exact Shapley Interactions to depend only on the receptive fields of the GNN.
The method requires linear global pooling and output layers (Assumption 3.4) for the theoretical guarantees to hold.
SI-Graphs provide adjustable explanation complexity, from Shapley Values (order 1) to Möbius Interactions (order n).
The approach yields faithful, additive decompositions of GNN predictions for graph classification and regression tasks.
Experiments show the method works effectively on real-world chemical and water distribution network datasets.
papers.limitation: The method requires the global pooling function (Ψ) and the output layer (σ) to be linear (Assumption 3.4).
future_direction: Exploring different node masking strategies beyond baseline imputation.
Extending the approach to GNNs with non-linear pooling and output layers.
papers.abstract: Albeit the ubiquitous use of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in machine learning (ML) prediction tasks involving graph-structured data, their interpretability remains challenging. In explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), the Shapley Value (SV) is the predominant method to quantify contributions of individual features to a ML model's output. Addressing the limitations of SVs in complex prediction models, Shapley Interactions (SIs) extend the SV to groups of features. In this work, we explain single graph predictions of GNNs with SIs that quantify node contributions and interactions among multiple nodes. By exploiting the GNN architecture, we show that the structure of interactions in node embeddings are preserved for graph prediction. As a result, the exponential complexity of SIs depends only on the receptive fields, i.e. the message-passing ranges determined by the connectivity of the graph and the number of convolutional layers. Based on our theoretical results, we introduce GraphSHAP-IQ, an efficient approach to compute any-order SIs exactly. GraphSHAP-IQ is applicable to popular message passing techniques in conjunction with a linear global pooling and output layer. We showcase that GraphSHAP-IQ substantially reduces the exponential complexity of computing exact SIs on multiple benchmark datasets. Beyond exact computation, we evaluate GraphSHAP-IQ's approximation of SIs on popular GNN architectures and compare with existing baselines. Lastly, we visualize SIs of real-world water distribution networks and molecule structures using a SI-Graph.

papers.title: Interpreting Neural Networks through the Polytope Lens
papers.research_question: What are the fundamental primitives of neural network representations, and can polytopes serve as a better unit of description than neurons or directions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the polytope lens, a perspective that accounts for nonlinearities in neural networks, and demonstrates that polytopes can identify monosemantic regions and that polytope boundaries correspond to semantic boundaries.
papers.conclusion: The polytope lens provides a more accurate description of neural networks by incorporating nonlinearities, but further work is needed to develop it into a practical tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Polysemantic directions overlap with multiple monosemantic polytope regions.
Polytope boundaries reflect semantic boundaries, with denser boundaries between different classes than within the same class.
Polytopes partially define when feature-directions are on- and off-distribution, with dense boundaries near the origin but class changes also occur in low-density regions.
Clustering activations or spline codes yields monosemantic clusters in both image classifiers and language models.
The polytope lens provides a more complete description of neural networks by incorporating nonlinearities, but it is not yet clear how to use it for decomposable descriptions.
papers.limitation: The polytope lens sacrifices globally valid feature directions for locally valid ones, making descriptions more complex and less decomposable.
future_direction: Develop the polytope lens into a practical tool for mechanistic interpretability.
Build more robust and scalable methods based on the polytope lens.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to explain what a neural network has learned at a nuts-and-bolts level. What are the fundamental primitives of neural network representations? Previous mechanistic descriptions have used individual neurons or their linear combinations to understand the representations a network has learned. But there are clues that neurons and their linear combinations are not the correct fundamental units of description: directions cannot describe how neural networks use nonlinearities to structure their representations. Moreover, many instances of individual neurons and their combinations are polysemantic (i.e. they have multiple unrelated meanings). Polysemanticity makes interpreting the network in terms of neurons or directions challenging since we can no longer assign a specific feature to a neural unit. In order to find a basic unit of description that does not suffer from these problems, we zoom in beyond just directions to study the way that piecewise linear activation functions (such as ReLU) partition the activation space into numerous discrete polytopes. We call this perspective the polytope lens. The polytope lens makes concrete predictions about the behavior of neural networks, which we evaluate through experiments on both convolutional image classifiers and language models. Specifically, we show that polytopes can be used to identify monosemantic regions of activation space (while directions are not in general monosemantic) and that the density of polytope boundaries reflect semantic boundaries. We also outline a vision for what mechanistic interpretability might look like through the polytope lens.

papers.title: Towards Automated Circuit Discovery for Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we automate the discovery of circuits in neural networks for mechanistic interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper systematizes the mechanistic interpretability workflow and introduces the ACDC algorithm to automate circuit discovery by using activation patching to find important connections in the computational graph.
papers.conclusion: ACDC is a step towards automating circuit discovery in mechanistic interpretability, showing promise on several tasks but with limitations that need to be addressed in future work.
papers.key_findings:
ACDC successfully rediscovers known circuits, such as the Greater-Than circuit in GPT-2 Small and the IOI circuit.
ACDC selects a sparse set of edges (e.g., 68 out of 32,000 in GPT-2 Small for IOI) that match manually found circuits.
ACDC performs competitively with gradient-based methods like Subnetwork Probing and Head Importance Score for Pruning.
ACDC is not robust in all settings, e.g., it fails on tracr tasks when using corrupted activations.
ACDC can miss negative components when optimizing for logit difference.
papers.limitation:
ACDC can fail in some settings, such as on tracr tasks when using corrupted activations.
ACDC may miss negative components when optimizing for logit difference.
The ground-truth circuits from previous work are not 100% reliable, limiting the evaluation.
future_direction: Automating the functional interpretation of model components.
Improving circuit discovery methods to handle more complex behaviors and models.
papers.abstract: Through considerable effort and intuition, several recent works have reverse-engineered nontrivial behaviors of transformer models. This paper systematizes the mechanistic interpretability process they followed. First, researchers choose a metric and dataset that elicit the desired model behavior. Then, they apply activation patching to find which abstract neural network units are involved in the behavior. By varying the dataset, metric, and units under investigation, researchers can understand the functionality of each component. We automate one of the process' steps: to identify the circuit that implements the specified behavior in the model's computational graph. We propose several algorithms and reproduce previous interpretability results to validate them. For example, the ACDC algorithm rediscovered 5/5 of the component types in a circuit in GPT-2 Small that computes the Greater-Than operation. ACDC selected 68 of the 32,000 edges in GPT-2 Small, all of which were manually found by previous work. Our code is available at https://github.com/ArthurConmy/Automatic-Circuit-Discovery.

papers.title: Query Circuits: Explaining How Language Models Answer User Prompts
papers.research_question: How can we explain why a language model produces a particular output for a specific input query by tracing the information flow inside the model?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces query circuit discovery for local, input-level explanations of LLMs, proposes a robust evaluation metric (NDF) and sampling-based methods (BoN) to efficiently identify sparse, faithful circuits.
papers.conclusion: Query circuit discovery, aided by BoN sampling and NDF, demonstrates that compact sub-networks can explain much of an LLM's behavior on individual queries, offering a promising path for scalable, faithful explanations of LLM decisions.
papers.key_findings:
Extremely sparse query circuits (e.g., 1.3% of edges) can recover a large portion (e.g., 60%) of model performance on individual queries.
Best-of-N (BoN) sampling effectively discovers faithful query circuits, outperforming baseline methods.
Normalized Deviation Faithfulness (NDF) is a more robust evaluation metric for query circuits compared to Normalized Faithfulness Score (NFS).
Query circuits enable local, prompt-level explanations of LLM decisions, offering a step towards scalable interpretability.
papers.limitation:
The method neglects combinatorial interactions among edges, which is a fundamental limitation of using indirect effects as edge scores.
The work focuses on queries with single-token outputs (e.g., option IDs) and does not address multi-token generations.
There is no automated method for interpreting the functionalities of identified edges and nodes; manual investigation is not scalable.
future_direction: Develop methods to account for combinatorial interactions among edges in circuit discovery.
Extend query circuit discovery to multi-token generations.
Integrate automated interpretability methods to explain the functionalities of discovered circuits.
papers.abstract: Explaining why a language model produces a particular output requires local, input-level explanations. Existing methods uncover global capability circuits (e.g., indirect object identification), but not why the model answers a specific input query in a particular way. We introduce query circuits, which directly trace the information flow inside a model that maps a specific input to the output. Unlike surrogate-based approaches (e.g., sparse autoencoders), query circuits are identified within the model itself, resulting in more faithful and computationally accessible explanations. To make query circuits practical, we address two challenges. First, we introduce Normalized Deviation Faithfulness (NDF), a robust metric to evaluate how well a discovered circuit recovers the model's decision for a specific input, and is broadly applicable to circuit discovery beyond our setting. Second, we develop sampling-based methods to efficiently identify circuits that are sparse yet faithfully describe the model's behavior. Across benchmarks (IOI, arithmetic, MMLU, and ARC), we find that there exist extremely sparse query circuits within the model that can recover much of its performance on single queries. For example, a circuit covering only 1.3% of model connections can recover about 60% of performance on an MMLU questions. Overall, query circuits provide a step towards faithful, scalable explanations of how language models process individual inputs.

papers.title: Discovering Invariant Rationales for Graph Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we discover invariant rationales in graph neural networks that capture causal patterns and improve interpretability and generalization on out-of-distribution data?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a novel invariant learning algorithm, DIR, for intrinsically interpretable graph neural networks, which discovers causal rationales that are invariant across distributions to improve generalization and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: DIR discovers invariant rationales by constructing interventional distributions to distill causal features, improving both interpretability and generalization in graph neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
DIR outperforms baselines in generalization ability and interpretability on both synthetic and real-world graph classification datasets.
DIR remains effective under different degrees of spurious bias, while baselines often fail.
Data augmentation via interventional distributions is beneficial, and the variance regularization further boosts performance.
DIR exhibits better intrinsic interpretability, accurately discovering causal features as rationales.
The training process of DIR shows an adaption-fitting pattern, where rationales are explored and then consolidated.
papers.limitation:
The memory bank only contains spurious patterns seen in training, which may fail for unseen spurious patterns.
The expressiveness of rationale generators could be limited.
The method assumes separable causal and non-causal features, which may not hold in all cases.
future_direction: Building more reliable and expressive interpretable models under various assumptions.
Exploring higher-level interpretability (e.g., representation interpretability, interpretations on disentangled variables).
Handling unseen spurious patterns via attribute perturbation, external knowledge base, or subgraph matching.
papers.abstract: Intrinsic interpretability of graph neural networks (GNNs) is to find a small subset of the input graph's features -- rationale -- which guides the model prediction. Unfortunately, the leading rationalization models often rely on data biases, especially shortcut features, to compose rationales and make predictions without probing the critical and causal patterns. Moreover, such data biases easily change outside the training distribution. As a result, these models suffer from a huge drop in interpretability and predictive performance on out-of-distribution data. In this work, we propose a new strategy of discovering invariant rationale (DIR) to construct intrinsically interpretable GNNs. It conducts interventions on the training distribution to create multiple interventional distributions. Then it approaches the causal rationales that are invariant across different distributions while filtering out the spurious patterns that are unstable. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets validate the superiority of our DIR in terms of interpretability and generalization ability on graph classification over the leading baselines. Code and datasets are available at https://github.com/Wuyxin/DIR-GNN.

papers.title: Open Roles In Interpretability Scaling Laws for Dictionary Learning Update on how we train SAEs How Strongly do Dictionary Learning Features Influence Model Behavior? Interpretability Architectures Project Caloric and the Utility of Incorrect Theories Open Problem: Attribution Dictionary Learning Isolating Circuits Paths of Different Lengths
papers.core_contribution: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.
papers.key_findings:
Scaling laws for dictionary learning show that loss decreases approximately as a power law with compute, with optimal allocations of training steps and features scaling as power laws.
An improved SAE training setup with modified loss function and initialization reduces loss and allows scaling to millions of features without issues.
Ablating dictionary learning features causes significantly more loss increase than random perturbations, indicating that features are high-leverage for model behavior.
Feature ablations have a larger effect than feature doublings, suggesting that feature influence may saturate at higher activations.
The impact of feature ablations is more pronounced for residual stream features compared to MLP features, hinting at different functional roles.
papers.limitation:
The relationship between SAE loss and qualitative usefulness of SAE features is imperfect and may break down at sufficient scale.
The SAE training initialization may need improvement and could cause issues for large feature counts.
The results on feature influence are preliminary and require further investigation.
future_direction: Exploring interpretable model architectures
Investigating attribution dictionary learning
Improving SAE training methods such as initialization and post-training
papers.abstract: This blog post reports several developments in mechanistic interpretability, including scaling laws for dictionary learning, updates on SAE training techniques, and preliminary evidence that dictionary learning features significantly influence model behavior. The updates demonstrate progress in dictionary learning and circuit analysis, with SAE features showing causal influence on model behavior, and open problems like attribution dictionary learning offering directions for further research.

papers.title: LLM Circuit Analyses Are Consistent Across Training and Scale
papers.research_question: Do circuit analyses of LLMs generalize across training time and model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Circuit analyses are consistent across training and scale: task abilities and supporting functional components emerge at similar token counts across model sizes, and the overarching algorithms implemented by circuits remain stable even when individual components change.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analyses generalize well over both training and scale, suggesting that studies on small models at the end of pre-training can inform understanding of larger models and models with longer training.
papers.key_findings:
Task abilities and functional components (e.g., induction heads, name-mover heads) emerge consistently at similar token counts across different model scales.
The algorithm implemented by a circuit remains stable over training even when the specific attention heads implementing it change.
Circuit size correlates with model size and can fluctuate over time while the algorithm remains the same.
Components like induction heads emerge around 2B tokens across scales, paralleling task learning curves.
Circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training provide insights that generalize to larger models and longer training runs.
papers.limitation:
The study does not include fine-tuning or other post-training techniques.
Circuit completeness is challenging to verify.
The findings need validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
future_direction: Validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
Investigating the load-balancing mechanism that maintains task performance when components change.
papers.abstract: Most currently deployed large language models (LLMs) undergo continuous training or additional finetuning. By contrast, most research into LLMs' internal mechanisms focuses on models at one snapshot in time (the end of pre-training), raising the question of whether their results generalize to real-world settings. Existing studies of mechanisms over time focus on encoder-only or toy models, which differ significantly from most deployed models. In this study, we track how model mechanisms, operationalized as circuits, emerge and evolve across 300 billion tokens of training in decoder-only LLMs, in models ranging from 70 million to 2.8 billion parameters. We find that task abilities and the functional components that support them emerge consistently at similar token counts across scale. Moreover, although such components may be implemented by different attention heads over time, the overarching algorithm that they implement remains. Surprisingly, both these algorithms and the types of components involved therein can replicate across model scale. These results suggest that circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training can provide insights that still apply after additional pre-training and over model scale.

papers.title: Tensor Product Decomposition Networks: Uncovering Representations of Structure Learned by Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How do neural networks encode compositional symbolic structure in their vector representations, and do they use tensor product representations?
papers.core_contribution: TPDNs show that RNNs can learn structured representations similar to tensor product representations for artificial tasks, but for real-world NLP tasks, representations are less structured, approximated by bag-of-words, suggesting training tasks may not induce robust structural representations.
papers.conclusion: RNNs trained on structure-sensitive tasks learn representations well approximated by tensor-product representations, but sentence encoders for NLP tasks show less structure, approximated by bag-of-words.
papers.key_findings:
TPDNs can closely approximate RNN representations for digit sequence copying tasks, indicating structured encoding.
Linear RNNs use bidirectional role schemes, while tree RNNs use tree position roles for representation.
For natural language processing models like InferSent and Skip-thought, representations are well approximated by bag-of-words, showing limited structure.
The nature of learned representations is related to the RNN's structure and the training task.
Training tasks influence whether networks discover structured or unstructured representations.
papers.abstract: We introduce an analysis technique for understanding compositional structure present in the vector representations used by neural networks. The inner workings of neural networks are notoriously difficult to understand, and in particular it is far from clear how they manage to perform remarkably well on tasks that depend on compositional structure even though they use continuous vector representations with no obvious compositional structure. Using our analysis technique, we show that the representations of these models can be closely approximated by Tensor Product Representations, a type of interpretable structure that lends significant insight into the workings of these hard-to-interpret models.

papers.title: Learning Transformer Programs
papers.research_question: How can we train Transformers that are mechanistically interpretable by design, rather than reverse-engineering black-box models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method for training Transformers that are interpretable by design, which can be automatically converted into discrete, human-readable programs after training.
papers.conclusion: Transformer Programs represent a promising step towards building intrinsically interpretable machine learning models.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer Programs can achieve reasonable performance on a variety of tasks, including algorithmic problems and NLP tasks, comparable to standard Transformers of similar size.
The learned programs are easy to interpret and can be analyzed using standard code analysis tools, such as debuggers, to understand model behavior and debug errors.
The method faces optimization challenges, especially when scaling to larger vocabularies and sequence lengths, and the learned programs can be non-intuitive.
papers.limitation:
Optimization challenges make it difficult to scale to larger vocabularies and sequence lengths.
The learned programs can be complicated and non-intuitive, differing from human-written solutions.
future_direction: Scaling Transformer Programs to larger models and more complex tasks.
Developing methods for automatically analyzing the resulting programs and imposing inductive biases for more interpretable programs.
papers.abstract: Recent research in mechanistic interpretability has attempted to reverse-engineer Transformer models by carefully inspecting network weights and activations. However, these approaches require considerable manual effort and still fall short of providing complete, faithful descriptions of the underlying algorithms. In this work, we introduce a procedure for training Transformers that are mechanistically interpretable by design. We build on RASP [Weiss et al., 2021], a programming language that can be compiled into Transformer weights. Instead of compiling human-written programs into Transformers, we design a modified Transformer that can be trained using gradient-based optimization and then automatically converted into a discrete, human-readable program. We refer to these models as Transformer Programs. To validate our approach, we learn Transformer Programs for a variety of problems, including an in-context learning task, a suite of algorithmic problems (e.g. sorting, recognizing Dyck languages), and NLP tasks including named entity recognition and text classification. The Transformer Programs can automatically find reasonable solutions, performing on par with standard Transformers of comparable size; and, more importantly, they are easy to interpret. To demonstrate these advantages, we convert Transformers into Python programs and use off-the-shelf code analysis tools to debug model errors and identify the "circuits" used to solve different sub-problems. We hope that Transformer Programs open a new path toward the goal of intrinsically interpretable machine learning.

papers.title: Protein Circuit Tracing via Cross-layer Transcoders
papers.research_question: How can we uncover the computational circuits in protein language models that underlie their predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ProtoMech, a framework using cross-layer transcoders to discover computational circuits in protein language models, achieving high performance recovery and enabling protein design.
papers.conclusion: ProtoMech establishes a principled framework for protein circuit tracing, revealing interpretable computational pathways and enabling effective protein design.
papers.key_findings:
ProtoMech recovers 82–89% of the original ESM2 performance on protein family classification and function prediction tasks.
ProtoMech identifies compact circuits using <1% of the latent space while retaining up to 79% of model accuracy.
Steering along the discovered circuits enables high-fitness protein design, outperforming baseline methods in more than 70% of cases.
The circuits correspond to known structural and functional motifs, such as binding sites and catalytic loops.
ProtoMech provides a more accurate approximation of ESM2's computation than per-layer transcoder baselines.
papers.limitation: Full replacement models, where both attention and MLP computations are replaced, lead to substantial performance degradation due to compounding reconstruction errors.
future_direction: Developing robust full replacement models remains an active area of research.
Using a tanh loss for constraining sparsity is an interesting future direction.
papers.abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) have emerged as powerful predictors of protein structure and function. However, the computational circuits underlying their predictions remain poorly understood. Recent mechanistic interpretability methods decompose pLM representations into interpretable features, but they treat each layer independently and thus fail to capture cross-layer computation, limiting their ability to approximate the full model. We introduce ProtoMech, a framework for discovering computational circuits in pLMs using cross-layer transcoders that learn sparse latent representations jointly across layers to capture the model's full computational circuitry. Applied to the pLM ESM2, ProtoMech recovers 82-89% of the original performance on protein family classification and function prediction tasks. ProtoMech then identifies compressed circuits that use <1% of the latent space while retaining up to 79% of model accuracy, revealing correspondence with structural and functional motifs, including binding, signaling, and stability. Steering along these circuits enables high-fitness protein design, surpassing baseline methods in more than 70% of cases. These results establish ProtoMech as a principled framework for protein circuit tracing.

papers.title: Interpreting Physics in Video World Models
papers.research_question: Whether video-based models rely on factorized representations of physical variables or implicitly represent them in a task-specific, distributed manner, and how physical information is organized within video encoders.
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a sharp intermediate-depth transition (Physics Emergence Zone) where physical variables become accessible in video encoders, revealing that models use distributed, task-specific representations rather than factorized, physics-engine-like representations.
papers.conclusion: The findings argue against compact, reusable latent physics states and instead support a distributed, task-specific representational regime, aligning with heuristic-based accounts of intuitive physics.
papers.key_findings:
A Physics Emergence Zone at approximately one-third network depth marks where physical information becomes linearly accessible.
Scalar motion quantities (speed, acceleration magnitude) are available from early layers, while motion direction emerges only at the Physics Emergence Zone.
Direction and possible–impossible physics judgments occupy nearly orthogonal representational subspaces, indicating task-specific representations.
Local spatiotemporal attention heads within the Physics Emergence Zone are causally important for both direction encoding and physics judgments.
Direction is encoded as a high-dimensional population code with circular geometry, requiring coordinated intervention across many dimensions to steer.
papers.limitation:
Analysis limited to encoder-based video transformers trained with masked objectives; autoregressive or diffusion models may exhibit different representational structure.
Focus on possible–impossible discrimination and controlled motion variables does not isolate richer physical computations such as contact dynamics, force inference, or long-horizon interaction.
Methods characterize representational accessibility and coarse causal influence rather than a complete circuit-level mechanism.
Synthetic toy-ball dataset may not reflect how physical structure is represented in natural video.
papers.abstract: A long-standing question in physical reasoning is whether video-based models need to rely on factorized representations of physical variables in order to make physically accurate predictions, or whether they can implicitly represent such variables in a task-specific, distributed manner. While modern video world models achieve strong performance on intuitive physics benchmarks, it remains unclear which of these representational regimes they implement internally. Here, we present the first interpretability study to directly examine physical representations inside large-scale video encoders. Using layerwise probing, subspace geometry, patch-level decoding, and targeted attention ablations, we characterize where physical information becomes accessible and how it is organized within encoder-based video transformers. Across architectures, we identify a sharp intermediate-depth transition -- which we call the Physics Emergence Zone -- at which physical variables become accessible. Physics-related representations peak shortly after this transition and degrade toward the output layers. Decomposing motion into explicit variables, we find that scalar quantities such as speed and acceleration are available from early layers onwards, whereas motion direction becomes accessible only at the Physics Emergence Zone. Notably, we find that direction is encoded through a high-dimensional population structure with circular geometry, requiring coordinated multi-feature intervention to control. These findings suggest that modern video models do not use factorized representations of physical variables like a classical physics engine. Instead, they use a distributed representation that is nonetheless sufficient for making physical predictions.

papers.title: Mechanistic Neural Networks for Scientific Machine Learning
papers.research_question: How can we design neural networks that explicitly learn and solve ordinary differential equations (ODEs) as representations in a parallel and scalable way to enhance interpretability and efficiency in scientific machine learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces Mechanistic Neural Networks, a novel neural network design that incorporates a Mechanistic Block to explicitly learn governing differential equations as representations, and a parallel, differentiable ODE solver (NeuRLP) for efficient and scalable training in scientific machine learning.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic Neural Networks are a powerful and versatile approach for scientific machine learning, capable of discovering and modeling complex dynamical systems with high interpretability and efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic Neural Networks can discover governing equations from data and outperform the SINDy method in some cases, including for nonlinear and rational function derivatives.
The NeuRLP solver is efficient, parallel, and allows for faster training and longer rollouts compared to traditional sequential ODE solvers like Runge-Kutta.
The method is versatile and achieves competitive or state-of-the-art performance on a range of scientific ML tasks, including PDE solving, equation discovery, and dynamical systems modeling.
The NeuRLP solver can learn adaptive time steps, becoming finer in regions where the fit is poor.
The method can handle multiple independent trajectories and learn a single governing equation from them, improving generalization.
papers.limitation: The cumulative error of the NeuRLP solver can become large for equations where the coefficients c0/c2 and c1/c2 are large relative to the step size.
papers.abstract: This paper presents Mechanistic Neural Networks, a neural network design for machine learning applications in the sciences. It incorporates a new Mechanistic Block in standard architectures to explicitly learn governing differential equations as representations, revealing the underlying dynamics of data and enhancing interpretability and efficiency in data modeling. Central to our approach is a novel Relaxed Linear Programming Solver (NeuRLP) inspired by a technique that reduces solving linear ODEs to solving linear programs. This integrates well with neural networks and surpasses the limitations of traditional ODE solvers enabling scalable GPU parallel processing. Overall, Mechanistic Neural Networks demonstrate their versatility for scientific machine learning applications, adeptly managing tasks from equation discovery to dynamic systems modeling. We prove their comprehensive capabilities in analyzing and interpreting complex scientific data across various applications, showing significant performance against specialized state-of-the-art methods.

papers.title: Global Concept-Based Interpretability for Graph Neural Networks via Neuron Analysis
papers.research_question: What concepts do GNN neurons detect, and how can they be used for global explanations of GNNs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that GNN neurons act as concept detectors and introduces a method for global concept-based explanations of GNNs.
papers.conclusion: This work is an initial step in neuron-level analysis of GNNs, providing a method for global concept-based explanations that offers advantages in transparency and user-friendliness.
papers.key_findings:
GNN neurons have alignment with concepts formulated as logical compositions of node and neighborhood properties.
There is a trade-off between training duration and neuron-level interpretability: longer training reduces interpretability.
The proposed global explainability approach has advantages over the state-of-the-art (XGNN) by being concept-based and providing logical descriptions.
Interpretable concepts are detected by GNN neurons, and they vary across different tasks (e.g., chemical substructures, social network motifs).
Not all detected concepts are useful for the model's predictions; some are redundant or have low contribution.
future_direction: Explore the relationship between neuron interpretability and theoretical issues such as the information bottleneck, over-smoothing and over-squashing.
Investigate model pruning by manually removing or suppressing certain concepts to reduce parameters while preserving performance.
papers.abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are highly effective on a variety of graph-related tasks; however, they lack interpretability and transparency. Current explainability approaches are typically local and treat GNNs as black-boxes. They do not look inside the model, inhibiting human trust in the model and explanations. Motivated by the ability of neurons to detect high-level semantic concepts in vision models, we perform a novel analysis on the behaviour of individual GNN neurons to answer questions about GNN interpretability, and propose new metrics for evaluating the interpretability of GNN neurons. We propose a novel approach for producing global explanations for GNNs using neuron-level concepts to enable practitioners to have a high-level view of the model. Specifically, (i) to the best of our knowledge, this is the first work which shows that GNN neurons act as concept detectors and have strong alignment with concepts formulated as logical compositions of node degree and neighbourhood properties; (ii) we quantitatively assess the importance of detected concepts, and identify a trade-off between training duration and neuron-level interpretability; (iii) we demonstrate that our global explainability approach has advantages over the current state-of-the-art -- we can disentangle the explanation into individual interpretable concepts backed by logical descriptions, which reduces potential for bias and improves user-friendliness.

papers.title: Same Task, Different Circuits: Disentangling Modality-Specific Mechanisms in VLMs
papers.research_question: Why do Vision-Language models (VLMs) perform worse on visual tasks compared to analogous textual tasks?
papers.core_contribution: VLMs use largely disjoint circuits for visual and textual tasks, but the functional difference lies in data processing; patching visual token embeddings from later layers to earlier layers (back-patching) reduces the performance gap without training.
papers.conclusion: The performance gap in VLMs arises from disjoint circuits for different modalities, and back-patching provides a training-free method to reduce it by aligning visual representations earlier.
papers.key_findings:
Vision and language circuits are structurally disjoint but implement similar functionalities for query and generation.
The performance gap stems from differences in processing modality-specific data tokens.
Visual token representations become aligned with textual counterparts only in later layers.
Back-patching visual token embeddings from later to earlier layers improves visual task accuracy, closing about a third of the performance gap on average.
The intervention is effective across multiple models and tasks.
papers.limitation:
Focused on single-image question-answering tasks with single-token completions.
Current open models struggle with complex visual reasoning, limiting analysis.
Circuit analysis methods are limited to single-token completions.
Back-patching closes only 32% of the performance gap; causes for the remaining gap are unclear.
Analysis is limited to adapter-based VLMs; may not apply to other fusion approaches.
future_direction: Explore multi-image scenarios, different prompt orders, and more complex visual reasoning tasks.
Investigate varied computational resources per token, especially for visual inputs.
Extend analysis to VLMs with different fusion approaches.
papers.abstract: Vision-Language models (VLMs) show impressive abilities to answer questions on visual inputs (e.g., counting objects in an image), yet demonstrate higher accuracies when performing an analogous task on text (e.g., counting words in a text). We investigate this accuracy gap by identifying and comparing the \textit{circuits} - the task-specific computational sub-graphs - in different modalities. We show that while circuits are largely disjoint between modalities, they implement relatively similar functionalities: the differences lie primarily in processing modality-specific data positions (an image or a text sequence). Zooming in on the image data representations, we observe they become aligned with the higher-performing analogous textual representations only towards later layers, too late in processing to effectively influence subsequent positions. To overcome this, we patch the representations of visual data tokens from later layers back into earlier layers. In experiments with multiple tasks and models, this simple intervention closes a third of the performance gap between the modalities, on average. Our analysis sheds light on the multi-modal performance gap in VLMs and suggests a training-free approach for reducing it.

papers.title: A Unified Theory of Sparse Dictionary Learning in Mechanistic Interpretability: Piecewise Biconvexity and Spurious Minima
papers.research_question: Why do sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, and what is the theoretical understanding of these phenomena?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a unified theoretical framework for sparse dictionary learning (SDL) that explains failure modes like feature absorption and dead neurons via piecewise biconvex optimization and non-identifiability, and proposes feature anchoring to improve feature recovery.
papers.conclusion: The theoretical framework explains persistent failure modes in SDL methods, and feature anchoring provides an effective, method-agnostic technique to improve feature recovery by reducing underdetermination.
papers.key_findings:
SDL optimization exhibits piecewise biconvex structure, enabling analysis of its landscape.
SDL suffers from non-identifiability, leading to spurious minima that result in polysemantic features.
Feature absorption arises naturally from hierarchical concept structures and corresponds to partial minima.
Feature anchoring, which constrains a subset of features to known directions, significantly improves feature recovery across SDL methods.
Dead neuron resampling helps escape spurious local minima in large language models.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical analysis relies on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, which assumes features are linear directions; this may not hold for all representations.
The synthetic benchmark, while controlled, may not capture all complexities of real-world data.
Feature anchoring requires anchor features, which may be difficult to obtain in some settings.
future_direction: Extending the theory to non-linear representations.
Applying feature anchoring to more domains and real-world tasks.
Integrating anchoring with other SDL improvements and scaling to larger models.
papers.abstract: As AI models achieve remarkable capabilities across diverse domains, understanding what representations they learn and how they encode concepts has become increasingly important for both scientific progress and trustworthy deployment. Recent works in mechanistic interpretability have widely reported that neural networks represent meaningful concepts as linear directions in their representation spaces and often encode diverse concepts in superposition. Various sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods, including sparse autoencoders, transcoders, and crosscoders, are utilized to address this by training auxiliary models with sparsity constraints to disentangle these superposed concepts into monosemantic features. These methods are the backbone of modern mechanistic interpretability, yet in practice they consistently produce polysemantic features, feature absorption, and dead neurons, with very limited theoretical understanding of why these phenomena occur. Existing theoretical work is limited to tied-weight sparse autoencoders, leaving the broader family of SDL methods without formal grounding. We develop the first unified theoretical framework that casts all major SDL variants as a single piecewise biconvex optimization problem, and characterize its global solution set, non-identifiability, and spurious optima. This analysis yields principled explanations for feature absorption and dead neurons. To expose these pathologies under full ground-truth access, we introduce the Linear Representation Bench. Guided by our theory, we propose feature anchoring, a novel technique that restores SDL identifiability, substantially improving feature recovery across synthetic benchmarks and real neural representations.

papers.title: A Mathematical Philosophy of Explanations in Mechanistic Interpretability -- The Strange Science Part I.i
papers.research_question: What is the nature of explanations in mechanistic interpretability? How can we define mechanistic interpretability and what are its inherent limits?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a philosophical framework for mechanistic interpretability, including the Explanatory View Hypothesis, a definition of mechanistic interpretability as producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations, and the Principle of Explanatory Optimism.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that if the Principle of Explanatory Optimism holds, interpretability could enable humans to understand machine knowledge, making it a crucial scientific endeavor for the future of human understanding.
papers.key_findings:
The Explanatory View Hypothesis posits that neural networks contain implicit explanations of their behavior that can be extracted and understood.
Explanatory Faithfulness is defined as the extent to which an explanation matches the model's internal ur-explanations, and is well-defined under the Explanatory View.
Mechanistic Interpretability is defined as the practice of producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations of neural networks.
Mechanistic Interpretability has inherent limits, such as theory-ladenness and the potential for high explanatory complexity that may make models incomprehensible to humans.
The Principle of Explanatory Optimism, which states that the algorithmic structure of generalizing neural networks is human-understandable, is a necessary precondition for the success of Mechanistic Interpretability.
papers.limitation:
Mechanistic interpretability may be limited by the theory-ladenness of observations, where the interpreter's prior theories influence what they can discover.
There is a risk that the explanatory complexity of models might be too high for humans to understand, which would make mechanistic interpretability intractable.
future_direction: Formalize the conjectures of Strong and Weak Explanatory Optimism, including defining explanatory complexity classes and explanatory universality.
Prove the formalized conjectures to assess the truth value of the Principle of Explanatory Optimism.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability aims to understand neural networks through causal explanations. We argue for the Explanatory View Hypothesis: that Mechanistic Interpretability research is a principled approach to understanding models because neural networks contain implicit explanations which can be extracted and understood. We hence show that Explanatory Faithfulness, an assessment of how well an explanation fits a model, is well-defined. We propose a definition of Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) as the practice of producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations of neural networks, allowing us to distinguish MI from other interpretability paradigms and detail MI's inherent limits. We formulate the Principle of Explanatory Optimism, a conjecture which we argue is a necessary precondition for the success of Mechanistic Interpretability.

papers.title: Decoding Structure-Spectrum Relationships with Physically Organized Latent Spaces
papers.research_question: The paper investigates how to construct an interpretable latent space that maps individual structure descriptors to spectral trends in XANES spectra, enabling the discovery of structure-spectrum relationships.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces RankAAE, a semi-supervised method that constructs an interpretable latent space for spectra, enabling the discovery of structure-spectrum relationships by disentangling contributions from multiple structural descriptors.
papers.conclusion: The RankAAE methodology has great potential to assist researchers in interpreting complex scientific data, testing physical hypotheses, and revealing new patterns that extend scientific insight.
papers.key_findings:
RankAAE produces a regularized latent space that ensures decoded spectra are physical, unlike standard autoencoders.
The method aligns individual latent dimensions with specific structure descriptors (e.g., oxidation state, coordination number) through a rank constraint.
RankAAE reveals new structure-spectrum relationships that are visually indiscernible in large datasets.
The method works consistently across eight transition metal oxide families (Ti to Cu).
RankAAE enables comparison of different sets of structure descriptors and assesses their importance in capturing spectral variations.
