papers.abstract: A new semi-supervised machine learning method for the discovery of structure-spectrum relationships is developed and demonstrated using the specific example of interpreting X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectra. This method constructs a one-to-one mapping between individual structure descriptors and spectral trends. Specifically, an adversarial autoencoder is augmented with a novel rank constraint (RankAAE). The RankAAE methodology produces a continuous and interpretable latent space, where each dimension can track an individual structure descriptor. As a part of this process, the model provides a robust and quantitative measure of the structure-spectrum relationship by decoupling intertwined spectral contributions from multiple structural characteristics. This makes it ideal for spectral interpretation and the discovery of new descriptors. The capability of this procedure is showcased by considering five local structure descriptors and a database of over fifty thousand simulated XANES spectra across eight first-row transition metal oxide families. The resulting structure-spectrum relationships not only reproduce known trends in the literature, but also reveal unintuitive ones that are visually indiscernible in large data sets. The results suggest that the RankAAE methodology has great potential to assist researchers to interpret complex scientific data, test physical hypotheses, and reveal new patterns that extend scientific insight.

papers.title: Transcoders Find Interpretable LLM Feature Circuits
papers.research_question: How can we perform fine-grained circuit analysis through MLP sublayers in transformers, given the polysemanticity of neurons? The paper proposes transcoders as a solution to enable input-invariant circuit analysis.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces transcoders, a method for approximating MLP sublayers with sparse, interpretable features, enabling input-invariant circuit analysis through MLPs.
papers.conclusion: Transcoders are an effective tool for decomposing model computations involving MLPs into interpretable circuits, enabling scalable and interpretable circuit analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Transcoders are as interpretable as SAEs and perform similarly or better in terms of sparsity and faithfulness.
Transcoders enable circuit analysis that factorizes into input-invariant and input-dependent terms, allowing for general claims about model behavior.
Blind case studies demonstrate that transcoders can reverse-engineer features without looking at activating examples.
Analysis of the GPT2-small greater-than circuit reveals new insights, such as the role of the MLP0 layer.
papers.limitation:
Transcoders may not capture all nuances of the original MLP, as seen in the 'caught' feature example where the transcoder did not accurately model the difference between 'was caught' and 'caught the ball'.
Blind case studies had some failures, indicating that circuit analysis with transcoders is not always perfect.
future_direction: Scaling transcoders to larger models.
Applying transcoders to more tasks and models.
papers.abstract: A key goal in mechanistic interpretability is circuit analysis: finding sparse subgraphs of models corresponding to specific behaviors or capabilities. However, MLP sublayers make fine-grained circuit analysis on transformer-based language models difficult. In particular, interpretable features -- such as those found by sparse autoencoders (SAEs) -- are typically linear combinations of extremely many neurons, each with its own nonlinearity to account for. Circuit analysis in this setting thus either yields intractably large circuits or fails to disentangle local and global behavior. To address this we explore transcoders, which seek to faithfully approximate a densely activating MLP layer with a wider, sparsely-activating MLP layer. We introduce a novel method for using transcoders to perform weights-based circuit analysis through MLP sublayers. The resulting circuits neatly factorize into input-dependent and input-invariant terms. We then successfully train transcoders on language models with 120M, 410M, and 1.4B parameters, and find them to perform at least on par with SAEs in terms of sparsity, faithfulness, and human-interpretability. Finally, we apply transcoders to reverse-engineer unknown circuits in the model, and we obtain novel insights regarding the "greater-than circuit" in GPT2-small. Our results suggest that transcoders can prove effective in decomposing model computations involving MLPs into interpretable circuits. Code is available at https://github.com/jacobdunefsky/transcoder_circuits/.

papers.title: Shapley Flow: A Graph-based Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions
papers.research_question: How can we interpret model predictions by accounting for dependencies among features using causal graphs?
papers.core_contribution: Shapley Flow is a novel edge attribution method that generalizes Shapley values to causal graphs, providing a complete view of feature importance by accounting for both direct and indirect effects.
papers.conclusion: Shapley Flow extends Shapley value axioms to causal graphs, resulting in a unique edge attribution method that unifies previous approaches and enables joint understanding of direct and indirect feature impacts.
papers.key_findings:
Shapley Flow uniquely satisfies a generalization of Shapley value axioms for directed acyclic graphs.
It unifies previous feature attribution methods including SHAP, Asymmetric Shapley Values (ASV), and Owen values.
Shapley Flow enables understanding of both direct and indirect impacts of features on model predictions.
The method is model-agnostic and can be applied to arbitrary machine learning pipelines.
Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that Shapley Flow provides more comprehensive explanations compared to existing approaches.
papers.limitation: Shapley Flow relies on access to a complete causal graph, which may not always be available or accurate.
future_direction: Can Shapley Flow work with partially defined causal graphs?
How to explore Shapley Flow attribution when the causal graph is complex?
Can Shapley Flow be useful for feature selection?
papers.abstract: Many existing approaches for estimating feature importance are problematic because they ignore or hide dependencies among features. A causal graph, which encodes the relationships among input variables, can aid in assigning feature importance. However, current approaches that assign credit to nodes in the causal graph fail to explain the entire graph. In light of these limitations, we propose Shapley Flow, a novel approach to interpreting machine learning models. It considers the entire causal graph, and assigns credit to \textit{edges} instead of treating nodes as the fundamental unit of credit assignment. Shapley Flow is the unique solution to a generalization of the Shapley value axioms to directed acyclic graphs. We demonstrate the benefit of using Shapley Flow to reason about the impact of a model's input on its output. In addition to maintaining insights from existing approaches, Shapley Flow extends the flat, set-based, view prevalent in game theory based explanation methods to a deeper, \textit{graph-based}, view. This graph-based view enables users to understand the flow of importance through a system, and reason about potential interventions.

papers.title: What Does BERT Learn about the Structure of Language?
papers.research_question: What linguistic structure does BERT learn? Specifically, can we unveil the representations learned by BERT to proto-linguistics structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that BERT captures hierarchical linguistic structure, with surface features in lower layers, syntactic in middle, and semantic in higher layers, and that it uses deeper layers for long-distance dependencies and implicitly captures tree-like structures.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that BERT captures structural properties of English language, with a hierarchy of linguistic signals and compositional modeling that parallels traditional syntactic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers, which gets diluted in higher layers.
BERT embeds a rich hierarchy of linguistic signals: surface information at the bottom, syntactic in the middle, and semantic at the top.
BERT requires deeper layers to handle long-distance dependency information, such as subject-verb agreement with more attractors.
BERT implicitly implements a tree-based compositional scheme, as shown by Tensor Product Decomposition Networks (TPDN) approximating BERT's representations.
The untrained version of BERT in higher layers outperforms the trained version in predicting sentence length, indicating that training trades off basic surface features for more complex information.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to English and may not generalize to other languages or noisy user-generated content.
future_direction: Investigating if the results transfer to other domains with higher syntactic variability, such as noisy user-generated content or morphologically-rich languages.
papers.abstract: BERT is a recent language representation model that has surprisingly performed well in diverse language understanding benchmarks. This result indicates the possibility that BERT networks capture structural information about language. In this work, we provide novel support for this claim by performing a series of experiments to unpack the elements of English language structure learned by BERT. We first show that BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers. We also show that BERT's intermediate layers encode a rich hierarchy of linguistic information, with surface features at the bottom, syntactic features in the middle and semantic features at the top. BERT turns out to require deeper layers when long-distance dependency information is required, e.g. to track subjectverb agreement. Finally, we show that BERT representations capture linguistic information in a compositional way that mimics classical, tree-like structures.

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of LoRA-Adapted Language Models for Nuclear Reactor Safety Applications
papers.research_question: How does LoRA adaptation alter neuron activation patterns in an LLM for a nuclear reactor safety domain, and what is the causal role of these altered neurons?
papers.core_contribution: This paper presents a methodology for tracing domain expertise in a LoRA-adapted LLM to a sparse set of neurons and demonstrates that the model's expertise is an emergent property of a neural circuit, providing a pathway for nuclear-grade AI assurance.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates a replicable methodology for moving beyond treating LLMs as opaque black boxes towards a mechanistic understanding of their function, offering a pathway to achieve nuclear-grade AI assurance by identifying, monitoring, and causally testing knowledge-bearing neural circuits.
papers.key_findings:
LoRA fine-tuning on a BWR dataset induced systematic changes in the activation patterns of a small set of neurons in the final MLP layer.
Silencing the entire group of six key neurons collectively caused a statistically significant degradation in BLEU score, while silencing most individual neurons did not, supporting a circuit-based view of knowledge encoding.
Qualitative analysis revealed distinct functional roles for key neurons, such as encoding core technical concepts (#1066, #1086), suppressing generalist language (#941), and representing procedural logic (#176).
The adapted model produced more concise and precise answers than the base model, as measured by a decrease in average answer length and an increase in BLEU score.
The findings suggest that verifying the integrity of distributed neural circuits, rather than individual components, is crucial for safety assurance in nuclear applications.
papers.limitation: The reliance on the BLEU score, while justified for measuring output precision, does not verify factual accuracy.
future_direction: Development of domain-specific evaluation metrics that can automatically verify technical correctness against a trusted knowledge base.
Extending the methodology to other critical nuclear systems, including Pressurized Water Reactors (PWRs) and advanced reactor designs.
Validating the approach across different model architectures, model scales, and technical documentation corpora.
papers.abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into safety-critical domains, such as nuclear engineering, necessitates a deep understanding of their internal reasoning processes. This paper presents a novel methodology for interpreting how an LLM encodes and utilizes domain-specific knowledge, using a Boiling Water Reactor system as a case study. We adapted a general-purpose LLM (Gemma-3-1b-it) to the nuclear domain using a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique known as Low-Rank Adaptation. By comparing the neuron activation patterns of the base model to those of the fine-tuned model, we identified a sparse set of neurons whose behavior was significantly altered during the adaptation process. To probe the causal role of these specialized neurons, we employed a neuron silencing technique. Our results demonstrate that while silencing most of these specialized neurons individually did not produce a statistically significant effect, deactivating the entire group collectively led to a statistically significant degradation in task performance. Qualitative analysis further revealed that silencing these neurons impaired the model's ability to generate detailed, contextually accurate technical information. This paper provides a concrete methodology for enhancing the transparency of an opaque black-box model, allowing domain expertise to be traced to verifiable neural circuits. This offers a pathway towards achieving nuclear-grade artificial intelligence (AI) assurance, addressing the verification and validation challenges mandated by nuclear regulatory frameworks (e.g., 10 CFR 50 Appendix B), which have limited AI deployment in safety-critical nuclear operations.

papers.title: Partnering with Radical AI to Advance Materials Science With Interpretability
papers.core_contribution: This blog announces a partnership between Radical AI and Goodfire to apply interpretability methods to AI-driven materials discovery models, aiming to extract underlying physical and chemical principles for scientific insight and more explainable AI.
papers.conclusion: The collaboration represents a significant step towards interpretable AI that bridges correlation and causation, accelerating materials discovery and fundamental understanding of how AI learns about the physical world.
papers.abstract: This blog announces a partnership between Radical AI and Goodfire to apply interpretability methods to AI-driven materials discovery models, aiming to extract underlying physical and chemical principles for scientific insight and more explainable AI. The collaboration represents a significant step towards interpretable AI that bridges correlation and causation, accelerating materials discovery and fundamental understanding of how AI learns about the physical world.

papers.title: On the Symmetries of Deep Learning Models and their Internal Representations
papers.research_question: How do the symmetries of a network architecture (via intertwiner groups) relate to the symmetries in the network's internal representations of data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces intertwiner groups to connect architectural symmetries with symmetries in internal representations, and shows that for ReLU networks, the activation basis is special for interpretability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that intertwiner groups connect architectural symmetries to representation symmetries, and provide a justification for focusing on activation basis in ReLU networks for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Intertwiner groups describe weight space symmetries and propagate to symmetries in internal representations.
Stitching with GReLU transformations incurs a small accuracy penalty, indicating that much of the variation between networks can be accounted for by GReLU.
GReLU-Procrustes and GReLU-CKA are effective dissimilarity measures invariant to GReLU transformations.
For ReLU networks, interpretability is higher in the activation basis than in arbitrary linear combinations, but this is not the case for networks without ReLU.
papers.limitation:
The theory does not fully account for residual connections, as noted in remark 3.6.
Stitching with GReLU does not achieve full accuracy, indicating that internal representations are not perfectly aligned by permutations and scalings.
papers.abstract: Symmetry is a fundamental tool in the exploration of a broad range of complex systems. In machine learning symmetry has been explored in both models and data. In this paper we seek to connect the symmetries arising from the architecture of a family of models with the symmetries of that family's internal representation of data. We do this by calculating a set of fundamental symmetry groups, which we call the intertwiner groups of the model. We connect intertwiner groups to a model's internal representations of data through a range of experiments that probe similarities between hidden states across models with the same architecture. Our work suggests that the symmetries of a network are propagated into the symmetries in that network's representation of data, providing us with a better understanding of how architecture affects the learning and prediction process. Finally, we speculate that for ReLU networks, the intertwiner groups may provide a justification for the common practice of concentrating model interpretability exploration on the activation basis in hidden layers rather than arbitrary linear combinations thereof.

papers.title: Factorized Explainer for Graph Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we avoid trivial solutions and improve the accuracy of explanations for Graph Neural Networks, particularly in multi-motif scenarios?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies trivial solutions in Graph Information Bottleneck (GIB)-based explanation methods for GNNs, proposes a modified GIB principle to avoid them, and introduces a factorized explainer (K-FactExplainer) that addresses locality and lossy aggregation issues to improve explanation accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed factorized explainer (K-FactExplainer) addresses the trivial solution problem in GIB-based explanations and improves explanation accuracy by mitigating locality and lossy aggregation issues in Graph Neural Networks.
papers.key_findings:
The original Graph Information Bottleneck (GIB) formulation for GNN explanation admits trivial solutions where the explanation subgraph signals the predicted label but is independent of the input graph.
Existing parametric explainers (e.g., PGExplainer) are local explanation methods and suffer from suboptimality due to locality and lossy aggregation in GNNs, especially in multi-motif classification tasks.
A modified GIB objective using cross-entropy between the ground truth label and the prediction on the explanation subgraph avoids the trivial solution problem.
The proposed K-FactExplainer, which combines multiple local explainers via a factorized model, mitigates locality and aggregation losses and achieves better explanation faithfulness than existing methods.
Empirical results on synthetic and real-world datasets show that K-FactExplainer consistently outperforms GIB-based baselines in terms of AUC-ROC.
papers.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have received increasing attention due to their ability to learn from graph-structured data. To open the black-box of these deep learning models, post-hoc instance-level explanation methods have been proposed to understand GNN predictions. These methods seek to discover substructures that explain the prediction behavior of a trained GNN. In this paper, we show analytically that for a large class of explanation tasks, conventional approaches, which are based on the principle of graph information bottleneck (GIB), admit trivial solutions that do not align with the notion of explainability. Instead, we argue that a modified GIB principle may be used to avoid the aforementioned trivial solutions. We further introduce a novel factorized explanation model with theoretical performance guarantees. The modified GIB is used to analyze the structural properties of the proposed factorized explainer. We conduct extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets to validate the effectiveness of our proposed factorized explainer.

papers.title: MIB: A Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark
papers.research_question: How can we know whether new mechanistic interpretability methods achieve real improvements? The paper proposes a benchmark to provide a basis for comparisons.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes MIB, a benchmark for mechanistic interpretability with two tracks (circuit localization and causal variable localization) to enable meaningful comparisons of interpretability methods.
papers.conclusion: MIB provides a standardized benchmark for comparing mechanistic interpretability methods, enabling meaningful evaluations and demonstrating progress in the field.
papers.key_findings:
Attribution and mask optimization methods perform best on circuit localization.
Supervised Distributed Alignment Search (DAS) performs best on causal variable localization.
Sparse autoencoder (SAE) features are not better than non-featurized hidden vectors (neurons) for causal variable localization.
MIB enables meaningful comparisons and shows real progress in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.limitation:
The set of models and tasks is incomplete, limiting generalizability.
The metrics may not capture all aspects of interpretability that researchers care about.
The benchmark focuses on localization and featurization, leaving out other mechanistic interpretability goals like editing or control.
future_direction: Expand MIB to include more models and tasks.
Develop more comprehensive metrics that capture other aspects of interpretability.
Extend the benchmark to other modalities beyond language.
papers.abstract: How can we know whether new mechanistic interpretability methods achieve real improvements? In pursuit of lasting evaluation standards, we propose MIB, a Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark, with two tracks spanning four tasks and five models. MIB favors methods that precisely and concisely recover relevant causal pathways or causal variables in neural language models. The circuit localization track compares methods that locate the model components - and connections between them - most important for performing a task (e.g., attribution patching or information flow routes). The causal variable localization track compares methods that featurize a hidden vector, e.g., sparse autoencoders (SAEs) or distributed alignment search (DAS), and align those features to a task-relevant causal variable. Using MIB, we find that attribution and mask optimization methods perform best on circuit localization. For causal variable localization, we find that the supervised DAS method performs best, while SAE features are not better than neurons, i.e., non-featurized hidden vectors. These findings illustrate that MIB enables meaningful comparisons, and increases our confidence that there has been real progress in the field.

papers.title: Neural Mechanisms Underlying Visual Object Recognition
papers.research_question: How does the brain achieve invariant visual object recognition? The paper seeks to build falsifiable, predictive models of the encoding (from images to neural activity) and decoding (from neural activity to behavior) processes underlying core object recognition.
papers.core_contribution: The paper builds predictive models of the neural mechanisms for visual object recognition: a hierarchical neural network (HMO) optimized for object recognition performance predicts neural responses in V4 and IT cortex, and a simple linear decoder from IT neural activity accurately predicts human behavior across many object recognition tasks.
papers.conclusion: Core object recognition is largely supported by a feed-forward cascade of neural activity, with encoding via a hierarchical nonlinear network and decoding via a simple linear readout from IT cortex.
papers.key_findings:
A simple linear decoder from IT neural population activity accurately predicts human object recognition behavior across a wide range of tasks.
Inactivation of face-selective IT subregions causally impairs face gender discrimination, and the impairment correlates with local linear separability of neural responses.
Hierarchical convolutional neural networks optimized for object recognition performance predict neural responses in V4 and IT cortex.
The HMO model achieves near-human performance on object categorization and explains a large fraction of neural response variance.
Combining the encoding (HMO) and decoding (linear) models provides an end-to-end mechanistic model of core object recognition.
papers.limitation:
The encoding and decoding models are imperfect and do not capture all of the variance in neural responses and behavior.
Only a subset of possible behavioral tasks has been explored, leaving open the possibility of failure on other tasks.
The origin of cortical heterogeneity (e.g., spatial clustering of face-selective neurons) and the functional significance of multiple cortical layers in each visual area are not explained.
The role of feedback circuits in complex visual behaviors (e.g., visual memory, learning, top-down inference) is not addressed.
future_direction: Extend causal methods to a battery of object recognition tests and build stronger quantitative links between neural activity and behavior.
Understand the role of feedback circuits in complex visual behaviors involving visual memory, learning, top-down inference, and sensorimotor integration over extended time periods.
papers.abstract: Invariant visual object recognition and the underlying neural representations are fundamental to higher-level human cognition. To understand these neural underpinnings, we combine human and monkey psychophysics, large-scale neurophysiology, neural perturbation methods, and computational modeling to construct falsifiable, predictive models that aim to fully account for the neural encoding and decoding processes that underlie visual object recognition. A predictive encoding model must minimally describe the transformation of the retinal image to population patterns of neural activity along the entire cortical ventral stream of visual processing and must accurately predict the responses to any retinal image. A predictive decoding model must minimally describe the transformation from those population patterns of neural activity to observed object recognition behavior (i.e., subject reports), and, given that population pattern of activity, it must accurately predict behavior for any object recognition task. To date, we have focused on core object recognition-a remarkable behavior that is accomplished with image viewing durations of <200 msec. Our work thus far reveals that the neural encoding process is reasonably well explained by a largely feed-forward, highly complex, multistaged nonlinear neural network-the current best neuronal simulation models predict approximately one-half of the relevant neuronal response variance across the highest levels of the ventral stream (areas V4 and IT). Remarkably, however, the decoding process from IT to behavior for all object recognition tasks tested thus far is very accurately predicted by simple direct linear conversion of the inferior temporal neural population state to behavior choice. We have recently examined the behavioral consequences of direct suppression of IT neural activity using pharmacological and optogenetic methods and find them to be well-explained by the same linear decoding model.

papers.title: Brain-optimized deep neural network models of human visual areas learn non-hierarchical representations
papers.research_question: Does hierarchical representation in deep neural networks (DNNs) improve the accuracy of predicting brain activity in human visual areas V1-V4?
papers.core_contribution: Hierarchical representations are not necessary to accurately predict human brain activity in V1-V4, and DNNs with diverse architectures (from strict serial hierarchies to multiple independent branches) can encode brain-like visual representations.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that hierarchical representations are not necessary for accurately predicting brain activity in human visual areas V1-V4, and brain-optimized DNNs can learn non-hierarchical representations while maintaining high accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Brain-optimized DNNs (GNet) predict brain activity in V1-V4 more accurately than task-optimized AlexNet for both natural and artificial stimuli.
Single-branch (GNet8j) and multi-branch (GNet8r) brain-optimized models yield similar prediction accuracy despite architectural differences.
Both single-branch and multi-branch models exhibit integration hierarchy, with receptive field sizes expanding from V1 to V4.
Only single-branch models (AlexNet and GNet8j) learn compositional and entailment hierarchies; multi-branch models (GNet8r) do not.
Hierarchical representations are not essential for accurate prediction of brain activity, as non-hierarchical models can achieve state-of-the-art accuracy.
papers.limitation: The best models leave much variance unexplained, accounting for at most 78% of explainable variance in brain activity.
future_direction: Developing new analytical tools for uncovering the function of representations encoded in different human visual areas using brain-optimized networks.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) optimized for visual tasks learn representations that align layer depth with the hierarchy of visual areas in the primate brain. One interpretation of this finding is that hierarchical representations are necessary to accurately predict brain activity in the primate visual system. To test this interpretation, we optimized DNNs to directly predict brain activity measured with fMRI in human visual areas V1-V4. We trained a single-branch DNN to predict activity in all four visual areas jointly, and a multi-branch DNN to predict each visual area independently. Although it was possible for the multi-branch DNN to learn hierarchical representations, only the single-branch DNN did so. This result shows that hierarchical representations are not necessary to accurately predict human brain activity in V1-V4, and that DNNs that encode brain-like visual representations may differ widely in their architecture, ranging from strict serial hierarchies to multiple independent branches.

papers.title: Extending Token Computation for LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: What is the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance? Can extending the Chain-of-Thought chain within the same prompt improve reasoning outcomes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel algorithm that extends computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought process by optimizing attention mechanisms, which improves reasoning capabilities, especially in non-STEM domains.
papers.conclusion: The study introduces an attention optimization method that enhances LLM reasoning, particularly in non-STEM domains, and sets the groundwork for more transparent and adaptable models for real-world applications.
papers.key_findings:
Increasing the number of computed tokens enhances LLM reasoning performance.
Attention patterns in middle layers are skewed by non-semantic tokens with high attention scores, which hinders reasoning.
The proposed algorithm re-balances attention distributions by emulating early layer attention patterns, leading to more extended and logical reasoning steps.
The method improves reasoning in non-STEM domains but may reduce accuracy in memory-dependent questions due to error propagation.
Larger models (e.g., 13B) show greater improvement with the method compared to smaller models (e.g., 7B).
papers.limitation:
The method reduces accuracy by 3 percentage points in memory-dependent questions from the MMLU dataset.
Extended reasoning may amplify error propagation in STEM categories where the model's reasoning capabilities are not robust.
Scarcity of logical process examples for STEM questions in training data may hinder performance.
future_direction: Integrate a training phase to enhance memory recall for early-answering questions.
Reduce memory and computational demands using techniques like ghost attention mechanisms.
Enhance interpretability of attention patterns across layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are pivotal in advancing natural language processing but often struggle with complex reasoning tasks due to inefficient attention distributions. In this paper, we explore the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance and introduce a novel method for extending computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process, utilizing attention mechanism optimization. By fine-tuning an LLM on a domain-specific, highly structured dataset, we analyze attention patterns across layers, identifying inefficiencies caused by non-semantic tokens with outlier high attention scores. To address this, we propose an algorithm that emulates early layer attention patterns across downstream layers to re-balance skewed attention distributions and enhance knowledge abstraction. Our findings demonstrate that our approach not only facilitates a deeper understanding of the internal dynamics of LLMs but also significantly improves their reasoning capabilities, particularly in non-STEM domains. Our study lays the groundwork for further innovations in LLM design, aiming to create more powerful, versatile, and responsible models capable of tackling a broad range of real-world applications.

papers.title: Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens (CORAL): Transferrable and Calibration-Aware Inference-Time Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve both accuracy and calibration of LLMs during inference by directly steering using correctness signals from internal activations, rather than optimizing proxies?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CORAL, a lightweight inference-time steering method that uses regularized MLP probes on residual activations to improve accuracy and calibration in MCQA tasks, with demonstrated transferability across benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: CORAL provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference by extracting distributed correctness signals via regularized probes.
papers.key_findings:
CORAL consistently improves accuracy and calibration across three 7B models and multiple MCQA benchmarks.
CORAL's learned steering directions transfer without retraining to four held-out benchmarks, averaging 14% accuracy and 49% ECE improvements.
Correctness signals are distributed across many neurons and require supervised aggregation; sparse methods like SAE fail to capture them.
Middle layers (17-21) contain the most useful correctness signals for steering.
Regularized probes capture distributed correctness signals that sparse methods miss.
papers.limitation:
Limited to multiple-choice question answering; generalization to free-form generation is open.
Requires labeled data to train probes, which may not be available for all domains or languages.
Adds inference latency due to activation extraction and probe prediction.
Transfer performance depends on similarity between source and target tasks; dissimilar tasks yield smaller improvements.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit persistent miscalibration, especially after instruction tuning and preference alignment. Modified training objectives can improve calibration, but retraining is expensive. Inference-time steering offers a lightweight alternative, yet most existing methods optimize proxies for correctness rather than correctness itself. We introduce CORAL (Correctness-Optimized Residual Activation Lens), a regularized inference-time steering method that captures distributed correctness signals from model internal activations using weight-decay MLP probes. We evaluate CORAL across three 7B-parameter models and find that it consistently improves accuracy by 10\% and expected calibration error (ECE) by 50\% on average. We additionally demonstrate that these gains transfer without retraining to the complete published test sets of four held-out benchmarks (ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, Math-MC, OpenBookQA), averaging 14\% accuracy improvements and 49\% ECE improvements. Our results support the hypothesis that distributed information in model internals can be extracted using regularized probes when individual neurons are insufficient. CORAL thus provides a compute-efficient, transferable, and calibration-aware approach to improve MCQA performance during inference.

papers.title: Understanding polysemanticity in neural networks through coding theory
papers.research_question: How can coding theory and eigenspectrum analysis provide insights into polysemanticity and improve interpretability in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a coding theory perspective to neural network interpretability, using eigenspectrum analysis of activation covariance and random projections to understand polysemanticity, redundancy, and the trade-off between capacity and robustness in network codes.
papers.conclusion: The eigenspectrum analysis and random projections offer a top-down perspective on neural network interpretability, advancing understanding of code structure and suggesting new avenues for circuit-level interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks learn codes that balance capacity and redundancy, with eigenspectrum decay indicating the level of redundancy.
Dropout during training leads to faster eigenspectrum decay, more robust codes, and smoother random projections.
Random projections of hidden activations reveal the smoothness of the code, which is linked to eigenspectrum decay and can complement single-neuron interpretability methods.
In large language models, random projections provide explanatory power in layers where single-neuron methods perform poorly, suggesting complementary approaches.
The framework explains polysemanticity as an efficient encoding strategy and provides theoretical insights into optimal coding and error correction.
papers.limitation: Identifying the exact error-correcting code is beyond the scope of this paper.
future_direction: A systematic study of how eigenspectrum decay changes with network size.
Investigating the role of nonlinearities in the network code.
Further research into the underlying structure and behavior of deep learning models from a coding perspective.
papers.abstract: Despite substantial efforts, neural network interpretability remains an elusive goal, with previous research failing to provide succinct explanations of most single neurons' impact on the network output. This limitation is due to the polysemantic nature of most neurons, whereby a given neuron is involved in multiple unrelated network states, complicating the interpretation of that neuron. In this paper, we apply tools developed in neuroscience and information theory to propose both a novel practical approach to network interpretability and theoretical insights into polysemanticity and the density of codes. We infer levels of redundancy in the network's code by inspecting the eigenspectrum of the activation's covariance matrix. Furthermore, we show how random projections can reveal whether a network exhibits a smooth or non-differentiable code and hence how interpretable the code is. This same framework explains the advantages of polysemantic neurons to learning performance and explains trends found in recent results by Elhage et al.~(2022). Our approach advances the pursuit of interpretability in neural networks, providing insights into their underlying structure and suggesting new avenues for circuit-level interpretability.

papers.title: Interpretability Beyond Feature Attribution: Quantitative Testing with\n Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV)
papers.research_question: How can we interpret neural networks using human-defined concepts and quantify the sensitivity of predictions to these concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) to represent human-friendly concepts in a model's activation space, and a method (TCAV) to quantify the importance of these concepts to model predictions using directional derivatives.
papers.conclusion: TCAV provides a human-friendly linear interpretation of neural networks, allowing analysts to quantify the importance of user-defined concepts to model predictions, and has been shown to be a useful technique in various applications including bias detection and medical image analysis.
papers.key_findings:
CAVs align with intended concepts, validated by sorting images and activation maximization (deep dream).
TCAV can reveal biases in models, such as gender and race biases in image classifiers.
TCAV quantifies the importance of specific concepts to model classes (e.g., stripes for zebras, red for fire engines).
TCAV can help interpret model errors in medical applications, such as diabetic retinopathy grading.
In a controlled experiment, TCAV more accurately communicated concept importance to humans compared to saliency maps.
future_direction: Applying TCAV to other types of data (audio, video, sequences).
Using TCAV to identify adversarial examples.
Automatically identifying concepts.
papers.abstract:
The interpretation of deep learning models is a challenge due to their size,
complexity, and often opaque internal state. In addition, many systems, such as
image classifiers, operate on low-level features rather than high-level
concepts. To address these challenges, we introduce Concept Activation Vectors
(CAVs), which provide an interpretation of a neural net's internal state in
terms of human-friendly concepts. The key idea is to view the high-dimensional
internal state of a neural net as an aid, not an obstacle. We show how to use
CAVs as part of a technique, Testing with CAVs (TCAV), that uses directional
derivatives to quantify the degree to which a user-defined concept is important
to a classification result--for example, how sensitive a prediction of "zebra"
is to the presence of stripes. Using the domain of image classification as a
testing ground, we describe how CAVs may be used to explore hypotheses and
generate insights for a standard image classification network as well as a
medical application.

papers.title: Efficiently Democratizing Medical LLMs for 50 Languages via a Mixture of Language Family Experts
papers.research_question: How to efficiently adapt medical Large Language Models to many languages, especially low-resource ones, by analyzing internal information flow and using language family experts?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an efficient method to scale medical LLMs to 50 languages via language family experts and a Post-MoE architecture, based on the discovery of the 'Spread Out in the End' information flow mechanism.
papers.conclusion: The proposed Apollo-MoE method efficiently democratizes medical LLMs to 50 languages, demonstrating strong generalization and scalability.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered the 'Spread Out in the End' mechanism in multilingual MoE models: early layers concentrate cross-lingual information flow, later layers exhibit language-specific divergence.
Proposed Post-MoE architecture (MoE only in later layers) improves generalization to low-resource languages.
Introduced language family experts, enabling scaling to many languages without adding parameters.
Hybrid-k routing (language-specific experts with cross-lingual routing) outperforms Top-k and Language-Specific routing.
papers.abstract: Adapting medical Large Language Models to local languages can reduce barriers to accessing healthcare services, but data scarcity remains a significant challenge, particularly for low-resource languages. To address this, we first construct a high-quality medical dataset and conduct analysis to ensure its quality. In order to leverage the generalization capability of multilingual LLMs to efficiently scale to more resource-constrained languages, we explore the internal information flow of LLMs from a multilingual perspective using Mixture of Experts (MoE) modularity. Technically, we propose a novel MoE routing method that employs language-specific experts and cross-lingual routing. Inspired by circuit theory, our routing analysis revealed a Spread Out in the End information flow mechanism: while earlier layers concentrate cross-lingual information flow, the later layers exhibit language-specific divergence. This insight directly led to the development of the Post-MoE architecture, which applies sparse routing only in the later layers while maintaining dense others. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach enhances the generalization of multilingual models to other languages while preserving interpretability. Finally, to efficiently scale the model to 50 languages, we introduce the concept of language family experts, drawing on linguistic priors, which enables scaling the number of languages without adding additional parameters.

papers.title: Integrating clinical reasoning into large language model-based diagnosis through etiology-aware attention steering
papers.research_question: How can we enhance the diagnostic accuracy and clinical reasoning ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) in complex clinical scenarios?
papers.core_contribution: This study proposes an Etiology-Aware Attention Steering Framework that integrates structured clinical reasoning into LLM-based diagnosis by identifying and steering attention heads crucial for etiology reasoning, significantly improving diagnostic accuracy and reasoning focus.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework integrates etiology-aware attention guidance with authoritative clinical guidelines, significantly improving diagnostic accuracy, attention stability, and reasoning interpretability, holding strong potential for real-world clinical deployment in complex diagnostic environments.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed framework improves average diagnostic accuracy by 15.65% and boosts the average Reasoning Focus Score by 31.6% over baselines on the Consistent Diagnosis Cohort.
External validation on the Discrepant Diagnosis Cohort confirms the framework's effectiveness in enhancing diagnostic accuracy in real-world complex scenarios.
The Etiology-Aware Head Identification algorithm successfully pinpoints attention heads that exhibit strong alignment with etiological reasoning.
Ablation studies demonstrate the importance of each component (CRS annotation, Etiology-Aware Head Identification, Reasoning-Guided Loss) for overall performance.
The framework enhances the model's attention stability and reasoning interpretability across diverse diagnostic tasks.
future_direction: Extending the framework to a broader range of diseases and clinical scenarios.
Integrating multimodal data (e.g., medical images, lab waveforms) to enhance diagnostic reasoning.
Incorporating contrastive or self-supervised objectives to further enhance model robustness in low-resource or noisy environments.
papers.abstract: Objective: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate significant capabilities in medical text understanding and generation. However, their diagnostic reliability in complex clinical scenarios remains limited. This study aims to enhance LLMs' diagnostic accuracy and clinical reasoning ability. Method: We propose an Etiology-Aware Attention Steering Framework to integrate structured clinical reasoning into LLM-based diagnosis. Specifically, we first construct Clinical Reasoning Scaffolding (CRS) based on authoritative clinical guidelines for three representative acute abdominal emergencies: acute appendicitis, acute pancreatitis, and acute cholecystitis. Next, we develop the Etiology-Aware Head Identification algorithm to pinpoint attention heads crucial for the model's etiology reasoning. To ensure reliable clinical reasoning alignment, we introduce the Reasoning-Guided Parameter-Efficient Fine-tuning that embeds etiological reasoning cues into input representations and steers the selected Etiology-Aware Heads toward critical information through a Reasoning-Guided Loss function. Result: On the Consistent Diagnosis Cohort, our framework improves average diagnostic accuracy by 15.65% and boosts the average Reasoning Focus Score by 31.6% over baselines. External validation on the Discrepant Diagnosis Cohort further confirms its effectiveness in enhancing diagnostic accuracy. Further assessments via Reasoning Attention Frequency indicate that our models exhibit enhanced reliability when faced with real-world complex scenarios. Conclusion: This study presents a practical and effective approach to enhance clinical reasoning in LLM-based diagnosis. By aligning model attention with structured CRS, the proposed framework offers a promising paradigm for building more interpretable and reliable AI diagnostic systems in complex clinical settings.

papers.title: Learning local discrete features in explainable-by-design convolutional neural networks
papers.research_question: How can we design a convolutional neural network that is both high-performance and explainable by using a lateral inhibition mechanism to learn local discrete features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ExplaiNet, an explainable-by-design CNN that uses a lateral inhibition layer to learn local discrete feature vectors, enabling high accuracy and providing explanations via a probabilistic graph and motif discovery.
papers.conclusion: The ExplaiNet framework breaks the performance-explainability trade-off by introducing an explainable-by-design CNN that retains or surpasses baseline performance while providing causal explanations based on discrete feature motifs.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed ExplaiNet model achieves comparable or better performance than baseline ResNet and DenseNet architectures on tiny image datasets while providing explanations.
The lateral inhibition layer amplifies gradients of winner neurons, leading to ordered activations and the formation of local discrete feature vectors.
Feature motif discovery using the EXTREME algorithm reduces the vocabulary of local discrete features, providing concise explanations.
The explainer probabilistic graph can infer causal relationships between motifs of adjacent levels and attribute the model's output to global motifs.
Experiments show that the explainer can sometimes correctly classify samples that the neural predictor misclassifies, suggesting potential for ensemble use or adversarial sample detection.
papers.limitation:
Further research on regularization aspects of the lateral inhibition function is required to investigate the magnitude of weights and activations during training.
Experiments are limited to tiny image datasets due to computational resources; the method has not been tested on medium-resolution images or high numbers of classes.
future_direction: Investigate the proper amount of weight decay and restriction of input values for positively monotonic gradient amplification in the lateral inhibition function.
Scale up the method to train models on medium-resolution images, high number of classes, and with millions of parameters.
Adjust the EXTREME algorithm to support custom numeric system bases, making the conversion to the quaternary system optional.
papers.abstract: Our proposed framework attempts to break the trade-off between performance and explainability by introducing an explainable-by-design convolutional neural network (CNN) based on the lateral inhibition mechanism. The ExplaiNet model consists of the predictor, that is a high-accuracy CNN with residual or dense skip connections, and the explainer probabilistic graph that expresses the spatial interactions of the network neurons. The value on each graph node is a local discrete feature (LDF) vector, a patch descriptor that represents the indices of antagonistic neurons ordered by the strength of their activations, which are learned with gradient descent. Using LDFs as sequences we can increase the conciseness of explanations by repurposing EXTREME, an EM-based sequence motif discovery method that is typically used in molecular biology. Having a discrete feature motif matrix for each one of intermediate image representations, instead of a continuous activation tensor, allows us to leverage the inherent explainability of Bayesian networks. By collecting observations and directly calculating probabilities, we can explain causal relationships between motifs of adjacent levels and attribute the model's output to global motifs. Moreover, experiments on various tiny image benchmark datasets confirm that our predictor ensures the same level of performance as the baseline architecture for a given count of parameters and/or layers. Our novel method shows promise to exceed this performance while providing an additional stream of explanations. In the solved MNIST classification task, it reaches a comparable to the state-of-the-art performance for single models, using standard training setup and 0.75 million parameters.

papers.title: Multimodal Task Vectors Enable Many-Shot Multimodal In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How to enable Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) to perform many-shot in-context learning without being limited by context length, by compressing examples into implicit representations (task vectors) in the model's attention heads?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Multimodal Task Vectors (MTV), compact implicit representations of in-context examples stored in attention heads, enabling many-shot multimodal in-context learning without fine-tuning and overcoming context length limitations.
papers.conclusion: MTV enables many-shot multimodal in-context learning, scales with examples, and generalizes to similar tasks without requiring fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
MTV outperforms zero-shot and few-shot ICL on various vision-language tasks.
MTV performance scales with the number of compressed examples (shots and iterations).
MTV can be used alongside explicit few-shot examples, freeing up context length.
MTV attention heads extracted on one task can generalize to similar out-of-domain tasks.
papers.limitation:
MTV requires interleaved LMMs and may not work as well on non-interleaved models.
Computing mean activations requires multiple forward passes, which can be computationally expensive.
papers.abstract: The recent success of interleaved Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) in few-shot learning suggests that in-context learning (ICL) with many examples can be promising for learning new tasks. However, this many-shot multimodal ICL setting has one crucial problem: it is fundamentally limited by the model's context length set at pretraining. The problem is especially prominent in the multimodal domain, which processes both text and images, requiring additional tokens. This motivates the need for a multimodal method to compress many shots into fewer tokens without finetuning. In this work, we enable LMMs to perform multimodal, many-shot in-context learning by leveraging Multimodal Task Vectors (MTV) -- compact implicit representations of in-context examples compressed in the model's attention heads. Specifically, we first demonstrate the existence of such MTV in LMMs and then leverage these extracted MTV to enable many-shot in-context learning for various vision-and-language tasks. Our experiments suggest that MTV can scale in performance with the number of compressed shots and generalize to similar out-of-domain tasks without additional context length for inference. Code: https://github.com/Brandon3964/MultiModal-Task-Vector

papers.title: Counterfactual reasoning: an analysis of in-context emergence
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether language models can perform in-context counterfactual reasoning, i.e., predicting consequences of hypothetical scenarios by inferring unobserved latent concepts and copying contextual noise from factual observations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that language models are capable of in-context counterfactual reasoning, and through analysis of Transformers, finds that self-attention, model depth, and pre-training data diversity drive performance, with mechanistic evidence that the latent concept is linearly represented in the residual stream and that designated noise abduction heads emerge.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can perform counterfactual reasoning by leveraging self-attention and depth, and this ability extends to sequential data, suggesting potential for counterfactual story generation.
papers.key_findings:
Language models can perform in-context counterfactual reasoning on synthetic linear regression tasks.
Self-attention is crucial for counterfactual reasoning; MLP-only models fail.
Model depth improves counterfactual reasoning performance.
Pre-training data diversity improves performance and out-of-distribution generalization.
The latent parameter is linearly encoded in the residual stream, and designated noise abduction heads emerge in attention layers.
papers.limitation: The synthetic setup may not fully capture the complexity of natural language counterfactual reasoning.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to natural language tasks and more complex functions.
Further exploration of the role of attention heads in counterfactual reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large-scale neural language models exhibit remarkable performance in in-context learning: the ability to learn and reason about the input context on the fly. This work studies in-context counterfactual reasoning in language models, that is, the ability to predict consequences of a hypothetical scenario. We focus on a well-defined, synthetic linear regression task that requires noise abduction. Accurate prediction is based on (1) inferring an unobserved latent concept and (2) copying contextual noise from factual observations. We show that language models are capable of counterfactual reasoning. Further, we enhance existing identifiability results and reduce counterfactual reasoning for a broad class of functions to a transformation on in-context observations. In Transformers, we find that self-attention, model depth and pre-training data diversity drive performance. Moreover, we provide mechanistic evidence that the latent concept is linearly represented in the residual stream and we introduce designated \textit{noise abduction heads} central to performing counterfactual reasoning. Lastly, our findings extend to counterfactual reasoning under SDE dynamics and reflect that Transformers can perform noise abduction on sequential data, providing preliminary evidence on the potential for counterfactual story generation. Our code is available under https://github.com/mrtzmllr/iccr.

papers.title: From Sequence to Structure: Uncovering Substructure Reasoning in Transformers
papers.research_question: How can a decoder-only Transformer architecture understand underlying graph structures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Induced Substructure Filtration (ISF) perspective to explain how transformers extract substructures from graph data, and shows that this perspective applies to LLMs and can be extended to attributed graphs.
papers.conclusion: The ISF process explains how transformers understand graph structures and can be extended to complex graph reasoning, offering a new perspective for graph foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers perform a layer-wise node aggregation process (ISF) to detect substructures.
The number of transformer layers needed correlates with the size of the substructure.
Transformers can extract multiple substructures simultaneously.
Both adjacency list and edge list representations can be used, but adjacency list is more efficient.
Transformers abstract substructures into a sequence of tokens in the question prompt.
papers.limitation: The work focuses primarily on the fundamentals of substructure extraction, leaving other substructure-related tasks and more detailed theoretical analysis for future research.
future_direction: Extend to other substructure-related tasks.
Develop a more comprehensive theoretical understanding.
papers.abstract: Recent studies suggest that large language models (LLMs) possess the capability to solve graph reasoning tasks. Notably, even when graph structures are embedded within textual descriptions, LLMs can still effectively answer related questions. This raises a fundamental question: How can a decoder-only Transformer architecture understand underlying graph structures? To address this, we start with the substructure extraction task, interpreting the inner mechanisms inside the transformers and analyzing the impact of the input queries. Specifically, through both empirical results and theoretical analysis, we present Induced Substructure Filtration (ISF), a perspective that captures the substructure identification in the multi-layer transformers. We further validate the ISF process in LLMs, revealing consistent internal dynamics across layers. Building on these insights, we explore the broader capabilities of Transformers in handling diverse graph types. Specifically, we introduce the concept of thinking in substructures to efficiently extract complex composite patterns, and demonstrate that decoder-only Transformers can successfully extract substructures from attributed graphs, such as molecular graphs. Together, our findings offer a new insight on how sequence-based Transformers perform the substructure extraction task over graph data.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning is Subgraph Search: A New Lens on Learning Dynamics
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how fine-tuning works from a mechanistic interpretability perspective, viewing fine-tuning as a search for and optimization of a subgraph within the model's computational graph.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit-tuning, a fine-tuning method that dynamically localizes and optimizes subgraphs (circuits) within a model's computational graph, enabling analysis of learning dynamics and balancing task performance with general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Circuit-tuning provides a new method for studying learning dynamics from a mechanistic interpretability perspective, offering insights into how fine-tuning works and enabling more precise fine-tuning that balances task performance and general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit-tuning provides better training stability and preserves language modeling ability better than full fine-tuning.
The functionality of specific attention heads (Subject Attribute Heads) can reverse during fine-tuning to adapt to new tasks.
Some attention heads (Subject Identification Heads) preserve their functions and are shared before and after fine-tuning.
Nodes within a circuit cooperate through division of labor and indirect interactions to complete tasks.
Edges in the computational graph exhibit strengthening and weakening akin to Hebbian learning during fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: The study of mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer a model to explain its behaviors. While recent studies have focused on the static mechanism of a certain behavior, the learning dynamics inside a model remain to be explored. In this work, we develop a fine-tuning method for analyzing the mechanism behind learning. Inspired by the concept of intrinsic dimension, we view a model as a computational graph with redundancy for a specific task, and treat the fine-tuning process as a search for and optimization of a subgraph within this graph. Based on this hypothesis, we propose circuit-tuning, an algorithm that iteratively builds the subgraph for a specific task and updates the relevant parameters in a heuristic way. We first validate our hypothesis through a carefully designed experiment and provide a detailed analysis of the learning dynamics during fine-tuning. Subsequently, we conduct experiments on more complex tasks, demonstrating that circuit-tuning could strike a balance between the performance on the target task and the general capabilities. Our work offers a new analytical method for the dynamics of fine-tuning, provides new findings on the mechanisms behind the training process, and inspires the design of superior algorithms for the training of neural networks.

papers.title: Site-Net: Using global self-attention and real-space supercells to capture long-range interactions in crystal structures
papers.research_question: How can global self-attention and real-space supercells be used to capture long-range interactions in crystal structures for property prediction?
papers.core_contribution: Site-Net is a transformer architecture that uses global self-attention and real-space supercells to capture long-range interactions in crystal structures, achieving state-of-the-art performance on band gap prediction.
papers.conclusion: Site-Net effectively captures long-range interactions in crystal structures and achieves competitive performance on band gap prediction, with potential for improvement via more extensive hyperparameter tuning and the use of larger supercells.
papers.key_findings:
Site-Net achieves a mean absolute error of 0.251 eV on the Matbench band gap regression task, demonstrating competitive performance.
Attention heads in Site-Net become specialized to deal with primarily short- or long-range interactions.
Enforcing a distance cutoff limit of 5 Å on the attention decreases model performance, confirming that longer-range interactions meaningfully contribute to predictions.
Site-Net learns from interactions beyond the nearest neighbor atomic sites.
The model performance is consistent across band gap values.
papers.limitation:
The model is computationally intensive and has a quadratic dependence on the number of atoms in the crystal in terms of VRAM and computational load.
The hyperparameter search was only preliminary, and the hyperparameters used are likely far from optimal.
The cutoff limit of 100 atoms excludes about 3% of crystal structures in the dataset during training due to memory constraints.
Model performance may be limited by the size of the supercell and could improve with larger supercells.
future_direction: More extensive hyperparameter tuning.
Using larger supercells to improve performance.
Applying the method to disordered crystal structures.
papers.abstract: Site-Net is a transformer architecture that models the periodic crystal structures of inorganic materials as a labelled point set of atoms and relies entirely on global self-attention and geometric information to guide learning. Site-Net processes standard crystallographic information files to generate a large real-space supercell, and the importance of interactions between all atomic sites is flexibly learned by the model for the prediction task presented. The attention mechanism is probed to reveal Site-Net can learn long-range interactions in crystal structures, and that specific attention heads become specialized to deal with primarily short- or long-range interactions. We perform a preliminary hyperparameter search and train Site-Net using a single graphics processing unit (GPU), and show Site-Net achieves state-of-the-art performance on a standard band gap regression task.

papers.title: Hierarchical Sparse Circuit Extraction from Billion-Parameter Language Models through Scalable Attribution Graph Decomposition
papers.research_question: How can sparse computational circuits be efficiently extracted from billion-parameter language models using hierarchical decomposition and attribution graphs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Hierarchical Attribution Graph Decomposition (HAGD), a framework that reduces circuit discovery complexity from exponential to polynomial, enabling extraction of interpretable circuits from billion-parameter models with high behavioral preservation.
papers.conclusion: HAGD enables circuit extraction from large models with preserved behavior, but limitations include incomplete attention modeling, reconstruction residuals, and interpretability challenges for large circuits.
papers.key_findings:
HAGD reduces circuit discovery complexity to O(n^2 log n) and extracts circuits from models up to 70B parameters.
Behavioral preservation ranges from 82% to 97% on algorithmic tasks and 74% to 88% on natural language benchmarks.
Cross-architecture transfer shows 52%-82% structural similarity, indicating shared computational patterns.
Circuit size grows sublinearly with model parameters, but natural language tasks yield larger, less modular circuits.
The method outperforms baselines like ACDC in scalability while maintaining comparable circuit quality.
papers.limitation:
Attention circuits are not modeled, leaving significant computational pathways unanalyzed.
Reconstruction dark matter of 15-20% unexplained variance means extracted circuits are incomplete.
Validation circularity arises from using ablation experiments that assume circuit completeness.
GNN meta-model requires ground-truth circuit labels that are expensive to obtain.
Large circuits with hundreds of nodes may exceed human interpretability limits.
future_direction: Integrate attention and MLP circuit analysis.
Characterize reconstruction residuals (dark matter).
Develop label-efficient training methods for GNN meta-model.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to reverse-engineer neural network computations into human-understandable algorithms, yet extracting sparse computational circuits from billion-parameter language models remains challenging due to exponential search complexity and pervasive polysemanticity. The proposed Hierarchical Attribution Graph Decomposition (HAGD) framework reduces circuit discovery complexity from O(2^n) exhaustive enumeration to O(n^2 log n) through multi-resolution abstraction hierarchies and differentiable circuit search. The methodology integrates cross-layer transcoders for monosemantic feature extraction, graph neural network meta-learning for topology prediction, and causal intervention protocols for validation. Empirical evaluation spans GPT-2 variants, Llama-7B through Llama-70B, and Pythia suite models across algorithmic tasks and natural language benchmarks. On modular arithmetic tasks, the framework achieves up to 91% behavioral preservation ($\pm$2.3\% across runs) while maintaining interpretable subgraph sizes. Cross-architecture transfer experiments suggest that discovered circuits exhibit moderate structural similarity (averaging 67%) across model families, indicating potential shared computational patterns. These results provide preliminary foundations for interpretability at larger model scales while identifying significant limitations in current attribution methodologies that require future advances.

papers.title: Exploring Cancer Genomics with Graph Convolutional Networks: A Comparative Explainability Study with Integrated Gradients and SHAP
papers.research_question: How do SHAP and Integrated Gradients compare in explaining the predictions of Graph Convolutional Networks applied to multiomics cancer data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a framework that integrates SHAP and Integrated Gradients to improve the interpretability of Graph Convolutional Networks for cancer gene identification from multiomics data.
papers.conclusion: SHAP is ideal for tasks requiring interpretability and consistency, while IG is better for faster, scalable analyses in explaining GCN predictions.
papers.key_findings:
SHAP provides more intuitive visualizations and consistent feature importance rankings for GCN predictions.
Integrated Gradients is computationally more efficient but has diffused attributions and variability for lower-impact genes.
The GCN model achieves 76% accuracy and 0.78 AUC-ROC in cancer gene identification.
SHAP and IG are complementary methods, with SHAP better for interpretability and IG for scalability.
papers.limitation:
SHAP is computationally intensive due to its game-theoretic approach.
IG shows variability in identifying lower-impact genes across runs.
future_direction: Improving scalability of GCNs for larger datasets.
Integrating explainability techniques for more robust feature attributions.
Exploring GCN applications in clinical settings for real-time predictions.
papers.abstract: In the rapidly advancing field of cancer genomics, identifying new cancer genes and understanding their molecular mechanisms are essential for advancing targeted therapies and improving patient outcomes. This study explores the capability of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) for integrating complex multiomics data to uncover intricate biological relationships. However, the inherent complexity of GCNs often limits their interpretability, posing challenges for practical applications in clinical settings. To enhance explainability, we systematically compare two state-of-the-art interpretability methods: Integrated Gradients (IG) and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). We quantify model performance through various metrics, achieving an accuracy of 76% and an Area Under the ROC curve is 0.78, indicating the model’s effective identification of both overall predictions and positive instances. We analyze and compare explanations provided by IG and SHAP to gain more knowledge in the decision-making processes of GCNs. Our framework interpret the contributions of various omics features in GCN models, with the highest SHAP score observed for feature MF:UCEC and the highest IG score for KIF11. This approach identifies novel cancer genes and clarifies their molecular mechanisms, enhancing GCN interpretability. The study improves GCN accessibility in personalized medicine and contributes to understanding cancer biology.

papers.title: The Molecular Structure of Thought: Mapping the Topology of Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models learn and represent effective Long Chain-of-Thought?
papers.core_contribution: The paper models Long Chain-of-Thought as a molecular structure with three bond types and introduces Mole-Syn, a method to synthesize effective Long CoT structures, improving performance and RL stability.
papers.conclusion: The molecular structure view explains how LLMs learn Long CoT, and Mole-Syn enables effective synthesis of these structures for improved reasoning performance.
papers.key_findings:
Long CoT reasoning exhibits stable molecular-like structures formed by deep-reasoning, self-reflection, and self-exploration bonds.
Semantic isomers with compatible bond structures are crucial for effective Long CoT learning, while incompatible structures lead to instability.
Distillation from strong reasoning LLMs successfully imparts Long CoT structures, but distillation from weak instruction LLMs or human traces fails.
Mole-Syn can synthesize effective Long CoT structures by transferring behavior distributions, boosting performance across benchmarks.
Conflict between two stable molecular structures during training causes structural chaos and degrades performance.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often fail to learn effective long chain-of-thought (Long CoT) reasoning from human or non-Long-CoT LLMs imitation. To understand this, we propose that effective and learnable Long CoT trajectories feature stable molecular-like structures in unified view, which are formed by three interaction types: Deep-Reasoning (covalent-like), Self-Reflection (hydrogen-bond-like), and Self-Exploration (van der Waals-like). Analysis of distilled trajectories reveals these structures emerge from Long CoT fine-tuning, not keyword imitation. We introduce Effective Semantic Isomers and show that only bonds promoting fast entropy convergence support stable Long CoT learning, while structural competition impairs training. Drawing on these findings, we present Mole-Syn, a distribution-transfer-graph method that guides synthesis of effective Long CoT structures, boosting performance and RL stability across benchmarks.

papers.title: Physics Steering: Causal Control of Cross-Domain Concepts in a Physics Foundation Model
papers.research_question: Whether scientific foundation models learn abstract, domain-general representations of physical phenomena that can be causally manipulated via activation steering.
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that a physics foundation model learns linearly steerable representations of physical concepts (e.g., vorticity, diffusion, temporal progression), and that injecting these directions during inference enables fine-grained causal control over simulation behavior. The concept directions are domain-general and transfer across unrelated physical systems.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability techniques from LLMs can be successfully adapted to scientific foundation models, providing evidence that these models develop abstract, domain-general representations of fundamental physical concepts that are linearly encoded and causally steerable.
papers.key_findings:
Single directions in the model's activation space correspond to specific physical concepts like vorticity, diffusion, and simulation speed.
Injecting (adding or subtracting) these concept directions during inference causally steers model predictions, allowing induction or suppression of vortices, enhancement or suppression of diffusion, and speeding up or slowing down simulations.
The extracted concept directions transfer successfully between unrelated physical systems (e.g., from fluid dynamics to chemical reaction-diffusion), indicating they represent abstract, domain-general physical principles.
The results support the Linear Representation Hypothesis for scientific foundation models, showing physical concepts are represented linearly in activation space.
Steering effects are more physically plausible and interpretable when using spatially-averaged concept directions that discard spatial structure, compared to using full spatial tensors.
papers.limitation:
The physical plausibility of the steered results is an open question; including spatial dimensions in the steering tensor can lead to less physically realistic outcomes.
The effectiveness of steering depends on the initial conditions of the simulation; steering becomes more difficult and can produce distorted fields when the initial state is far from the target regime.
future_direction: Exploring the layer-dependence of concept representations and steering effects.
Further work to definitively assess the physicality and self-consistency of steered simulation results.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have revealed that large language models (LLMs) develop internal representations corresponding not only to concrete entities but also distinct, human-understandable abstract concepts and behaviour. Moreover, these hidden features can be directly manipulated to steer model behaviour.
